true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write of retryCount

The counter is written as `reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read at the start of the run. If two cron invocations overlap (the job makes many external calls and can run long), both can read the same value and write the same increment, so failures are under-counted and a reminder gets an extra attempt. Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }` performs the increment atomically in the database and avoids this. The same pattern appears in the catch block at line 195.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

The second branch of the `OR` (`retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. Any WorkflowReminder of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, or a future channel) with retryCount > 1 is deleted, regardless of its `scheduled` state. Only the SMS path increments the column today, so the practical impact is currently small, but the delete condition is broader than the stated intent and will cause data loss once another channel uses the column. The branch should be scoped as `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` plus `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment describes only the date-based deletion

The comment says this block deletes 'all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date'. After this PR the same `deleteMany` also deletes reminders whose retryCount is greater than 1, including unscheduled ones that failed twice. The comment is now wrong and does not explain the retry threshold either.

No tests for the new retry and deletion behavior

The PR changes control flow in three places: failed scheduling increments retryCount, errors increment retryCount, and reminders with retryCount > 1 are deleted. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. A test that drives the handler with a mocked twilio.scheduleSMS returning null or throwing, and checks the retryCount updates and the deletion on the next run, would catch regressions such as the catch-block issue above.

OR with an unindexed retryCount predicate forces a full table scan

The new `OR` in deleteMany combines a predicate that uses the composite index `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` with `retryCount > 1`, which has no index (schema.prisma line 1000 adds the column without one). Postgres can only use a BitmapOr when every arm is indexable, so this cron query now falls back to a sequential scan of WorkflowReminder on every run. That table grows over time, so the cost increases with it. Consider an index on `retryCount` or splitting the delete into two queries.

Reminders with no sendTo or empty message never accrue retries

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` (the else branch at line 178 and the catch block). If `sendTo` is null (for example an SMS_ATTENDEE step where `booking.smsReminderNumber` is missing) or the message is empty, nothing is scheduled and retryCount is not incremented. Such a reminder stays unscheduled and is reprocessed on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes, with the template/DB work repeated each time. This is the 'keep retrying until the date is reached' behavior the PR is meant to stop, and the PR leaves this path uncovered. Either count these as failed attempts or delete them explicitly.

Retry budget of two attempts is spent within a few cron ticks with no backoff

Each cron tick makes one attempt, and the row is deleted on the first tick after the second failure. Two failures can therefore occur only minutes apart, and a Twilio or network outage longer than that permanently drops the reminder with no log beyond a console line and no alert. The magic `gt: 1` also does not state the 'two failures' rule anywhere in code. The threshold or the lack of backoff should be a deliberate, documented choice.

Unguarded DB update inside catch can abort the whole batch

The new `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` in the catch block has no try/catch, and it is not inside any outer try. Before this PR the catch only logged, so it could not throw. Now, if this update fails, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler rejects. The most plausible trigger is a reminder deleted after `findMany` (for example when its booking is cancelled, which makes Prisma throw P2025), or any transient DB error. The consequence is that every remaining reminder in the batch is skipped for this cron run and the response is an error instead of the normal success response. The increment should be guarded so one bad row does not stop processing of the rest.

The description says the change only updates the integration tests and that the service was 'previously converted'. getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, deleteMeeting, deleteEvent and payment app lookup all changed from synchronous to async, and several callers moved from sync forEach to async callbacks. The PR adds no tests or test updates covering what happens when credential or app lookup or CalendarService construction throws during cancel, reschedule, or video deletion. Those error paths are exactly what changed, so they should have coverage.

Async forEach in requestReschedule turns calendar failures into unhandled rejections

Previously a synchronous throw from getCalendar inside this forEach propagated and failed the mutation. Now getCalendar is async, so the error is returned from the discarded async callback and becomes an unhandled promise rejection while the mutation reports success. The calendar deleteEvent calls are also not awaited before sendRequestRescheduleEmail runs. Use for...of with await so errors are handled and deletions finish before the email is sent.

Object-literal import() calls still load every app eagerly, so nothing is lazy

Each `import("./...")` is a property initializer in the object literal, so every app module is requested as soon as this file is evaluated. Awaiting at the call sites only defers the wait; it does not avoid loading the apps. Deferred loading needs thunks (e.g. `googlecalendar: () => import("./googlecalendar")`) with callers invoking them. The PR description gives no goal, so it is unclear whether the intent was laziness. Also, a module whose import rejects produces an unhandled rejection at load time unless that key is awaited, rather than an error at the lookup site.

Recurring-cancel calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

The outer `.forEach(async (credential) => ...)` does not return its promise, so the handler continues without waiting for it. The final `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` copies apiDeletes before these callbacks reach their `apiDeletes.push(...)` calls, so these per-occurrence calendar deletions are never awaited. Their results and errors are dropped and failures become unhandled rejections. The PR rewrote the sibling non-recurring loop in the else branch to for...of with await but left this one as forEach(async); it should be converted the same way.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the pending deletions

On the paid-cancellation path, `await apiDeletes;` does not wait for the promises inside the array. The handler returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' before calendar and video deletions settle, and their rejections are unhandled. This is pre-existing, but the PR touches these calls and the async change makes the difference observable. Use `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)` if the deletions are meant to complete before responding.

forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective for calendar errors

Same change as in the vital reschedule: getCalendar is now async, so errors thrown while creating the calendar service escape the try/catch on line 124-139 and become unhandled rejections. The deleteEvent/deleteMeeting calls are not awaited before the function returns true and sends the reschedule email. Use for...of with await inside the try so failures are logged and ordering is preserved.

getCalendarCredentials still calls the now-async getCalendar without await

getCalendarCredentials stays synchronous and stores `getCalendar(credential)` directly, so each returned `calendar` field is a Promise<Calendar | null>, not a Calendar. Only getConnectedCalendars currently remembers to await `item.calendar`; any other consumer that uses the field as a Calendar will get undefined methods or a Promise where a value is expected. Make this function async and await the calendar, or document that the field is a Promise.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end check compares the slot start, not the slot end

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, the same value as `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` never checks the slot's end. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past the end is accepted. With working hours ending at 17:00 and a 60-minute event, the 16:30 slot passes this check. The fixed host's own end boundary is only enforced here, so a fixed host can be booked beyond their hours in round-robin events, which is the scenario this PR is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length override check compares object references

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares object identity, which is always false for two distinct dayjs instances. The zero-length override early return is therefore dead code. It should use `.isSame(...)` or compare timestamps.

false_positives.candidate:
Availability checks use eventType.length instead of the requested duration

`availabilityCheckProps.eventLength` is `eventType.length`, but slot generation at line 451 uses `input.duration || eventType.length`. For events with multiple duration options, the new working-hours and date-override checks compute the slot end from the wrong length, so a 60-minute booking is validated as a 30-minute one. This matters more now that these checks depend on the slot end.

Multiple date overrides on one day make every slot on that day unavailable

`dateOverrides.find` returns the first override whose callback returns truthy, and the callback returns true when the slot lies outside that override. With two overrides on the same date (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the availability UI supports as multiple ranges per date), a slot inside the first range is rejected because the second range reports it as outside, and the converse holds for the second range. Every slot on that day is therefore rejected. The correct semantics is 'available if inside at least one override on that day'. The flag `dateOverrideExist` is also mutated as a side effect inside the predicate, which relies on `find` short-circuiting and is fragile.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host override fix or for busy times on override days

The PR's headline fix (fixed-host date overrides constraining round-robin slots, and busy times on override days) has no test. The only added assertion is an invitee-timezone variant of an existing single-override scenario. Missing coverage: a round-robin event where a fixed host's override limits availability; an existing booking inside an override still blocking the slot (this would catch the busy-skip bug); split working hours on one weekday; two overrides on one date; and an override that shifts across midnight for an invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic is subtle and currently untested beyond the single happy path.

Override end check ignores slots that start inside the override but run past it

The override boundary test compares `slotStartTime` with the override end instead of `slotEndTime`. A slot that starts inside an override and extends beyond its end (override ends 18:00, 60-minute slot at 17:30) fails all three checks and falls through to `return true` at line 133. The fixed host is then treated as available for time after the override ends. The earlier check at line 119 does use the slot end, so the two checks are inconsistent.

Same-day override check depends on the server process timezone

`dayjs(date.start)` is created in local mode, so `.add(...).format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's process timezone. `slotStartTime` is converted with `.utc()` and formats in UTC. On any server whose TZ is not UTC (developer machines, self-hosted deployments), the same-day comparison fails for overrides whose local date differs from the UTC date. The override is then not detected, and the slot falls through to the working-hours/busy logic, so date-override behaviour depends on where the process runs. The shifted value should be put in UTC mode before formatting.

Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check

When a same-day date override exists and the slot lies inside it, execution reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. Existing bookings and calendar busy times are therefore ignored for every slot inside a date override window. Personal events are treated as fixed-host events (isFixed is true when there is no schedulingType), so this affects ordinary personal bookings too: a host with an override 14:00-18:00 who already has a 15:00 booking is still offered 15:00 and can be double-booked. The override should only replace the working-hours check; busy times must still be evaluated.

Split working hours on one weekday reject every slot

`workingHours.find(...)` returns the first entry for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is outside that entry. Working hours come one entry per availability row, so a host with two ranges on the same weekday (for example 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) has every slot outside at least one of those entries. Every slot on that day then hits `return false` at line 150. This check now runs for every fixed host, including personal events, so users with split days get no slots at all. The intended test is 'reject only if no entry contains the slot'. The test suite only uses single-row schedules, so this is not caught.

Timezone conversions run inside the per-slot override loop

`dayjs.tz(...)` (which formats through Intl) is evaluated inside the `find` predicate for every override, for every slot, for every fixed host, although the offset depends only on the override. Over a long date range with many overrides this multiplies into a very large number of timezone conversions per getSchedule call. The override windows should be computed once per call.

Timezone-shifted override minutes drop the date and land on the wrong day across midnight

The converted override time is reduced to minute-of-day with `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding the timezone offset, which discards the date. When the shifted time crosses midnight, the slot is attributed to the wrong day. Example: an override 15:00-17:00 on Jan 10 for an organizer in America/New_York (stored as 15:00Z-17:00Z) and an invitee in Asia/Kolkata. The real slots are Jan 11 01:30-03:30 IST. The day filter at line 207 selects the override using the unshifted instant, which falls on Jan 10 IST, and line 219 yields 01:30. The slot is therefore offered (or later dropped by checkIfIsAvailable) on Jan 10, and the override never appears on Jan 11. The full converted timestamp should be computed and bucketed by its own date.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when an existing Integration has no sender metadata

integration.metadata['sender']['login'] assumes every existing Integration has a 'sender' entry. build_integration only writes sender when state.get('sender') is truthy (lines 376-377), so Integrations created by the pipeline without a webhook-provided sender, or created before this metadata existed, lack the key. For such a row that is ACTIVE but has no OrganizationIntegration, this line raises KeyError and the request returns a 500 instead of the error template. Use a safe lookup and treat a missing sender as a failed verification that renders the error page.

OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Installer check is skipped when no Integration record exists yet

The new sender check (lines 501-505) runs only after the `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch above has returned. When no Integration row exists for the installation_id (the installation webhook has not been processed, or never reaches Sentry, e.g. a self-hosted instance without webhook delivery), this line returns pipeline.next_step() immediately. The OAuth-authenticated GitHub user is never compared with the user who installed the app, and build_integration then links the installation to the org. test_basic_flow exercises exactly this path (no webhook posted, authenticated user 'octocat', no check), so the PR's main guarantee does not hold in the default path. Someone handed an installation_id belonging to another GitHub account can complete the install whenever the webhook record has not landed yet. The installer must be verified on this path too, or the pipeline must fail closed.

Integration lookup is not scoped to the GitHub provider

Both lookups by external_id=installation_id (this one and the one at line 478) omit provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key. external_id is only unique per provider, so the row found may belong to another provider and has no GitHub 'sender' in its metadata. The new check then indexes metadata['sender'] on a non-GitHub integration. Before this PR that case fell through to next_step. Add the provider filter to the lookup.

Mismatch test asserts only a generic error that every failure path shares

The mismatch test asserts only 'Invalid installation request.', which is the message for every failure in this pipeline: state mismatch, failed token exchange, missing login, missing Integration, and sender mismatch. It would still pass if the OAuth exchange broke, so it does not prove the sender check fired. It also does not assert that no OrganizationIntegration was created for org_2, which is the security-relevant outcome. Assert the absence of the OrganizationIntegration and/or give the sender mismatch its own error text.

Network and HTTP failures in the OAuth exchange escape as 500s

safe_urlopen (line 423) is outside the try block, so a connection error or timeout raises out of the view instead of rendering the failure template; the try only guards reading the body. get_user_info (line 434) is also unguarded, so if it raises on a non-2xx response or on undecodable JSON, the user gets a 500 rather than the 'could not verify' page. Wrap the token exchange and user lookup and route failures to error(...).

No test covers a successful install through the sender check or the new OAuth failure branches

test_basic_flow never posts an installation webhook, so it never reaches the Integration-exists branch with a matching sender. The only test of that branch (test_github_user_mismatch) covers rejection. Nothing verifies that the matching installer is accepted with the check active. The new OAuth failure branches (state mismatch at integration.py line 412, missing access_token at line 431, missing login at line 435) have no tests either. Add a case that posts the installation event with sender 'octocat' (the stubbed /user login) and expects success, plus cases for a bad state and a failed token exchange.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the not-found path

The test now sends a wrong state (ddd023...), so it fails at OAuthLoginView's state check and returns 'Invalid installation request.'. The original assertion for 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' (the 404 branch in build_integration, integration.py line 356) is no longer exercised anywhere in this file, despite the test name. Restore that assertion using the valid state, and keep the bad-state case as a separate test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import, so every instance gets the same timestamp

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default, so `timezone.now()` runs once when the module is imported. Every AssignmentSource created in that process then carries the process-start time, not the time the assignment was queued. The value is serialized by `to_dict()` into the task payload. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The existing `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it would not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`to_dict()` puts a raw datetime into a dict passed as a Celery task argument

`asdict(self)` keeps `queued` as a `datetime`. This dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` in `apply_async` kwargs (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py, around line 141). A datetime is not JSON-native, so the type does not survive a JSON-serialized task round trip, and the consumer receives a string instead. Serializing `queued` to an ISO string, or excluding it, would make the payload type-stable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Loop check excludes the whole integration, not the originating external issue

The check `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` suppresses outbound assignee sync to every external issue of that integration linked to the group. A group linked to two Jira issues on the same Jira site would no longer receive assignee updates to issue B when issue A's assignee is changed by an inbound webhook. The description only mentions preventing the echo back to the triggering issue. This suppression of legitimate updates to other linked issues is not mentioned or tested.

New positional argument to `should_sync` and new kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound` break existing overrides

The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` and `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` on every installation. The actual inbound-webhook loop path and the deassign path are untested

Unused `assignment_source` parameter added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` contract

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter, but no caller in this PR passes it and no implementation is required to use it. Occurrences are produced to Kafka before detector state is committed

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the loop without terminating the remaining flusher processes

In the new join loop, once `remaining_time <= 0` the `break` at line 341 exits the loop before the `terminate()` at line 347 for every remaining process. In the old single-process code, the deadline only ended the wait and the process was still terminated. Now, if the deadline is hit during process i, process i is terminated, but processes i+1..n are neither waited on nor terminated. They keep running and can be mid-flush or mid-produce after join() returns. The termination should happen for every process that is still alive, independent of the deadline.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the per-shard flusher is not enabled by default

The PR's stated goal and the SpanFlusher docstring (flusher.py lines 31-32) say the flusher runs one process per redis shard. But the new CLI option defaults to `1`, and SpanFlusher caps process count at `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`. With the default, all shards in the consumer are flushed by one process, so the deployed behavior is essentially unchanged unless the flag is set explicitly. The factory default (`flusher_processes=None` in factory.py line 41, which becomes `len(shards)`) is per-shard, so direct construction and the CLI disagree. Either the CLI default should match the stated design, or the description and docstring should make clear that the flag must be raised to get the new behavior.

If a callable reaches `SpanFlusher`, `min(self.max_processes, ...)` in flusher.py raises TypeError when the consumer starts. The new parameter should be added after `produce_to_pipe`, or the call sites should be confirmed to use keyword arguments.

New test only checks counts; per-process restart and shard flushing are untested

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts only the number of processes, `max_processes`, `num_processes`, and that the shard map sums to 4. The new logic that matters most is not exercised: each process flushing exactly its own shards, `_ensure_processes_alive` restarting a single multi-shard process (including the per-process MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS accounting), per-process backpressure in `submit`, and the case where `flusher_processes` exceeds the number of shards. A regression in the shard-to-process mapping or restart path would not be caught.

Unrelated documentation change bundled into a span flusher PR

The added 'Use hasattr() for unions' anti-pattern has nothing to do with the multiprocessed span flusher. It should be split into its own change so the reviewed PR stays scoped to the flusher and its consumer option.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and nearly duplicates _create_process_for_shards

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is added but never called. `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. The two near-identical names make it easy to call the wrong one, and the unused method suggests a restart-by-shard path that does not exist. It should be removed or wired in.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the failing batch is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring

The docstring says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages'. Offsets 100 and 101 both complete: the first raises, the worker logs it and completes the offset in its finally, and the second succeeds. The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. It passes only because the commit thread's first cycle fires about one second after creation while the test checks after roughly 0.2 seconds. On a slower run the commit happens and the test fails. The test should wait for the commit and assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition

get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing

Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s

The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order

The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers

The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Explicit denial-cache test passes without the denial cache

The test is meant to show the denial entry short-circuits the check, but it cannot fail if that logic is removed. The permission cache entry for dash1 is set to false (line 982), so checkPermission returns false, and the DB fallback also denies because setupService's fakeStore has no userPermissions. The result is false with or without permDenialCache. The comment 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' contradicts the value set. Set the cached permission for dash1 to true so only the denial entry produces the deny, and/or assert the store was not called. No test also checks that a DB-confirmed denial actually populates permDenialCache.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous: different resources can collide

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent folder with '_' without escaping. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so the tuple is ambiguous: dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c' and dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' both produce '...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c'. A denial recorded for one resource then makes Check return denied for the other for 30s without consulting permissions. The result is false denials of legitimate access for the feature this PR targets. Encode the tuple unambiguously (length-prefixed fields, a JSON array, or a hash of the tuple).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Every unmatched name now triggers an uncached permissions query

On a permission-cache miss for a name, which is the normal case for any resource the user cannot access, Check always runs the uncached GetUserPermissions query. Before this PR those denials were answered from the cached permission map with no DB access. The denial cache is keyed by exact (action, name, folder), so a caller checking many distinct names the user cannot access costs one DB permissions query per name per 30s. The DB cost of this path should be considered or documented.

List has no requery path, so newly created items stay out of results for up to 30s

List answers from the 30s permission-map entry on a hit and never requeries, because it cannot tell which resources are missing from the cached set. Dashboards and folders created by the user therefore stay absent from list results for up to 30 seconds, the same class of problem this PR claims to fix for Check. The PR does not mention or test this limitation.

Recorded denials pin a deny for 30s, bypassing the new requery and surviving grants

Check consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns Allowed=false on a hit, without consulting the permission cache or the DB. Entries are written whenever a DB-backed check denies (line 154) and are removed only by the 30s TTL; nothing clears them when a grant is written or a resource is created. The requery added by this PR only runs on a permission-cache miss, so a denial recorded before the creator's permission was visible (for example a GET racing the permission write, or any read of the UID before it existed) keeps returning denied for up to 30 seconds. That is the exact symptom the PR says it fixes, so the fix is incomplete for that window.

Requery on permission-cache miss still reads a stale folder tree

The requery only refreshes the permission set. checkInheritedPermissions (line 590) calls buildFolderTree, which returns the folderCache entry for up to 30s with no bypass. A folder created in that window is missing from the tree, so its ancestors cannot be resolved and a user whose access is inherited from an ancestor folder is denied for resources inside it. That denial is then cached (line 154). The requery therefore does not cover inherited access to newly created folders, and no test covers this case because the folder tests seed a complete tree.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

Silence menu item in the list view does nothing

In the list view `rule` (the RulerRuleDTO) is undefined. AlertRuleMenu shows the Silence item based on the Grafana promRule silence ability, and clicking it calls handleSilence, which sets showSilenceDrawer to true. false_positives.candidate:
Comment says this is a copy of RuleActionsButtons.tsx, which is no longer true

The header comment describes this file as a copy of RuleActionsButtons.tsx with only the View button removed. After this change it takes promRule, uses useGrafanaPromRuleAbility and getEditableIdentifier, and has different identifier and provenance logic, so it has diverged. The stale comment will mislead maintainers about which file to change.

Delete item is gated on rulerRule, which is always absent in the list view

`{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` hides Delete whenever rulerRule is undefined. Since the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, Delete is never shown for Grafana rules there even when the user has delete permission on the folder and canDelete is true via the promRule abilities. Delete is silently removed from the list view.

Duplicate becomes allowed for non-Grafana rules via skipToken

When promRule is not a Grafana rule, AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons pass skipToken, so useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities receives undefined. With no rule, MaybeSupported is AlwaysSupported and isPluginProvided is false, so Duplicate returns [true, user has AlertingRuleCreate]. AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler-based ability (canDuplicate = ruler || grafana), so any data source rule in the list shows Duplicate for users with Grafana create permission. This bypasses the ruler-availability check and the plugin-provided check (the ruler path marks plugin-provided rules as unsupported). The grafana hook should return NotSupported when no rule is supplied.

Federated rule group check dropped from useAllAlertRuleAbilities

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only has the group identifier and hardcodes `const isFederated = false` here. Every caller of useAlertRuleAbility, useAlertRuleAbilities and useAllAlertRuleAbilities therefore loses the immutability check for federated groups, so Update, Delete, Pause and related actions can be enabled for federated rules that cannot be modified.

Grafana rule links drop returnTo, breaking navigation back to the filtered list

The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `{ returnTo }` from createReturnTo(). The new href is just createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`), so navigating to a Grafana rule and back no longer returns to the filtered list. Data source rule links still pass returnTo, so behavior is now inconsistent between rule types. This is an unmentioned navigation regression.

New Grafana promRule abilities hook has no direct test coverage

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, useGrafanaPromRuleAbility(ies) and the skipToken path contain new permission logic that determines what the user can do in the list view (silence, export, duplicate, pause, delete). RulesTable.test.tsx mocks the whole hook surface, and GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx only checks that a few menu entries exist. None of the tests exercise the real decisions, including the skipToken/non-Grafana case where Duplicate is incorrectly allowed, or the federated check that was dropped.

Pause and Delete disappear from the alert list menu

In the list view `rulerRule` is now always undefined, but the Pause item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` here and the Delete item is gated on `rulerRule` at line 165. The new Grafana (promRule) abilities compute canPause/canDelete as allowed, yet the menu items are never rendered, so users lose pause and delete from the list view (they only remain on the details page). The regression is locked in by GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx line 207, which asserts exactly 4 menu items, and the `ui.menuItems.delete` helper defined in that test is never used. The menu gating needs to use the promRule path for these actions, or the abilities should not be advertised.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range guard now checks the interpolated expression and can be silently bypassed

querySupportsSplitting() is documented (lines 285-286) as refusing to split queries containing `$__range`, because `$__range` must be resolved on the backend against the split time range. This change interpolates templates at the start of runSplitQuery (line 299), so the guard on line 287 now tests the already-interpolated expression. If template replacement resolves `$__range` (it does when request.scopedVars carries `__range`), the token is gone, isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false, and queries like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` get split into chunks. Their results then no longer match what the guard was meant to protect. No test in the diff covers a `$__range` query, so this regression would not be caught. The guard should check the pre-interpolation expression, and the comment at lines 285-286 needs updating since its premise no longer holds.

Empty-expression check runs before interpolation, so variables that resolve to empty still execute

The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs on the raw expression, but the emptiness that matters is the one after interpolation, which this PR now introduces. A query whose expr is a variable resolving to an empty string (e.g. `$query` with an empty value) passes the filter, is classified by isLogsQuery('') as a metric query, and is sent to the backend with an empty expression. The same ordering exists in shardQuerySplitting.ts lines 50-52. Moving the empty-expr filter after the map in both places would make the check match the interpolated value the PR is meant to use.

New test only checks the runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions the change is meant to fix

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only asserts that the expr and step passed to runQuery are interpolated. It does not exercise what interpolating first changes: the isLogsQuery partitioning, querySupportsSplitting (including the $__range guard), and the step/resolution grouping computed by calculateStep. There is no case where a variable expands into a logs query, a step variable drives grouping, or a $__range query stays unsplit. Those are the behaviors the PR is supposed to fix, and they are untested.

Shard sub-requests are interpolated a second time (and the test locks this in)

runShardSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already applies applyTemplateVariables to each target. splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes every shard sub-request to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), and this line interpolates those targets again. The updated shard test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times (1 for the original target plus 4 sub-requests), which confirms the double application, and the assertion makes it look intended. Template replacement is not idempotent: a substituted value containing a `$name` token gets expanded on the second pass. Ad hoc filters are also passed on every pass, and the shard path now forwards request.filters, which it did not do before. The interpolation should happen at one point, or sub-requests should bypass it through an option.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

traceID dropped from the grafana-data-egress log line

The old logRequest explicitly appended a traceID field (tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)) to the 'Plugin Request Completed' event. That code is removed in this PR, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware/instrumentContext does not add a trace ID either. The egress event therefore no longer carries traceID, so plugin request logs can no longer be correlated with traces unless the infra logger injects trace IDs from ctx on its own, which this diff does not show. The event loses a field it previously always emitted when a trace was present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so its output is invisible to the test

FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now emits its only log line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so messages go to a throwaway object and never reach the TestLogger's InfoLogs/ErrorLogs counters. Any test that uses plog.TestLogger to assert on the egress log will observe zero calls. Returning f, or sharing the Logs state, would keep the fake observable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. false_positives.candidate:
FromContext doc comment is copied from New and misdescribes the method

The comment 'returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context' is the New() description. FromContext takes a context.Context and derives its attributes from that context value, which the comment does not say. Callers implementing the interface are given a misleading contract.

FromContext silently discards context attributes when the type assertion fails

If d.l.FromContext(ctx) does not return a *log.ConcreteLogger, the wrapper falls back to d.New(), which drops ctx entirely and logs nothing about the failure. The data-egress log now relies on FromContext to carry pluginId, endpoint, dsUID and similar fields, so this path would silently remove them from every plugin request log line. The fallback should preserve the attributes or surface the mismatch.

Moved egress-log fields have no test coverage and depend on implicit ordering

instrumentContext now carries pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname that LoggerMiddleware used to emit directly. They reach the 'grafana-data-egress' event only if (a) ConcreteLogger.FromContext renders contextual attributes from ctx, and (b) ContextualLoggerMiddleware is ordered outside LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. Nothing in this PR tests either condition: there is no unit test for ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and the existing metrics test no longer covers the enrichment it used to exercise. Reordering the middleware list or changing FromContext would silently strip plugin and datasource identifiers from the data-egress event with no failing test.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, so concurrent new devices can exceed the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices (line 110) and compares with the limit (line 115), then runs the upsert (lines 120-155) with no transaction or lock. Many concurrent logins from new devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of stored devices can exceed deviceLimit by up to the concurrency level. The check-and-insert needs to be atomic, for example in one transaction with a conditional insert, or the overshoot must be documented as acceptable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device is cached as tagged before the DB write, so a limit-rejected device is admitted on its retry

tagDeviceUI sets the local cache key (line 87) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice returns that error, and Authenticate rejects the login. The cache entry is not removed, so it stays for 29 minutes. The next request from the same device ID hits the cache check at lines 83-85, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and the anonymous login succeeds without the device ever being stored or counted. The same happens after any transient DB error. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or deleted when the write fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Dependency injection signature changed; wire files are not part of this diff

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB and builds the store itself, and anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64 that no provider in the graph supplies. If the wire provider set (wire.go or wire_gen.go) still binds anonstore.AnonStore or lists ProvideAnonDBStore, wire generation or compilation will fail. Those files are not in the changed list, so this should be checked.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, off the request path. Now Authenticate calls it synchronously with the request context and no timeout. Each first request per device per instance performs a DB write during login, and when a limit is configured each new device also runs a COUNT over the updated_at range (database.go line 110). Slow DB calls now delay or block anonymous page loads, and the panic recovery from the goroutine is gone. The limit-enforcement design needs the synchronous write, but the cost on the hot path, including the uncached COUNT, should be assessed.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented

The device_limit key is read here, but the PR changes no configuration documentation such as conf/defaults.ini or the docs for the [auth.anonymous] section, so operators have no way to learn that the key exists, that 0 means unlimited, or how the 30-day window counts devices. The PR description is also still the unfilled template, including the docs and feature-toggle checklist items.

No tests cover the Authenticate path, the cache interaction, or updates to existing devices at the limit

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device. Nothing tests that a rejected device retried within the cache window is still rejected, which would have caught the cache bypass in impl.go. Nothing tests that Authenticate returns the error to the caller, or that an existing device still gets its updated_at refreshed (the updateDevice path) once the count has reached the limit. The new enforcement behaviour is therefore only covered at the store level.

Requests without the device ID header are never counted or limited

TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent (lines 120-122). Authenticate only fails on ErrDeviceLimitReached, so an anonymous request that omits the header is neither stored nor rejected, and the limit does not apply to it. The header is client-supplied, so clients can also rotate IDs to get fresh slots. Before this change, tagging was only analytics and this gap did not matter. Now the feature is meant to enforce a limit, so the missing-header case should either be rejected while the limit is active or be documented as outside the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

Routine per-batch progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists

The new logging uses r.log.Error for routine progress: 'Annotations to clean by time' (with the full ids slice, up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries), 'cleaned annotations by time' (line 537), the matching 'by count' calls (lines 554 and 557), and 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' (lines 576 and 579). untilDoneOrCancelled always runs at least one batch, including the final empty one, so every cleanup cycle emits error-level entries even when nothing was deleted. true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated change: cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

This PR is about annotation-cleanup deadlocks, but it also changes the cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. false_positives.candidate:
One bind parameter per ID breaks large batch sizes on MySQL and PostgreSQL

The non-SQLite branch sends one bind parameter per ID. Previously the batch size was a literal in the LIMIT clause and could be any value. MySQL prepared statements and the PostgreSQL wire protocol cap bind parameters at 65535 per statement. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that now makes the DELETE fail on every cycle, and the diff adds no upper bound on the setting. The SQLite workaround only covers SQLite. Either cap the batch size or split the DELETE into statements of bounded parameter count.

Quadratic string building of the SQLite ID list

The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of n IDs costs O(n^2) bytes copied and allocated. With the batch size used in the new 40003-annotation test (32767), the final string is roughly 200KB and the loop copies several GB per batch, repeated for every batch and every annotation type. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

Every other method stores the request-scoped log (with name, kind and method values) in ctx. Delete uses d.Log, so anything downstream that logs via klog.FromContext, including the storage Delete path, loses those key/values. This is inconsistent with the rest of the file.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
