false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

The legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The request context is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after the unified-storage write completes. The legacy Create therefore almost always sees context.Canceled, the legacy copy is never written, and the only trace is a metric. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The detached goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a background context) before applying the timeout.

Dry-run requests are still dispatched to the legacy store

Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection never check options.DryRun before spawning the legacy write. A dry-run request is meant to have no side effects. Unified storage honors it, but the legacy call is dispatched unconditionally with the same options, and this file does not rely on the legacy store honoring DryRun. The legacy goroutine should be skipped when len(options.DryRun) > 0.

Legacy create mutates the same object the storage write used, racing with the response

The goroutine passes obj, the same pointer given to Storage.Create at line 42, to Legacy.Create while the handler continues to serialize the returned object. Legacy create paths typically assign UID, creationTimestamp and other metadata to the object in place. If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

Legacy write failures in mode 3 are counted but never logged

In Create the goroutine stores the legacy error in errObjectSt and only records a duration metric; no log line is emitted. Update (line 140), Delete (line 113) and DeleteCollection (line 166) have the same gap. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Since the async legacy write is now the only safety net, failures become invisible except as a counter with no object name or error text, so diverged objects cannot be identified.

Legacy writes in mode 3 are never verified by the tests

Each success case sets up a legacy expectation (for example here), but nothing asserts that it was called: there is no AssertExpectations and no wait for the goroutine. Legacy and storage also share one mock object (lines 53-54 construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock with the same m), so a legacy call would satisfy a storage expectation with the same method name and arguments. A regression that never calls Legacy, or calls it with the wrong object, passes these tests. Since asynchronous legacy behavior is the point of mode 3, tests should wait for the legacy call and check it against a separate legacy mock.

List test is named as 'not implemented' although List is implemented

The case name says listing 'is not implemented', but this PR implements List by calling Storage.List. The case only checks that an error returned by the storage mock is propagated. The name should describe that, for example 'error when listing from the unified store fails'.

Mode 3 update no longer sends the legacy store the object unified storage persisted

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. Now the raw objInfo is passed to Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated again against the legacy store's own copy. For patch and apply requests the legacy result can differ from what unified stored. Any resourceVersion precondition is checked against the legacy RV, which differs from the unified RV, so legacy updates can fail with a conflict. Both outcomes are silent (see the logging finding), so the two stores can silently diverge.

New mode 3 subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes

The new mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, which reads the legacy API right after k8s writes (getFromBothAPIs at lines 535 and 547, and later). With legacy writes now fire-and-forget, those reads race the goroutine and nothing waits for convergence. The subtests can be flaky, or fail deterministically if the legacy write fails (see the cancelled-context finding). The legacy-visibility checks should poll (for example with require.Eventually), or the test should document why these reads are unaffected in mode 3.

One unbounded goroutine per write, not tracked and not drained on shutdown

Each successful write spawns a goroutine that holds the request object and options until the legacy call returns. There is no bound on in-flight legacy writes. Nothing waits for them on shutdown, and Destroy (line 172) calls Legacy.Destroy while those goroutines may still be using Legacy. A slow legacy store causes goroutines and retained objects to grow with the write rate.

Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric

In Create, when the unified-storage write fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage errors are counted against the legacy series and the storage error metric is not updated. Update (line 129) makes the same mistake. Dashboards and alerts comparing the two stores will report wrong numbers.

Update doc comment describes the old synchronous ordering

The comment says Update writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage, which implies the legacy write is part of the synchronous call. It is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine and its errors are not returned. The Create comment (line 35) also does not say that the legacy write is asynchronous and best-effort, which callers need to know.

go.work.sum gets unrelated checksum entries and a duplicated line

The change adds checksums for modules unrelated to mode 3 (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporter and SDK versions, genproto rpc). This suggests a dependency tool was run and its output was committed. The github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery /go.mod line is also added even though an identical line already appears as context just above it, so it is duplicated. The unrelated lines should be reverted and the duplicate removed, or the PR should explain why they are needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, so waiters redo the full load

After Lock() at line 48, the function unconditionally reads and parses assets-manifest.json and then overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. It does this even when a goroutine that held the lock just before has already populated the cache. On a cold start, or after a failed load, N concurrent requests queue on the write lock and each performs the full file read and JSON decode, one after another. The redundant work existed before this change, but the lock now serializes it, so request latency grows with the number of waiters. Re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock in the non-dev case would complete the double-checked pattern that the RLock fast path starts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Dev mode now serializes every request through the exclusive lock

When cfg.Env == setting.Dev, the RLock fast path at lines 45-47 is never taken, so every GetWebAssets call acquires the exclusive write lock at line 48 and holds it across the file open, JSON decode and cache write. Concurrent dev-mode requests that previously ran in parallel are now fully serialized. The impact is limited to local development, but the change in concurrency behaviour is not mentioned and could be avoided by only taking the write lock when a reload is actually needed.

No regression test for the concurrent access fix

The change fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. The race is only detectable by calling GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines under `go test -race`. A test that uses a temporary static root with a valid assets-manifest.json, runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev configurations, and checks the cache behaviour would prevent a regression. Without it, removing the RWMutex would not be caught by CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag and always returns false

enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns false in both branches of the following `if`. The flag value is discarded, so the function is dead logic that reads as if it honours the flag. Anyone later restoring a flag-based gate will find an inverted-looking expression that never reaches a true result. It also dereferences `h.features` on every SQL query, so a nil feature set would panic on the SQL path, which previously never touched features. A plain rejection with a comment explaining the disablement would be clearer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL parsing and execution tests will fail, and no test files were updated

TablesList now always errors because DB.RunCommands is a stub returning "not implemented", and NewSQLCommand and SQLCommand.Execute depend on it. The PR changes no test files. If the repository's existing tests for TablesList, NewSQLCommand, SQL command execution, or the reader's SQL path (pkg/expr/sql, pkg/expr, reader tests) expect DuckDB results, they will fail in CI. Those tests should be removed, skipped with an explanation, or converted to assert the disabled behaviour.

false_positives.candidate:
Checksum removals unrelated to go-duck are unexplained

The go.work.sum hunk removes checksum lines for github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/storage/azblob v1.3.2 and github.com/google/go-replayers/grpcreplay and httpreplay. These are not part of the go-duck removal, and nothing in the PR explains them. This looks like side effects of a tidy run on a different module graph. Removing needed checksums can cause 'missing go.sum entry' failures in builds that run with -mod=readonly. Reviewers should confirm these modules are not needed, or drop the unrelated churn.

DuckDB-era string-built SQL is left in place; the fix depends entirely on the stub

TablesList still builds a SQL command with fmt.Sprintf and only escapes single quotes before sending it to the engine. The security property now relies entirely on the stub DB in db.go returning errors. Nothing in the reader or parser enforces the gate if the real engine is restored. Anyone who reinstates the DuckDB backend would reintroduce the injection surface without any warning in the code path. Either remove the dead parser code or add a comment and a guard tying its use to the feature gate.

Error message says 'not implemented' for a deliberate disablement

When a user enables the sqlExpressions flag, every SQL query now fails with "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is misleading: the feature is disabled by policy after a security fix, not missing. Users and support will read it as a bug. The feature toggle and its docs still describe SQL expressions as enabled by the flag, which the PR explicitly leaves untouched. The message and the flag documentation should say the feature is disabled for security reasons.

No regression test asserts that SQL expression queries are rejected

This is a security hotfix for RCE/LFI, but the PR adds no test showing that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL regardless of feature flags, and none that NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand fail for arbitrary SQL. Without such a test, a future change could silently re-enable the path (for example by restoring the DuckDB implementation in pkg/expr/sql/db.go) and nothing would catch it.

Stub DB named like a working in-memory engine with no doc comment

NewInMemoryDB and the DB type suggest a functional in-memory SQL engine, but every method unconditionally returns "not implemented". The type has no doc comment saying it is an intentional fail-closed stub that disables SQL expressions. A maintainer reading only this file could mistake the failures for a bug, or reinstate a DuckDB backend without knowing the stub is the security boundary.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key with no dedupe

The whole-function lock was the only serialization in BuildIndex. GetIndex returns nil for concurrent first requests, so each one runs a full ListIterator build. For file-backed indexes (size above FileThreshold), two builds now call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time (line 98). Previously the second build ran after the first and failed cleanly on the existing path. Now the two can interleave on-disk creation and fail or leave a bad store. For memory indexes, the second build replaces the first in the cache, orphaning it, and the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double counted. Add a per-key guard (the TODO in search.go mentions this) or re-check the cache under the lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without the lock, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. This PR adds a new caller of TotalDocs in init (search.go line 216), which runs right after the watch goroutine has started. That goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex, then build, then BuildIndex, and write b.cache concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error that cannot be recovered. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
Build errors in init's errgroup closures are shared-variable races and can be silently dropped

The errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` (declared at line 181) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` from up to `initWorkers` goroutines at once. The closure then does `return err`, which reads that shared variable, so a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build's nil. `init` then reports success while a namespace is missing from the index. `totalBatchesIndexed++` is also an unsynchronized write (lost updates, and the race detector flags it). This now runs inside NewResourceServer, which the code comments say must block startup on failure, so a swallowed error means a silently incomplete index. Use a closure-local error and an atomic counter.

Construction now performs DB init, full index build and watcher start synchronously, and can fail

NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle Init (DB open and ping), the full search index build for every namespace above the threshold, and starts the watcher. Any error makes construction fail. Previously this work happened on first RPC, so construction was cheap and a failure only affected calls. The consequences: the caller (module wiring) blocks for the entire build with no timeout (only Stop cancels, and that is not reached during startup); one bad namespace or a transient DB error prevents the whole storage module from starting; and any code that constructs a server before its DB or blob dependencies are ready now fails at construction. The PR asks what this could break, but the diff shows no update to callers and no bounded context for the build. This needs an explicit decision.

Error path after the new Init call leaks started resources

If any step after the new Init call fails, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel. The lifecycle backend may already be initialized, and search init may already have started the event goroutine (search.go line 207), which loops on a context.Background() watch forever. Nothing calls Stop on the discarded server. Call s.cancel() and the lifecycle Stop on the error path.

No tests cover the new construction-time failure and concurrency behaviour

The PR changes several behaviours without adding tests: NewResourceServer now returns an error when lifecycle init or the index build fails, RPCs no longer gate on initialization, and the BuildIndex lock was removed. Nothing checks that a failing index build makes NewResourceServer return an error, which would have caught the lost-error race in search.go. Nothing exercises concurrent BuildIndex and TotalDocs under the race detector, which would catch the cache races above.

Postgres skip disables the storage-server startup test without a tracked issue or mention in the description

A postgres branch is added that skips the only test in this file covering the storage-server startup path this PR changes. The skip has a TODO and no tracking issue, and the PR description does not mention disabling it. If construction-time init broke postgres startup, that regression is now hidden rather than fixed. Either fix the test or document the skip with an issue link in the description.

Span context is still discarded in WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator

The PR is described as fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down, but this file still discards the span context in WriteEvent (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` followed by `b.create(ctx, event)`). ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) do the same. The WriteEvent span is therefore not the parent of the create, update or delete spans, and the DB spans attach to the request instead. Only GetResourceStats was fixed here. Use `ctx, span :=` in these functions.

Stop no longer gates RPCs, since the Init calls that returned the stop error were removed

Stop stores 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped' in s.initErr. Before this PR every RPC called s.Init, which returned that stored error, so calls after Stop failed fast. This PR removes every s.Init call from the handlers, so nothing reads initErr anymore. After Stop, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List and Search keep reaching the backend. backend.Stop only cancels the poller and does not close the DB. This silently removes the shutdown guard. If it is still needed, check a stopped flag in the handlers or in a shared helper.

Watch loop dereferences nil event when the events channel is closed, causing a panic

The loop does `v := <-events` and passes `v` to handleEvent without checking whether the channel is open. The SQL poller does `defer close(stream)` when the backend is stopped (b.done). After that, every receive yields nil, and handleEvent immediately reads `evt.Type` (line 226), which panics with a nil pointer dereference. The same pattern in server.go initWatcher (`v.Type` on a possibly nil v) panics too. The watch context is context.Background(), so this loop never exits on its own. Use `v, ok := <-events` and return when ok is false.

Writes made during the initial index build are never indexed

init lists and builds each namespace first, and only afterwards calls WatchWriteEvents. The SQL WatchWriteEvents takes its starting point from the latest resource versions at subscription time (listLatestRVs), so any write committed after a namespace was read but before the subscription is never delivered to the index. The object stays missing from search until it is modified again. This PR makes the build window longer, since the whole build for all namespaces now runs synchronously at construction. The rv returned by build (line 309 onward) is computed for exactly this purpose but discarded here. Subscribe first, build, then replay events with a resource version above each namespace's list version.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes the literal alias "alias", so the 20 IdPs created in testCacheIDPForLogin leak

The cleanup `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove` (copied from the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg) never references the IdP that was created (`"idp-alias-" + i`). The 20 IdPs therefore remain in the realm after the test, and 10 of them (idp-alias-10..19) stay linked to orga. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts exact membership counts for orga (e.g. 6) and the new test asserts exact login counts, so their results depend on JUnit method execution order and can fail once the other runs first. The cleanup should reference the created alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache search key conflates null and "" organizationId, which the delegate treats differently

searchKey maps both null and "" to "". The delegate's default getForLogin only adds the ORGANIZATION_ID filter when organizationId != null. With null, ORG_ONLY/ALL return IdPs of any organization. With "", it adds an explicit ORGANIZATION_ID="" filter with different results. Because both share the same cache slot, a result computed for one input can be served for the other. Use a key that distinguishes null from the empty string.

Login-cache invalidation on update evaluates the stored IdP through the org-aware wrapper

update() obtains `idpById` via getById() (line 91), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization (or the OrganizationProvider) is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then runs getLoginPredicate() on this wrapper, but the login caches were built from raw DB rows where org state is irrelevant. Consequence: for an enabled, public IdP linked to a disabled org, an update that makes it not login-eligible (e.g. setHideOnLogin(true) or setLinkOnly(true)) gives test(original)=false and test(updated)=false, so no invalidation is registered. The cached ALL/ORG_ONLY lists still contain the IdP id. The consumer (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) only re-checks isEnabled(), not hideOnLogin/linkOnly, and enabling an org does not invalidate login caches. Once the org is re-enabled, the hidden IdP is shown on the login page. The original state should be taken from the raw stored model (not the org-aware wrapper) before evaluating the predicate.

No test covers invalidation when a login-eligible IdP is created or removed

testCacheIDPForLogin only creates a hidden IdP (line 424) and removes a disabled IdP (line 428). Both are paths where login caches must NOT be invalidated. The new registerIDPLoginInvalidation calls in create() and remove() for IdPs that are actually login-eligible are never exercised, so a regression there would go unnoticed. Also untested is the scenario where an org-linked IdP's login eligibility changes while its organization is disabled, which is where the wrapper-based classification in update() goes wrong.

remove() now always performs a DB lookup of the IdP

`idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was moved out of the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch, so every remove() now issues an extra DB query even when the alias entry is served from cache. The result is needed only for the new login invalidation and for the invalid branch. The lookup could be deferred or the cached model could be used for the login check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of a default KeyStore, not a BouncyCastle provider

The method creates a KeyStore of the default type and returns its provider (typically a JDK SUN/SunJSSE provider). The method name and the CryptoProvider contract say it returns the BouncyCastle provider. Callers that use it for Signature, Cipher or other lookups will silently get a non-BC provider, which may lack the required algorithms. A new KeyStore object is also allocated on every call just to read its provider. Return the real BC provider, or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods in this class.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances, encode rBigInteger and sBigInteger, and discard the results. The returned DER comes only from the writeDerSeq call below. The dead statements suggest the values feed into the output when they do not, and they should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length marker reaches new byte[-1] and throws an unchecked exception

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length marker 0x80. readInteger() passes that value straight to read(), where new byte[length] throws NegativeArraySizeException. The decoder's contract reports malformed DER through IOException, which the callers declare, so malformed input to asn1derToConcatenatedRS escapes as a RuntimeException. readNext() has the same problem. readLength should reject negative lengths with an IOException.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method on the public CryptoProvider SPI breaks existing implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside the three in-repo providers, including third-party or downstream ones, will stop compiling. If it is compiled against an older interface, it fails at runtime with AbstractMethodError when order() is called during provider sorting. A default implementation would keep existing providers loading, while the in-repo providers keep their explicit overrides.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient.create() installs a process-wide, one-shot crypto provider visible only to its own classloader

CryptoIntegration.init() is global and idempotent: it only runs detection while cryptoProvider is null, and later calls are no-ops. Here it is called with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(), so only providers visible from that loader are considered. If the real provider (Default, Elytron or FIPS) is only visible through another classloader, or is initialized later with a different loader, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider stub becomes the provider for the whole JVM and stays there. Every later crypto call then fails with UnsupportedOperationException. Before this PR, authz-client did not touch global crypto state at all. Consider not initializing global state from client construction, or only doing so when no provider has been set.

ECDSA conversion test is only a self round-trip, and uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512

The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. It checks the two conversions only against each other, so a shared encoding mistake (wrong DER SEQUENCE or INTEGER layout, for example) passes unnoticed. The produced DER is never checked with the JDK's Signature.verify. The key is also always generated as P-256 (KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")), so the ES384 and ES512 cases run with 32-byte R/S values padded to 48 and 66 bytes, not the real curve sizes. Verify each DER signature with the JDK verifier, and use P-384 and P-521 keys for ES384 and ES512. The 33-byte leading-zero INTEGER case should also be covered deterministically.

Most CryptoProvider methods are placeholder stubs throwing 'Not supported yet.'

getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getOCSPProver, getIdentityExtractorProvider, createECParams, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getSignature, wrapFactoryForTruststore and ECDSACryptoProvider.getPublicFromPrivate all throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."). This provider is registered through the service file and is selected whenever it is the only provider present. Any code path that reaches one of these methods then fails with a message that names nothing useful. The class Javadoc ("Simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client") does not mention these gaps. Document the supported operations, and make each unsupported operation name itself in the exception, or remove stubs that cannot be reached.

Providers with equal order() are picked arbitrarily, silently bypassing the old single-provider guard

The old code threw when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and takes the first element. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200 in this PR, so a tie is possible. Ties are then resolved by ServiceLoader/classpath order, which is not a defined contract. If a FIPS deployment has both the FIPS and the default (or elytron) provider jar on the classpath, the non-FIPS provider can be selected with no error. The only trace is a debug log line. The removed guard existed to prevent exactly this. Equal top-order providers should still fail fast, or the FIPS provider should be given a strictly higher order.

integerToBytes silently truncates over-long DER integers instead of rejecting them

When the decoded INTEGER has more bytes than the field length (qLength < bytes.length), the code keeps only the trailing bytes and discards the high-order ones. A malformed or non-canonical DER integer, for example r with an extra leading 0x01 byte, is turned into a different, valid-looking concatenated signature instead of an IOException. Verification then depends on the JDK rejecting the altered value. The conversion should check that the value fits in qLength bytes, allowing only a single leading zero.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-removal cleanup is skipped in V2-only deployments, leaving stale per-client resources

The whole listener body is now gated on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1). Deployments that enable only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (the mode management()/evaluator() select V2 for) therefore skip ClientRemovedEvent handling entirely. Per-client resources named by the deleted client's UUID, and scope permissions referencing them, persist after the client is deleted. The guard should check the feature that actually selects the implementation, or V2 should implement the cleanup.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission never returns individual clients and can return the literal 'Clients'

getClientsWithPermission enumerates resources with resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...). Per-client resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104) via resourceStore.create(...) without setting a type, so they never match the type filter. Only the all-clients resource matches, because init() sets its type. Consequence: when the scope is granted on all clients, the method adds the resource name "Clients" to the result as if it were a client id, and no individual client id is ever returned. Set the type when per-client resources are created, or look them up another way.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing FGAP v2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes

init() returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists. Before this PR, V2 mode used the V1 ClientPermissions implementation for these calls, which returned values instead of throwing. Any caller that reaches these methods in V2 mode now gets an uncaught exception, which surfaces as a 500 rather than a denial. canExchangeTo is the most exposed: it is part of the evaluator contract and is used by client-to-client token-exchange logic. getEvaluationContext (line 262) is an unused private helper that looks intended for canExchangeTo, so the method seems to have been left unfinished.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting any client fails when both fine-grained feature flags are enabled

The ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException (ClientPermissionsV2.java line 193). The listener is gated only on the V1 flag, but evaluator()/management() prefer V2 whenever the V2 flag is set, so the two flags can coexist. In that configuration every client deletion propagates the exception and fails. The V2 implementation should be a no-op here, or the event handler should skip V2.

Javadoc for requireView() says it returns a boolean, but it is a void method that throws

The Javadoc for requireView() reads 'Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.' The method is void and is meant to throw ForbiddenException when canView() returns false. The same mistake appears on requireViewClientScopes() (line 101). Implementers reading this doc, including the V2 class, could easily get the contract backwards.

Negative per-client VIEW policy cannot hide a client from an admin with all-clients VIEW

Every other per-client check goes through hasPermission(client, ...), which uses the per-client resource when it exists and so honours negative policies. The user resource tests (testViewUserPermission) expect a per-object negative policy to override an all-objects positive permission. Here, an admin with all-clients VIEW and a NEGATIVE VIEW policy on a specific client still sees and can GET that client, and it still appears in listings. The short-circuit should be removed or the per-client result should take precedence.

The result is null for client permissions. The USERS branch returns 'All users' for the type resource and the username for a user resource. The CLIENTS equivalents (an 'All clients' label and the client's clientId) are missing.

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

canManage() on V2 grants manage when the caller only has VIEW on groups

Because VIEW is in the accepted scope list, a caller whose only grant on the all-groups resource is VIEW passes canManage(). The no-argument requireManage() is what GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (POST /groups) calls, so a VIEW-only admin can create top-level groups. canView() correctly accepts VIEW and MANAGE; canManage() should accept MANAGE only. true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns internal resource UUIDs instead of group IDs

Callers treat the returned set as group IDs: it is set as the UserModel.GROUPS session filter in UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource, and passed to getUsersCount. Here, granted.add(groupResource.getId()) adds the internal UUID of the authz Resource record, not the group ID. The resource name is the group ID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource/resolveGroup). The V1 implementation correctly uses getName() with the prefix stripped. Line 122 has the same problem: hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) looks up the resource by name, so the UUID never matches, and the code silently falls back to the all-groups resource. The all-groups 'Groups' resource is itself returned by findByType and can add its own UUID to the set. Result: user search and count are filtered by IDs that match no group, so admins with per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS lose results, and the all-groups case adds garbage IDs.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting any group fails when V2 admin permissions are enabled

The GroupRemovedEvent listener calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) for every group removal. In V2 mode management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, which now returns GroupPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled (GroupPermissionsV2 lines 173-175) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The listener runs on every group deletion, whether or not the realm uses fine-grained admin permissions. Before this PR, V2 used the V1 GroupPermissions, where this call was a no-op for realms without permissions. With both ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, group deletion will likely fail with an exception propagating out of event publishing. The test cleanup in GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest (realm.cleanup().add(r -> r.groups().group(...).remove())) would hit the same path.

Existing FGAP v2 realms never get the Groups resource type; null is dereferenced

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists (line 250). Realms that enabled FGAP v2 before this PR therefore never receive the Groups resource or the manage-members, view-members and manage-membership scopes. getResourceTypeResource(GROUPS) then returns null. Line 147 passes that null to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource), which will likely NPE on every group check that falls back to the type-level resource. Creating a group permission in such a realm also fails in getOrCreateResource with 'No scopes found.'. This is an upgrade break unless a migration exists elsewhere, and none is in this diff.

Group management-permissions endpoints now throw UnsupportedOperationException in V2 realms

MgmtPermissionsV2 did not override groups() before this PR, so V2 realms used the V1 GroupPermissions for group management permissions. The PR replaces that with GroupPermissionsV2, where isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource and the *Permission accessors all throw UnsupportedOperationException. GroupResource.getManagementPermissions and setManagementPermissionsEnabled reach these, so the endpoints return HTTP 500 in V2 mode. This is a regression for groups, and the PR does not document it or gate the endpoints with a clear error.

IMPERSONATE is evaluated against the target user's identity when a requester client is given

When requester != null, the evaluation context is built with new UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), i.e. the impersonated target user. The IMPERSONATE scope is an admin-side permission, and the requester==null path (line 70) evaluates with the admin's identity. The two paths therefore disagree. The target-identity context was copied from V1 isImpersonatable(), which uses it for the USER_IMPERSONATED scope, where it is correct. Here, user or role policies that should match the admin (or the requesting client via kc.client.id) are checked against the victim user, so canClientImpersonate/canImpersonate(user, client) can deny legitimate impersonation or match on the wrong identity.

No test checks that a VIEW-only all-groups admin is denied group creation

testViewGroups grants VIEW on all groups and only checks listing. The VIEW-only canManage() bug in GroupPermissionsV2 allows POST /groups for such an admin, and nothing in this test class catches it. A negative assertion (create top-level group with only all-groups VIEW gets FORBIDDEN) is needed. Similarly, nothing checks that group user-search or count results are correct when the admin has per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS, which the group-ID bug would break.

Removed global canView short-circuit makes the list path evaluate policies per group

The previous code computed canView() once and skipped per-group checks when it was true. Now filter(groupsEvaluator::canView) calls canView(group) for every group. In V2, canView(group) runs hasPermission, which resolves the per-group resource and evaluates the authorization policy engine each time, or falls back to the all-groups resource. For admins with global view, listing N groups costs N policy evaluations instead of one. GroupResource.getSubGroups has the same change.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc says Stream but the method returns Set

The @return tag says 'Stream of IDs of groups with view permission', but the method returns Set<String>. The javadoc also says it returns an empty set only when canView() is true, but the implementation also returns an empty set when the caller is not in the same realm or the server is missing.

init() does not add the Groups type to realms that already have admin permissions

The early return when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null means the new GROUPS resource type, its resource and its scopes are only created for newly enabled realms. This is the upgrade gap described in the GroupPermissionsV2 finding: existing realms have no 'Groups' resource and no group scopes, and nothing in the diff backfills them.

requireManageMembers javadoc references the wrong method

The javadoc for requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should reference canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is the method it actually calls.

switch on resourceType throws NPE for null, where the old code was null-safe

The previous code compared with USERS.getType().equals(resourceType), which is null-safe. The new switch (resourceType) throws NullPointerException when resourceType is null, instead of the intended error path. Callers must guarantee a non-null type or the failure becomes an NPE rather than a clear validation error.

The grant shortcut sits at index 4-5 of the encoded context (e.g. 'onrtac' -> 'ac' at 4-5), but this reads `substring(3, 5)`, which is 'ta' for that example. The check is also inverted: `if (...equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` rejects the case where the grant matches and accepts the case where it does not. New recovery-codes test covers only the happy path

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes, logs in once with code 0 and stops. The reuse gap in particular is exactly what this test should catch.

Recovery codes are sent to user storage in plaintext while local storage keeps only hashes

generatedCodes are the raw codes shown to the user. They are serialized to JSON and passed unhashed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), so any external user storage provider (LDAP, a custom DB) persists usable bearer login secrets. The local path stores only RS512 hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). A read of the external store therefore yields directly usable recovery codes, and the test provider compares raw strings. For a federated credential that state is rebuilt from the raw stored list by getCredentials (new model, no used-state), so allCodesUsed() can never become true. The result is that a recovery code which logged a user in once keeps working indefinitely, while the local provider consumes codes. getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser

supportsCredentialType throws NPE for a null type

Nothing in the core flow writes used-state back to user storage either. The new test performs only one successful login and never attempts a second use, so this goes undetected.

generatedCodes are the raw codes shown to the user. They are serialized to JSON and passed unhashed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), so any external user storage provider (LDAP, a custom DB) persists usable bearer login secrets. The local path stores only RS512 hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). A read of the external store therefore yields directly usable recovery codes, and the test provider compares raw strings. Either hash the codes before handing them to user storage (and hash the input on verification) or explicitly document and accept the difference.

It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused (which the user-storage path currently fails, see the isValid comment), that the stored codes are visible through the account/admin credential APIs (the new getCredentials override is not exercised), or that the local fallback still works when a storage provider does not support recovery codes. The sibling methods getDisableableCredentialTypesStream and isConfiguredFor guard against this case, so this one throws NullPointerException where the others return empty results.

The previous implementation was null-safe (CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(null) and isOTPType(null) return false). The new clause credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) is evaluated for a null argument and throws NullPointerException instead of logging and returning false. Comparing against the constant (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)) would avoid this.

disableCredentialType only handles OTP and logs 'Unsupported' for anything else, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream never includes the recovery type. Admin disable-credential requests for a federated user therefore silently leave the stored recovery codes in place, and the admin API does not offer them as disableable. The local path supports revoking these codes, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the feature being added.

The credentialModel passed in carries the user-provided userLabel and the generatedAt timestamp, and the local branch persists them. The user-storage branch builds only a UserCredentialModel from the type and the JSON codes, so these values are discarded. The test provider then stamps createdDate with the current time and has no label. Users who set a label or check creation dates will see different metadata depending on where the codes ended up, without any indication.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The whole-function lock was the only serialization in BuildIndex. GetIndex returns nil for concurrent first requests, so each one runs a full ListIterator build. For file-backed indexes (size above FileThreshold), two builds now call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time (line 98). Previously the second build ran after the first and failed cleanly on the existing path. Now the two can interleave on-disk creation and fail or leave a bad store. For memory indexes, the second build replaces the first in the cache, orphaning it, and the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double counted. Add a per-key guard (the TODO in search.go mentions this) or re-check the cache under the lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same race condition where removing the function-wide lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs iterates the index cache without the lock, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. This PR adds a new caller of TotalDocs in init (search.go line 216), which runs right after the watch goroutine has started. That goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex, then build, then BuildIndex, and write b.cache concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error that cannot be recovered. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue describe the exact same race condition: calling TotalDocs() in init right after starting the watch goroutine causes a concurrent map read/write on b.cache because TotalDocs iterates without synchronization while BuildIndex writes to it.

false_positives.candidate:
Build errors in init's errgroup closures are shared-variable races and can be silently dropped

The errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` (declared at line 181) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` from up to `initWorkers` goroutines at once. The closure then does `return err`, which reads that shared variable, so a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build's nil. `init` then reports success while a namespace is missing from the index. `totalBatchesIndexed++` is also an unsynchronized write (lost updates, and the race detector flags it). This now runs inside NewResourceServer, which the code comments say must block startup on failure, so a swallowed error means a silently incomplete index. Use a closure-local error and an atomic counter.

Watch loop dereferences nil event when the events channel is closed, causing a panic

The loop does `v := <-events` and passes `v` to handleEvent without checking whether the channel is open. The SQL poller does `defer close(stream)` when the backend is stopped (b.done). After that, every receive yields nil, and handleEvent immediately reads `evt.Type` (line 226), which panics with a nil pointer dereference. The same pattern in server.go initWatcher (`v.Type` on a possibly nil v) panics too. The watch context is context.Background(), so this loop never exits on its own. Use `v, ok := <-events` and return when ok is false.

Writes made during the initial index build are never indexed

init lists and builds each namespace first, and only afterwards calls WatchWriteEvents. The SQL WatchWriteEvents takes its starting point from the latest resource versions at subscription time (listLatestRVs), so any write committed after a namespace was read but before the subscription is never delivered to the index. The object stays missing from search until it is modified again. This PR makes the build window longer, since the whole build for all namespaces now runs synchronously at construction. The rv returned by build (line 309 onward) is computed for exactly this purpose but discarded here. Subscribe first, build, then replay events with a resource version above each namespace's list version.

Construction now performs DB init, full index build and watcher start synchronously, and can fail

NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle Init (DB open and ping), the full search index build for every namespace above the threshold, and starts the watcher. Any error makes construction fail. Previously this work happened on first RPC, so construction was cheap and a failure only affected calls. The consequences: the caller (module wiring) blocks for the entire build with no timeout (only Stop cancels, and that is not reached during startup); one bad namespace or a transient DB error prevents the whole storage module from starting; and any code that constructs a server before its DB or blob dependencies are ready now fails at construction. The PR asks what this could break, but the diff shows no update to callers and no bounded context for the build. This needs an explicit decision.

Stop no longer gates RPCs, since the Init calls that returned the stop error were removed

Stop stores 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped' in s.initErr. Before this PR every RPC called s.Init, which returned that stored error, so calls after Stop failed fast. This PR removes every s.Init call from the handlers, so nothing reads initErr anymore. After Stop, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List and Search keep reaching the backend. backend.Stop only cancels the poller and does not close the DB. This silently removes the shutdown guard. If it is still needed, check a stopped flag in the handlers or in a shared helper.

Error path after the new Init call leaks started resources

If any step after the new Init call fails, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel. The lifecycle backend may already be initialized, and search init may already have started the event goroutine (search.go line 207), which loops on a context.Background() watch forever. Nothing calls Stop on the discarded server. Call s.cancel() and the lifecycle Stop on the error path.

Span context is still discarded in WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator

The PR is described as fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down, but this file still discards the span context in WriteEvent (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` followed by `b.create(ctx, event)`). ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) do the same. The WriteEvent span is therefore not the parent of the create, update or delete spans, and the DB spans attach to the request instead. Only GetResourceStats was fixed here. Use `ctx, span :=` in these functions.

Nothing exercises concurrent BuildIndex and TotalDocs under the race detector, which would catch the cache races above.

A group linked to two Jira issues on the same Jira site would no longer receive assignee updates to issue B when issue A's assignee is changed by an inbound webhook. The description only mentions preventing the echo back to the triggering issue. This suppression of legitimate updates to other linked issues is not mentioned or tested.

Any installation subclass that still overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` or a concrete `sync_assignee_outbound` without `**kwargs` will now raise TypeError, even when no assignment source is involved. The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter, but no caller in this PR passes it and no implementation is required to use it. The docstring still describes only the status propagation. This is a misleading contract change for implementers, unrelated to the assignee fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the failing batch is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring

The docstring says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages'. Offsets 100 and 101 both complete: the first raises, the worker logs it and completes the offset in its finally, and the second succeeds. The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. It passes only because the commit thread's first cycle fires about one second after creation while the test checks after roughly 0.2 seconds. On a slower run the commit happens and the test fails. The test should wait for the commit and assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly points out that the test's implementation (specifically the final assertion) contradicts its own docstring regarding offset commits during error handling, which is the exact same issue described in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition

get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

Docstring promises no item is lost and commits only after success, but failed items are logged and committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches Exception and logs it, and the finally block (line 149) completes the offset anyway, so the offset is committed and the failed result is never retried. The result processor also swallows its own exceptions. The guarantees 'No item is lost' (line 252) and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' (line 254) therefore do not hold. This may match the existing batched modes, but the docstring should not claim otherwise.

Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing

Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order

The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers

The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s

The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.

false_positives.candidate:
Segment key type changed from SET to ZSET without migration, so in-flight keys break on deploy

The per-segment key type changes from a Redis SET to a sorted set: sadd becomes zadd here, sscan becomes zscan in _load_segment_data, and sunionstore becomes zunionstore in add-buffer.lua. The key names (span-buf:s:{...}) are unchanged and segment keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after, old-version SET keys still exist. New code then hits WRONGTYPE on zadd, on zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin inside the Lua script, and on zscan in the flusher. redis-py pipelines raise on command errors, so process_spans fails for any batch touching a legacy key, and flush_segments can fail for every segment in the same batch. That stalls ingestion and flushing until the old keys expire. The fix needs a new key prefix or explicit handling of the type mismatch.

zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores of members present in both sets

ZUNIONSTORE without an AGGREGATE option sums scores. When a member (same payload) already exists in set_key and is also in the source key, for example a redelivered span, its score becomes the sum of two end timestamps (about 3.4e9) instead of end_timestamp_precise. zpopmin uses these scores to choose which spans to evict, so eviction order is corrupted. The same problem applies at line 53 for the parent key. Use AGGREGATE MAX or MIN so scores remain timestamps.

Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no metric or log, and it replaces an observable limit

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin silently deletes the lowest-scored (earliest-ending) entries. The buffer.py change also removes the old flush-time guard, which logged an error and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded. Segments that used to be dropped and logged are now silently truncated, and operators have no signal that spans are being discarded. Add a counter or log for the number of evicted spans.

Redirect-chain walk bound lowered from 10000 to 1000 without explanation

The loop bound changed from 10000 to 1000 and the comment that documented the limit was deleted. The change is unrelated to span eviction and is not mentioned in the PR. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 now stop early, leaving set_span_id at an intermediate span, so later spans are attached to the wrong segment with no error or metric. Restore the original bound or justify the change explicitly.

New optimized_pagination branch and its admin gating have no tests

The branch that switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True, the superuser/global-access gate, and the fallback to DateTimePaginator are all untested. The negative-offset path that 500s for admins (paginator.py line 882) would be caught by even a single endpoint test. Add tests for the admin path, the non-admin fallback, and a negative cursor.

Comment claims a capability that this change does not implement

The added comment says it is a 'performance optimization' that allows negative offsets for 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions'. The only change is this comment: int(offset) was already unvalidated. Downstream, forward pages clamp negatives to 0 and prev pages pass them into queryset slicing, which raises. The comment advertises behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers.

Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* keys as sets

The glossary says span-buf:s:* keys are 'the actual set keys', and the flow above says payloads are added to 'the set'. After this change these keys are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, which is what the eviction and flush logic depends on. The docs should say so.

max_segment_spans is now a dead parameter; the eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000 in Lua

SpansBuffer still accepts max_segment_spans (default 1001), but nothing reads it. Its only use, the span-count check in _load_segment_data, was removed. The real limit is the hard-coded 1000 in add-buffer.lua line 62. Callers tuning this parameter get no effect, and the two limits disagree. Either pass the limit to the script through ARGV or remove the parameter.

Tests do not cover eviction, score ordering, or the set-to-zset change

The PR's purpose is eviction above 1000 spans, but no test inserts more than 1000 spans or checks which spans survive. Every fixture uses the same constant end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so score-based ordering is never exercised. The zunionstore SUM collision is also untested, as is the old-SET-key compatibility problem. Add a test that inserts more than 1000 spans with distinct end timestamps and checks that the latest 1000 survive, plus a case where the same payload arrives twice.

Unrelated audit-log, paginator, and cursor changes are bundled into a spans-buffer PR with a placeholder description

The PR title describes a spans buffer optimization, and the description is only 'Test 2'. The diff also changes the audit-log endpoint, adds an experimental pagination class to api/paginator.py, and changes utils/cursors.py. Nothing in the description explains why these belong together or how they are meant to behave. Split them into separate PRs with descriptions, or document the intent.

Sentry's options manager raises for unregistered keys. This call runs on every cache miss for any events-stats timeseries request, before the dataset check. The rewrite produces the literal string 'upsampled_count() as count'. Sentry's field grammar takes function(args) with nothing after the closing paren, so this string will not match the function form and will be treated as an unknown field or fail to parse. That turns affected requests into errors. The upsampled_count aggregate is only registered in DiscoverDatasetConfig (discover.py), yet _should_apply_sample_weight_transform also enables the rewrite for the `errors` dataset. Nothing in the diff shows this resolves through the errors query builder.

The docstring says the schema guarantees sample_weight for all events in allowlisted projects, so no null checks are needed. Nothing enforces that: the allowlist is per project, not per event. The discover gate is tested only with a plain 'event.type:error' query and a plain 'event.type:transaction' query. It is not tested with '!event.type:error', with 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction', or with the split-path query shapes. Those are exactly the inputs where the substring check gives the wrong answer, so the bug above would pass this suite.

The new class covers only plain count() timeseries for an error query, an all-allowlisted and a partial-allowlist case, and a transaction-only query. The new aggregate is registered without private=True, unlike the adjacent function in the same converter. Any discover or events query can therefore call upsampled_count() on any project. The allowlist check exists only in the count() rewrite, so users can request an upsampled value for non-allowlisted projects, where sample_weight is typically absent and the result is 0 or misleading. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but nothing in this change calls it. The eligibility cache set at line 38 has a 60 second TTL and is keyed only by org and project set. Removing a project from the allowlist therefore keeps upsampling it for up to a minute. The NOTE in _are_all_projects_error_upsampled (lines 50-53) says the allowlist is read fresh on every call and that this is intentional. The cache at lines 30-38 contradicts the second claim. The performance rationale is asserted without measurement, and the cache adds its own round trip on every request.

Comments claim caching and consistency that the code does not provide

The comments say 'this cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution' and describe a performance optimization. Nothing is cached in this function. The eligibility is recomputed on every _get_event_stats call, which can be up to four times per request in the split path. The topEvents validation message changes from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is a wording change to a public API response that the PR description does not mention and that no test update in this diff accompanies. Clients or tests matching the old string will break.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps both the lookup and the float conversion in bare 'except Exception: pass'. sample_weight is a non-integer float (1/sample_rate), and toInt64 truncates toward zero. A float sum that lands just below an integer, for example 9.9999999999, becomes 9. Round before casting, e.g. round(sum(...)), so the integer result is not systematically low.

Recorded denials pin a deny for 30s, bypassing the new requery and surviving grants

Entries are written whenever a DB-backed check denies (line 154) and are removed only by the 30s TTL; nothing clears them when a grant is written or a resource is created. The requery added by this PR only runs on a permission-cache miss, so a denial recorded before the creator's permission was visible (for example a GET racing the permission write, or any read of the UID before it existed) keeps returning denied for up to 30 seconds. Dashboards and folders created by the user therefore stay absent from list results for up to 30 seconds, the same class of problem this PR claims to fix for Check. The PR does not mention or test this limitation.

Someone handed an installation_id belonging to another GitHub account can complete the install whenever the webhook record has not landed yet. The installer must be verified on this path too, or the pipeline must fail closed.

Both lookups by external_id=installation_id (this one and the one at line 478) omit provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key. external_id is only unique per provider, so the row found may belong to another provider and has no GitHub 'sender' in its metadata. The new OAuth failure branches (state mismatch at integration.py line 412, missing access_token at line 431, missing login at line 435) have no tests either. Assert the absence of the OrganizationIntegration and/or give the sender mismatch its own error text.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, so waiters redo the full load

After Lock() at line 48, the function unconditionally reads and parses assets-manifest.json and then overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. It does this even when a goroutine that held the lock just before has already populated the cache. On a cold start, or after a failed load, N concurrent requests queue on the write lock and each performs the full file read and JSON decode, one after another. The redundant work existed before this change, but the lock now serializes it, so request latency grows with the number of waiters. Re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock in the non-dev case would complete the double-checked pattern that the RLock fast path starts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the cache is checked under a read lock, but not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing concurrent goroutines to redundantly reload the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Dev mode now serializes every request through the exclusive lock

When cfg.Env == setting.Dev, the RLock fast path at lines 45-47 is never taken, so every GetWebAssets call acquires the exclusive write lock at line 48 and holds it across the file open, JSON decode and cache write. Concurrent dev-mode requests that previously ran in parallel are now fully serialized. The impact is limited to local development, but the change in concurrency behaviour is not mentioned and could be avoided by only taking the write lock when a reload is actually needed.

No regression test for the concurrent access fix

The change fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. The race is only detectable by calling GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines under `go test -race`. A test that uses a temporary static root with a valid assets-manifest.json, runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev configurations, and checks the cache behaviour would prevent a regression. Without it, removing the RWMutex would not be caught by CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of n IDs costs O(n^2) bytes copied and allocated. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that now makes the DELETE fail on every cycle, and the diff adds no upper bound on the setting. The SQLite workaround only covers SQLite.
