false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

The legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The request context is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after the unified-storage write completes. The legacy Create therefore almost always sees context.Canceled, the legacy copy is never written, and the only trace is a metric. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The detached goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a background context) before applying the timeout.

Legacy write failures in mode 3 are counted but never logged

In Create the goroutine stores the legacy error in errObjectSt and only records a duration metric; no log line is emitted. Update (line 140), Delete (line 113) and DeleteCollection (line 166) have the same gap. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Since the async legacy write is now the only safety net, failures become invisible except as a counter with no object name or error text, so diverged objects cannot be identified.

Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric

In Create, when the unified-storage write fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage errors are counted against the legacy series and the storage error metric is not updated. Update (line 129) makes the same mistake. Dashboards and alerts comparing the two stores will report wrong numbers.

Legacy create mutates the same object the storage write used, racing with the response

The goroutine passes obj, the same pointer given to Storage.Create at line 42, to Legacy.Create while the handler continues to serialize the returned object. Legacy create paths typically assign UID, creationTimestamp and other metadata to the object in place. If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

Mode 3 update no longer sends the legacy store the object unified storage persisted

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. Now the raw objInfo is passed to Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated again against the legacy store's own copy. For patch and apply requests the legacy result can differ from what unified stored. Any resourceVersion precondition is checked against the legacy RV, which differs from the unified RV, so legacy updates can fail with a conflict. Both outcomes are silent (see the logging finding), so the two stores can silently diverge.

Dry-run requests are still dispatched to the legacy store

Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection never check options.DryRun before spawning the legacy write. A dry-run request is meant to have no side effects. Unified storage honors it, but the legacy call is dispatched unconditionally with the same options, and this file does not rely on the legacy store honoring DryRun. The legacy goroutine should be skipped when len(options.DryRun) > 0.

One unbounded goroutine per write, not tracked and not drained on shutdown

Each successful write spawns a goroutine that holds the request object and options until the legacy call returns. There is no bound on in-flight legacy writes. Nothing waits for them on shutdown, and Destroy (line 172) calls Legacy.Destroy while those goroutines may still be using Legacy. A slow legacy store causes goroutines and retained objects to grow with the write rate.

Update doc comment describes the old synchronous ordering

The comment says Update writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage, which implies the legacy write is part of the synchronous call. It is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine and its errors are not returned. The Create comment (line 35) also does not say that the legacy write is asynchronous and best-effort, which callers need to know.

Legacy writes in mode 3 are never verified by the tests

Each success case sets up a legacy expectation (for example here), but nothing asserts that it was called: there is no AssertExpectations and no wait for the goroutine. Legacy and storage also share one mock object (lines 53-54 construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock with the same m), so a legacy call would satisfy a storage expectation with the same method name and arguments. A regression that never calls Legacy, or calls it with the wrong object, passes these tests. Since asynchronous legacy behavior is the point of mode 3, tests should wait for the legacy call and check it against a separate legacy mock.

List test is named as 'not implemented' although List is implemented

The case name says listing 'is not implemented', but this PR implements List by calling Storage.List. The case only checks that an error returned by the storage mock is propagated. The name should describe that, for example 'error when listing from the unified store fails'.

New mode 3 subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes

The new mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, which reads the legacy API right after k8s writes (getFromBothAPIs at lines 535 and 547, and later). With legacy writes now fire-and-forget, those reads race the goroutine and nothing waits for convergence. The subtests can be flaky, or fail deterministically if the legacy write fails (see the cancelled-context finding). The legacy-visibility checks should poll (for example with require.Eventually), or the test should document why these reads are unaffected in mode 3.

go.work.sum gets unrelated checksum entries and a duplicated line

The change adds checksums for modules unrelated to mode 3 (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporter and SDK versions, genproto rpc). This suggests a dependency tool was run and its output was committed. The github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery /go.mod line is also added even though an identical line already appears as context just above it, so it is duplicated. The unrelated lines should be reverted and the duplicate removed, or the PR should explain why they are needed.

If template replacement resolves `$__range` (it does when request.scopedVars carries `__range`), the token is gone, isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false, and queries like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` get split into chunks. Their results then no longer match what the guard was meant to protect. No test in the diff covers a `$__range` query, so this regression would not be caught. The guard should check the pre-interpolation expression, and the comment at lines 285-286 needs updating since its premise no longer holds.

Shard sub-requests are interpolated a second time (and the test locks this in)

runShardSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already applies applyTemplateVariables to each target. splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes every shard sub-request to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), and this line interpolates those targets again. The updated shard test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times (1 for the original target plus 4 sub-requests), which confirms the double application, and the assertion makes it look intended. Template replacement is not idempotent: a substituted value containing a `$name` token gets expanded on the second pass. Ad hoc filters are also passed on every pass, and the shard path now forwards request.filters, which it did not do before. The interpolation should happen at one point, or sub-requests should bypass it through an option.

Empty-expression check runs before interpolation, so variables that resolve to empty still execute

The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs on the raw expression, but the emptiness that matters is the one after interpolation, which this PR now introduces. A query whose expr is a variable resolving to an empty string (e.g. `$query` with an empty value) passes the filter, is classified by isLogsQuery('') as a metric query, and is sent to the backend with an empty expression. The same ordering exists in shardQuerySplitting.ts lines 50-52. Moving the empty-expr filter after the map in both places would make the check match the interpolated value the PR is meant to use.

New test only checks the runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions the change is meant to fix

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only asserts that the expr and step passed to runQuery are interpolated. It does not exercise what interpolating first changes: the isLogsQuery partitioning, querySupportsSplitting (including the $__range guard), and the step/resolution grouping computed by calculateStep. There is no case where a variable expands into a logs query, a step variable drives grouping, or a $__range query stays unsplit. Those are the behaviors the PR is supposed to fix, and they are untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded by the controller filter, not by I18n.t

The translate override loads only `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)`). The fallback chain's other locales (the site default and :en) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, which is called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation made under `I18n.with_locale` outside a web request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers rendered in jobs, rake tasks) therefore has no guarantee that the fallback yml files are loaded. If the key is missing in the requested locale, the lookup falls back to a locale whose translations were never loaded and returns a 'translation missing' string. The fallback behavior depends on which entry point ran first, which is fragile.

Loading fallback locales does not invalidate the LRU translation cache

The cache at line 71 is keyed only on key, locale, and backend object_id, and is cleared only in `reload!`. Results now depend on which fallback locales are loaded and on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but neither is in the key. If a lookup runs before the fallback locale (e.g. :en) has been loaded, the 'translation missing' result is frozen into `@cache`. When `ensure_loaded!` later loads :en, that stale entry is still served for that locale until the process restarts. The same staleness applies when an admin changes `default_locale`, since cached fallback output for other locales is not recomputed.

Fallback chain is rebuilt and SiteSetting is read on every backend lookup

Fallbacks#translate in the i18n gem calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every backend translate, including the interpolated translations that bypass the LRU cache (`args.length > 0`). Each call reads `SiteSetting.default_locale`, calls `to_sym`, and allocates a new array with `uniq.compact`. This is a small per-translation cost on a hot path. Computing the chain once per locale, or caching it in the hash, would avoid it.

This PR changes locale resolution for the whole application: it adds a custom fallback order (user locale, site default, :en), a new `ensure_loaded!` path in the I18n accelerator, a new call in `set_locale`, and it removes `config.i18n.fallbacks` from three environment files. None of this is covered by a spec. Nothing checks that a missing key falls back in the expected order, that fallback locales get loaded, or that the behavior holds in production and profile environments after the config removal. Given the cache and loading issues above, targeted specs are needed before merge.

The feed poll needs its own global throttle or should not run inline per URL.

A retrieve job is enqueued on every request; the throttle only runs inside the job

When no topic exists, every request enqueues a retrieve_topic job, and the 60-second throttle is checked only when the job runs (topic_retriever.rb:27-28). Anonymous requests, and the loading page that reloads every 30 seconds, therefore create unbounded queue entries even when the URL was retrieved moments ago. The throttle check should happen before enqueueing, or duplicate jobs should be deduplicated.

PostCreator enqueues jobs inside an open transaction

PostCreator.create is called inside the outer Topic.transaction (line 21). PostCreator.create calls enqueue_jobs before returning, which queues process_post and feature_topic_users. Its own comment (post_creator.rb around line 290) says jobs must be enqueued after commit. With Sidekiq, a worker can start before this transaction commits and find no post, so the job silently does nothing. The TopicEmbed row is also created after those jobs are queued.

ALLOWALL is not a valid X-Frame-Options value

The only valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM. Browsers ignore unrecognized values, so this line only appears to allow framing by accident, and it overwrites any app-wide frame policy with a meaningless string. To allow framing, the header should be removed (for example response.headers.delete('X-Frame-Options')), not set to an invalid value.

Shipped migration now uses force: true, which drops an existing table

This changes an existing migration to create_table with force: true. If top_topics already exists with data in any environment where the migration version is not recorded (for example a database built from another branch), this migration drops the table and all its rows without warning. The flag is not needed for a table this migration is supposed to create for the first time and should be removed.

--category option removed with no replacement and no documentation

The method_option :category and its only use are deleted. Existing invocations that pass --category or -c now fail with an unknown-option error. The import also changes behaviour: the topic is now built by scraping the article with readability (TopicEmbed.import_remote) instead of a permalink post, and created_at is no longer set on the topic. The PR description is only 'Test 4', so none of this is documented.

Gate tests pass for the wrong reason; poll_feed itself is untested

feed_polling_enabled defaults to false (site_settings.yml). The 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples never enable feed_polling_enabled, so execute returns early at the first gate and the expectation holds regardless of the gate under test. Only the 'delegates' example enables all three, and it mocks poll_feed. The actual import loop, nil handling and failure behaviour have no coverage.

Protocol-relative URLs are rewritten to a wrong absolute URL

An href like //cdn.example.com/a.png starts with '/', so the sub(/^\/+/, '') strips both slashes and the result is prefix + '/cdn.example.com/a.png', i.e. http://host/cdn.example.com/a.png. The same problem exists for img src (line 71). Protocol-relative links should keep their host, or be resolved with URI.join against the article URL.

Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the posts table under lock

On PostgreSQL releases before 11, add_column with default: 1 and null: false rewrites the entire posts table while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a large forum this blocks all reads and writes to posts for the duration. The safer pattern is to add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then set the default and NOT NULL constraint.

setnx and expire are not atomic; a crash leaves the throttle key without a TTL

The key is set with setnx and then given a 60-second expiry in a separate command. If the process dies between the two, the key never expires and that embed URL is throttled permanently for non-staff users. A single atomic SET with NX and EX options would avoid this.

URL validation uses ^ instead of \A, so it matches any line

In Ruby, ^ matches at the start of any line. A value such as 'javascript:alert(1)' followed by a newline and 'http://x' passes this check. The later URI() call in absolutize_urls currently rejects it, so no harm follows, but the validation is ineffective and relies on an unrelated exception. The regex should be anchored with \A.

Test name says 404 but asserts only non-success; referer mismatch is untested

The example 'is 404 without an embed_url' does not set a host, so it fails on the host check and never exercises the missing-parameter path. It only asserts not-success, so it does not verify a 404. There is also no example for a referer whose host differs from embeddable_host, which is the main access check in ensure_embeddable.

Spec asserts raw HTML is stored and rendered verbatim

The assertion post.cooked.should == post.raw locks in the behaviour that imported content is stored as-is with no sanitization. Nothing tests escaping of the article URL in the footer, sanitization of feed or scraped HTML, the unchanged-content update path, or import_remote. The security-relevant paths of this feature are not covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

In Ruby the later definition replaces the earlier one, so the width/height form no longer exists. Any caller passing five arguments now gets ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments). Users can attempt uploads the site was configured to reject, and the 'file too large' message reports 10240 KB even when the configured limit is lower. Request-controlled 'type' ends up unquoted in a shell command via the tempfile name

For API URL uploads, the tempfile is created at line 55 with the name prefix 'discourse-upload-#{type}', where 'type' is the unvalidated params.require(:type) value. The new code passes tempfile.path to OptimizedImage.downsize, and convert_with (optimized_image.rb, around line 161) joins the instructions and runs them through backticks with the path unquoted. A 'type' containing shell metacharacters such as $(...), backticks, or ';' therefore becomes executed shell code. This is reached when an API caller uploads an image by URL that is larger than max_image_size_kb. It needs an API key, but it is still command execution that did not exist before this PR. The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times and ignores its return value. convert_with returns false (and swallows exceptions) on any failure, such as a missing binary, an unsupported format, or a corrupt file. After the loop there is no re-check of the size, so an image that is still above max_image_size_kb is passed to Upload.create_for as-is. The site's hard limit is therefore no longer enforced on the server. The input and output are also the same path, so a failed or partially written conversion overwrites the user's file with truncated data, and the next pass works on that damaged file. The download limit for API URL uploads changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to 10.megabytes. Two consequences. Second, if an admin raises max_image_size_kb above 10 MB, images between 10 MB and the new limit are rejected at download time (the rescue nil turns the failure into a nil tempfile), which is the opposite of what the feature is meant to allow. Derive the download cap from the setting, or justify the constant.

The animated branch in optimize is chosen by matching the GIF extension against 'from', which is the request tempfile path. Rack multipart tempfiles are typically created without the original extension, so the check fails for uploaded GIFs even when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. downsize_instructions then uses '#{from}[0]', which keeps only the first frame. The result is that an oversized animated GIF is silently reduced to a still image on upload. Determine animation from the original filename or from the file contents, and pass that decision explicitly.

The PR adds a server-side loop that rewrites uploaded files, changes the public OptimizedImage downsize/optimize API, and replaces the download and client size limits with constants. No specs were added or updated. The description is just 'Test 1'. Nothing covers an image above the limit being reduced below it, the loop giving up after five attempts, a failed convert, the GIF branch, or the duplicate downsize signature (which a spec calling the width/height form would have caught).

Synchronous API uploads run up to five full convert and optimize passes in the request

For synchronous API uploads, the request thread now performs up to five ImageMagick conversions, each followed by ImageOptim.optimize_image! (which runs several external optimizers), on an image up to the 10 MB download cap, before responding. Each pass rewrites the whole file. A single pass with a scale factor computed from the size ratio, or moving the reduction into the deferred job, would avoid this cost.

The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

The action mutates notification_level, but it is reachable via GET (config/routes.rb: `get 't/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe'` and `get 't/:topic_id/unsubscribe'`). Rails' forgery protection does not cover GET, so any page that embeds the URL (for example an img tag on another site) will mute a logged-in user's topic. Mail link scanners and prefetchers will also trigger the mutation without the user clicking. A state change like this should be a POST (with a GET confirmation page), or should use a signed token like the existing email/unsubscribe/:key flow.

Unsubscribe only steps watching/tracking down to regular, contradicting the email text

The email copy says 'You will stop receiving notifications for <title>', but for users at tracking or watching the action sets notification_level to regular. Regular still sends notifications for replies and mentions, so those users keep getting notified. Only users already at regular are muted. Either mute for every level or change the wording.

`user_id = user.is_a?(User) ? user.id : topic` falls back to `topic`, which is the topic id, instead of `user`. TopicsController calls `TopicUser.track_visit! topic_id, user_id` with integer ids, so `user_id` becomes the topic id. The update then hits (or creates) the topic_users row for whichever user has the same id as the topic, and the real user's last_visited_at is never recorded. This predates the PR, but the PR edits this same method (line 125), so the fix belongs in this change.

add_unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url or email building raises

The unsubscribe_link string now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}. html_part (line 67) and body (line 90) call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args), and template_args only contains unsubscribe_url if the caller passed it. Any caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link: true without unsubscribe_url, including plugins that use this public builder, will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument while building the email. Either default the URL in the builder or render the topic line only when the URL is present.

The diff rewrites the summary routes and drops `post_number: /<digits>/` from their constraints (both `t/:slug/:topic_id/summary` and `t/:topic_id/summary`). The unsubscribe feature has nothing to do with summary URLs, and the change is not mentioned. Either revert it or explain why it is safe, since the constraint's effect on a route with no post_number segment is not obvious.

The route is declared as a top-level `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', ...)`. The page could render blank or fall back to the application template. Either rename the template to match the route or nest the route under the topic resource as this.route('unsubscribe'). I have not verified the resolver behavior in the running app.

New unsubscribe action has no specs

Nothing covers the new action: the logged-out redirect, the 301 slug redirect that must happen before any state change, the notification_level transitions (tracking or watching to regular, regular to muted), or a missing TopicUser row. The message_builder_spec change only passes an extra argument and does not assert that the link appears in the body or HTML. A spec that re-reads the topic_user row after unsubscribe would have caught the auto-track persistence bug.

false_positives.candidate:

deleteCacheMutation's onSuccess (lines 42-46) only shows a toast and calls the parent's onSuccess (onChanged). Unlike disconnectMutation, it never invalidates trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, so the cacheUpdatedAt prop is not refreshed. The PR's own notes say the frontend reads CalendarCache.updatedAt and not SelectedCalendar.updatedAt, so this extra UPDATE has no consumer. It also changes the meaning of an existing column that is now selected into UserWithCalendars and the user session selects. Remove it, or justify it with a real consumer.

Adding the column with DEFAULT NOW() sets updatedAt for every pre-existing cache row to the deployment time. Immediately after deploy, the 'Last updated' label shows the deploy time for all Google calendars, even when the cached data is weeks old. Migration header warning contradicts the migration body

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, the same value as `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` never checks the slot's end. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past the end is accepted. With working hours ending at 17:00 and a 60-minute event, the 16:30 slot passes this check. The fixed host's own end boundary is only enforced here, so a fixed host can be booked beyond their hours in round-robin events, which is the scenario this PR is meant to fix.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `end` variable is mistakenly calculated using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime` when checking working hours.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length override check compares object references

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares object identity, which is always false for two distinct dayjs instances. The zero-length override early return is therefore dead code. It should use `.isSame(...)` or compare timestamps.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: using `===` to compare two `dayjs` instances checks object reference equality rather than value equality, which will always evaluate to false. Both suggest using the `.isSame()` method instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check

When a same-day date override exists and the slot lies inside it, execution reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. Existing bookings and calendar busy times are therefore ignored for every slot inside a date override window. Personal events are treated as fixed-host events (isFixed is true when there is no schedulingType), so this affects ordinary personal bookings too: a host with an override 14:00-18:00 who already has a 15:00 booking is still offered 15:00 and can be double-booked. The override should only replace the working-hours check; busy times must still be evaluated.

Split working hours on one weekday reject every slot

`workingHours.find(...)` returns the first entry for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is outside that entry. Working hours come one entry per availability row, so a host with two ranges on the same weekday (for example 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) has every slot outside at least one of those entries. Every slot on that day then hits `return false` at line 150. This check now runs for every fixed host, including personal events, so users with split days get no slots at all. The intended test is 'reject only if no entry contains the slot'. The test suite only uses single-row schedules, so this is not caught.

Override end check ignores slots that start inside the override but run past it

The override boundary test compares `slotStartTime` with the override end instead of `slotEndTime`. A slot that starts inside an override and extends beyond its end (override ends 18:00, 60-minute slot at 17:30) fails all three checks and falls through to `return true` at line 133. The fixed host is then treated as available for time after the override ends. The earlier check at line 119 does use the slot end, so the two checks are inconsistent.

Multiple date overrides on one day make every slot on that day unavailable

`dateOverrides.find` returns the first override whose callback returns truthy, and the callback returns true when the slot lies outside that override. With two overrides on the same date (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the availability UI supports as multiple ranges per date), a slot inside the first range is rejected because the second range reports it as outside, and the converse holds for the second range. Every slot on that day is therefore rejected. The correct semantics is 'available if inside at least one override on that day'. The flag `dateOverrideExist` is also mutated as a side effect inside the predicate, which relies on `find` short-circuiting and is fragile.

Same-day override check depends on the server process timezone

`dayjs(date.start)` is created in local mode, so `.add(...).format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's process timezone. `slotStartTime` is converted with `.utc()` and formats in UTC. On any server whose TZ is not UTC (developer machines, self-hosted deployments), the same-day comparison fails for overrides whose local date differs from the UTC date. The override is then not detected, and the slot falls through to the working-hours/busy logic, so date-override behaviour depends on where the process runs. The shifted value should be put in UTC mode before formatting.

Availability checks use eventType.length instead of the requested duration

`availabilityCheckProps.eventLength` is `eventType.length`, but slot generation at line 451 uses `input.duration || eventType.length`. For events with multiple duration options, the new working-hours and date-override checks compute the slot end from the wrong length, so a 60-minute booking is validated as a 30-minute one. This matters more now that these checks depend on the slot end.

Timezone conversions run inside the per-slot override loop

`dayjs.tz(...)` (which formats through Intl) is evaluated inside the `find` predicate for every override, for every slot, for every fixed host, although the offset depends only on the override. Over a long date range with many overrides this multiplies into a very large number of timezone conversions per getSchedule call. The override windows should be computed once per call.

Timezone-shifted override minutes drop the date and land on the wrong day across midnight

The converted override time is reduced to minute-of-day with `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding the timezone offset, which discards the date. When the shifted time crosses midnight, the slot is attributed to the wrong day. Example: an override 15:00-17:00 on Jan 10 for an organizer in America/New_York (stored as 15:00Z-17:00Z) and an invitee in Asia/Kolkata. The real slots are Jan 11 01:30-03:30 IST. The day filter at line 207 selects the override using the unshifted instant, which falls on Jan 10 IST, and line 219 yields 01:30. The slot is therefore offered (or later dropped by checkIfIsAvailable) on Jan 10, and the override never appears on Jan 11. The full converted timestamp should be computed and bucketed by its own date.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host override fix or for busy times on override days

The PR's headline fix (fixed-host date overrides constraining round-robin slots, and busy times on override days) has no test. The only added assertion is an invitee-timezone variant of an existing single-override scenario. Missing coverage: a round-robin event where a fixed host's override limits availability; an existing booking inside an override still blocking the slot (this would catch the busy-skip bug); split working hours on one weekday; two overrides on one date; and an override that shifts across midnight for an invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic is subtle and currently untested beyond the single happy path.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded DB update inside catch can abort the whole batch

The new `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` in the catch block has no try/catch, and it is not inside any outer try. Before this PR the catch only logged, so it could not throw. Now, if this update fails, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler rejects. The most plausible trigger is a reminder deleted after `findMany` (for example when its booking is cancelled, which makes Prisma throw P2025), or any transient DB error. The consequence is that every remaining reminder in the batch is skipped for this cron run and the response is an error instead of the normal success response. The increment should be guarded so one bad row does not stop processing of the rest.

Comment describes only the date-based deletion

The comment says this block deletes 'all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date'. After this PR the same `deleteMany` also deletes reminders whose retryCount is greater than 1, including unscheduled ones that failed twice. The comment is now wrong and does not explain the retry threshold either.

Reminders with no sendTo or empty message never accrue retries

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` (the else branch at line 178 and the catch block). If `sendTo` is null (for example an SMS_ATTENDEE step where `booking.smsReminderNumber` is missing) or the message is empty, nothing is scheduled and retryCount is not incremented. Such a reminder stays unscheduled and is reprocessed on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes, with the template/DB work repeated each time. This is the 'keep retrying until the date is reached' behavior the PR is meant to stop, and the PR leaves this path uncovered. Either count these as failed attempts or delete them explicitly.

OR with an unindexed retryCount predicate forces a full table scan

The new `OR` in deleteMany combines a predicate that uses the composite index `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` with `retryCount > 1`, which has no index (schema.prisma line 1000 adds the column without one). Postgres can only use a BitmapOr when every arm is indexable, so this cron query now falls back to a sequential scan of WorkflowReminder on every run. That table grows over time, so the cost increases with it. Consider an index on `retryCount` or splitting the delete into two queries.

Retry budget of two attempts is spent within a few cron ticks with no backoff

Each cron tick makes one attempt, and the row is deleted on the first tick after the second failure. Two failures can therefore occur only minutes apart, and a Twilio or network outage longer than that permanently drops the reminder with no log beyond a console line and no alert. The magic `gt: 1` also does not state the 'two failures' rule anywhere in code. The threshold or the lack of backoff should be a deliberate, documented choice.

No tests for the new retry and deletion behavior

The PR changes control flow in three places: failed scheduling increments retryCount, errors increment retryCount, and reminders with retryCount > 1 are deleted. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. A test that drives the handler with a mocked twilio.scheduleSMS returning null or throwing, and checks the retryCount updates and the deletion on the next run, would catch regressions such as the catch-block issue above.

getBaseConditions returns unparenthesized SQL that breaks precedence when composed

In two of the four branches, getBaseConditions returns authConditions or filterConditions as-is, without wrapping them in parentheses. Org and team auth conditions are top-level `(A) OR (B)` expressions, and the eventTypeId filter is also a top-level OR. Only the combined branch on line 73 wraps its parts. A caller that embeds this result next to other predicates, for example `WHERE ${base} AND status = ...`, gets SQL precedence `A OR (B AND status = ...)`. Rows that the org or team scope should exclude can then be returned. The fix is to wrap the returned fragment in parentheses in every branch so the method always yields one self-contained predicate.

Public findMany was removed; scope enforcement is no longer automatic

The public `findMany` method was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw SQL fragment. The old method applied the authorization and filter conditions as an AND on every query, so callers could not forget them. Callers now have to write their own `$queryRaw` and interpolate the fragment correctly. Nothing in this diff updates existing callers of `findMany`, so any remaining caller will fail to compile or will silently lose its scope restriction. Either keep a wrapper that always applies the conditions, or update all call sites in this PR.

Constructor options type no longer enforces teamId for team scope

The constructor's `options` parameter changed from the discriminated-union type `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the flat `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional for every scope. Code that passes `scope: 'team'` without `teamId` now type-checks. At runtime safeParse fails, `this.options` becomes null, and the service silently returns NOTHING (`1=0`) with no error. The compile-time check for team scope is lost. The constructor should keep the discriminated-union type.

PR description says only tests changed, but the service is rewritten

The description says the change only updates the integration tests and that the service was 'previously converted'. The diff rewrites the whole service: it removes findMany, adds getBaseConditions, changes SQL construction for org, team and filter conditions, changes the constructor option type, and changes isOrgOwnerOrAdmin. Reviewers following the description will not look at the service changes, which are the high-risk part. The description should list the service behavior changes.

Caching tests were deleted without replacement

The `Caching` describe block (cache authorization conditions, cache filter conditions) was removed and not replaced. The memoization in getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions still exists. The filter cache also stores null, which depends on the `=== undefined` check, and nothing covers that path now. The deletion is not mentioned in the PR description. The tests should be restored and adapted to Prisma.sql.

Org and team scope SQL is only checked as strings, never executed

The org and team scope tests compare the generated SQL template and parameter arrays for equality. Only the user scope is run against BookingTimeStatusDenormalized through $queryRaw. The AND/OR structure of the org and team conditions, which the PR description names as the high-risk part, is never executed. A wrong operator or a missing parenthesis would only show up in a live query. The tests should run org and team scope conditions against the view and assert which bookings are returned, including a booking from another team that must be excluded.

Zoom and Google route refreshed tokens through parseRefreshTokenResponse so the sync endpoint only needs to return an access token and expiry. Webex does not. When a provider returns invalid_grant, the code sets credential.invalid = true (googlecalendar, webex, zoom and invalidateCredential). This handler replaces the key with freshly synced tokens but never resets invalid. A credential flagged invalid therefore stays invalid after the self-hoster pushes working tokens, and any code path that skips invalid credentials keeps skipping it. The shared secret is compared with the !== operator, which short-circuits on the first mismatched character and can leak timing information about the secret. The outbound POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no shared secret or signature, so the endpoint cannot verify that the request came from this instance. At minimum add tests for refreshOAuthTokens in both modes and for parseRefreshTokenResponse's return shape.

The legacy provider should set Constants.GRANT_TYPE as well, or the gap should be documented.

Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed, so they can be replayed

isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code is in the stored list and never removes or marks it as used. The core RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (lines 80-92) decides when to retire the credential and force regeneration solely from the credential's allCodesUsed() state. For a federated credential that state is rebuilt from the raw stored list by getCredentials (new model, no used-state), so allCodesUsed() can never become true. The result is that a recovery code which logged a user in once keeps working indefinitely, while the local provider consumes codes. Nothing in the core flow writes used-state back to user storage either. The new test performs only one successful login and never attempts a second use, so this goes undetected.

Recovery codes are sent to user storage in plaintext while local storage keeps only hashes

generatedCodes are the raw codes shown to the user. They are serialized to JSON and passed unhashed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), so any external user storage provider (LDAP, a custom DB) persists usable bearer login secrets. The local path stores only RS512 hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). A read of the external store therefore yields directly usable recovery codes, and the test provider compares raw strings. Either hash the codes before handing them to user storage (and hash the input on verification) or explicitly document and accept the difference.

New recovery-codes test covers only the happy path

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes, logs in once with code 0 and stops. It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused (which the user-storage path currently fails, see the isValid comment), that the stored codes are visible through the account/admin credential APIs (the new getCredentials override is not exercised), or that the local fallback still works when a storage provider does not support recovery codes. The reuse gap in particular is exactly what this test should catch.

getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser

getMyUser(user) returns null when the user is not in the users map, and getCredentials immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp with no null check. The sibling methods getDisableableCredentialTypesStream and isConfiguredFor guard against this case, so this one throws NullPointerException where the others return empty results.

supportsCredentialType throws NPE for a null type

The previous implementation was null-safe (CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(null) and isOTPType(null) return false). The new clause credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) is evaluated for a null argument and throws NullPointerException instead of logging and returning false. Comparing against the constant (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)) would avoid this.

Recovery codes in user storage cannot be disabled or listed as disableable

disableCredentialType only handles OTP and logs 'Unsupported' for anything else, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream never includes the recovery type. Admin disable-credential requests for a federated user therefore silently leave the stored recovery codes in place, and the admin API does not offer them as disableable. The local path supports revoking these codes, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the feature being added.

userLabel and generatedAt are silently dropped in the user-storage branch

The credentialModel passed in carries the user-provided userLabel and the generatedAt timestamp, and the local branch persists them. The user-storage branch builds only a UserCredentialModel from the type and the JSON codes, so these values are discarded. The test provider then stamps createdDate with the current time and has no label. Users who set a label or check creation dates will see different metadata depending on where the codes ended up, without any indication.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

Per-client resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104) via resourceStore.create(...) without setting a type, so they never match the type filter. Only the all-clients resource matches, because init() sets its type. Consequence: when the scope is granted on all clients, the method adds the resource name "Clients" to the result as if it were a client id, and no individual client id is ever returned. The candidate matches the underlying issue even though it does not explicitly mention the downstream realm.getClientById failure.

Consequences: creating a client permission fails with ModelException("No scopes found.") (line 108), and getScope() throws 'Scope [...] does not exist'. It also recommends a null check, matching the golden comment despite including broader migration concerns.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative per-client VIEW policy cannot hide a client from an admin with all-clients VIEW

canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() (the all-clients VIEW check) succeeds, before evaluating the client's own resource. Every other per-client check goes through hasPermission(client, ...), which uses the per-client resource when it exists and so honours negative policies. The user resource tests (testViewUserPermission) expect a per-object negative policy to override an all-objects positive permission. Here, an admin with all-clients VIEW and a NEGATIVE VIEW policy on a specific client still sees and can GET that client, and it still appears in listings. The short-circuit should be removed or the per-client result should take precedence.

Deleting any client fails when both fine-grained feature flags are enabled

The ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException (ClientPermissionsV2.java line 193). The listener is gated only on the V1 flag, but evaluator()/management() prefer V2 whenever the V2 flag is set, so the two flags can coexist. In that configuration every client deletion propagates the exception and fails. The V2 implementation should be a no-op here, or the event handler should skip V2.

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2, which throws UnsupportedOperationException from canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, the *Permission(...) factories, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource and getPermissions. Before this PR, V2 mode used the V1 ClientPermissions implementation for these calls, which returned values instead of throwing. Any caller that reaches these methods in V2 mode now gets an uncaught exception, which surfaces as a 500 rather than a denial. canExchangeTo is the most exposed: it is part of the evaluator contract and is used by client-to-client token-exchange logic. getEvaluationContext (line 262) is an unused private helper that looks intended for canExchangeTo, so the method seems to have been left unfinished.

getResourceName special-cases only USERS. For CLIENTS it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). That value is never set for per-client resources, which are named by the client UUID (line 104), and it is also unset for the all-clients 'Clients' resource. The result is null for client permissions. The USERS branch returns 'All users' for the type resource and the username for a user resource. The CLIENTS equivalents (an 'All clients' label and the client's clientId) are missing.

The Javadoc for requireView() reads 'Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.' The method is void and is meant to throw ForbiddenException when canView() returns false. The same mistake appears on requireViewClientScopes() (line 101). Implementers reading this doc, including the V2 class, could easily get the contract backwards.

Nothing exercises canManage/canView(ClientScopeModel), MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, getClientsWithPermission, or a NEGATIVE per-client policy overriding an all-clients permission. The getClientsWithPermission type-filter bug and the canView short-circuit would both have been caught by tests of these paths.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting any group fails when V2 admin permissions are enabled

The GroupRemovedEvent listener calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) for every group removal. In V2 mode management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, which now returns GroupPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled (GroupPermissionsV2 lines 173-175) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The listener runs on every group deletion, whether or not the realm uses fine-grained admin permissions. Before this PR, V2 used the V1 GroupPermissions, where this call was a no-op for realms without permissions. MgmtPermissionsV2 did not override groups() before this PR, so V2 realms used the V1 GroupPermissions for group management permissions. The PR replaces that with GroupPermissionsV2, where isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource and the *Permission accessors all throw UnsupportedOperationException. GroupResource.getManagementPermissions and setManagementPermissionsEnabled reach these, so the endpoints return HTTP 500 in V2 mode. This is a regression for groups, and the PR does not document it or gate the endpoints with a clear error.

When requester != null, the evaluation context is built with new UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), i.e. the impersonated target user. The IMPERSONATE scope is an admin-side permission, and the requester==null path (line 70) evaluates with the admin's identity. The two paths therefore disagree. The target-identity context was copied from V1 isImpersonatable(), which uses it for the USER_IMPERSONATED scope, where it is correct. Here, user or role policies that should match the admin (or the requesting client via kc.client.id) are checked against the victim user, so canClientImpersonate/canImpersonate(user, client) can deny legitimate impersonation or match on the wrong identity.

The previous code computed canView() once and skipped per-group checks when it was true. Now filter(groupsEvaluator::canView) calls canView(group) for every group. In V2, canView(group) runs hasPermission, which resolves the per-group resource and evaluates the authorization policy engine each time, or falls back to the all-groups resource. For admins with global view, listing N groups costs N policy evaluations instead of one. GroupResource.getSubGroups has the same change.

A negative assertion (create top-level group with only all-groups VIEW gets FORBIDDEN) is needed. Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances, encode rBigInteger and sBigInteger, and discard the results. The returned DER comes only from the writeDerSeq call below. The dead statements suggest the values feed into the output when they do not, and they should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify redundant ASN1Encoder instances whose encoded results are discarded, while the returned DER is produced separately by the subsequent encoding operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method on the public CryptoProvider SPI breaks existing implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside the three in-repo providers, including third-party or downstream ones, will stop compiling. If it is compiled against an older interface, it fails at runtime with AbstractMethodError when order() is called during provider sorting. A default implementation would keep existing providers loading, while the in-repo providers keep their explicit overrides.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the backward-compatibility risk of adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider, which breaks existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Providers with equal order() are picked arbitrarily, silently bypassing the old single-provider guard

The old code threw when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and takes the first element. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200 in this PR, so a tie is possible. Ties are then resolved by ServiceLoader/classpath order, which is not a defined contract. If a FIPS deployment has both the FIPS and the default (or elytron) provider jar on the classpath, the non-FIPS provider can be selected with no error. The only trace is a debug log line. The removed guard existed to prevent exactly this. Equal top-order providers should still fail fast, or the FIPS provider should be given a strictly higher order.

AuthzClient.create() installs a process-wide, one-shot crypto provider visible only to its own classloader

CryptoIntegration.init() is global and idempotent: it only runs detection while cryptoProvider is null, and later calls are no-ops. Here it is called with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(), so only providers visible from that loader are considered. If the real provider (Default, Elytron or FIPS) is only visible through another classloader, or is initialized later with a different loader, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider stub becomes the provider for the whole JVM and stays there. Every later crypto call then fails with UnsupportedOperationException. Before this PR, authz-client did not touch global crypto state at all. Consider not initializing global state from client construction, or only doing so when no provider has been set.

Most CryptoProvider methods are placeholder stubs throwing 'Not supported yet.'

getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getOCSPProver, getIdentityExtractorProvider, createECParams, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getSignature, wrapFactoryForTruststore and ECDSACryptoProvider.getPublicFromPrivate all throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."). This provider is registered through the service file and is selected whenever it is the only provider present. Any code path that reaches one of these methods then fails with a message that names nothing useful. The class Javadoc ("Simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client") does not mention these gaps. Document the supported operations, and make each unsupported operation name itself in the exception, or remove stubs that cannot be reached.

ECDSA conversion test is only a self round-trip, and uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512

The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. It checks the two conversions only against each other, so a shared encoding mistake (wrong DER SEQUENCE or INTEGER layout, for example) passes unnoticed. The produced DER is never checked with the JDK's Signature.verify. The key is also always generated as P-256 (KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")), so the ES384 and ES512 cases run with 32-byte R/S values padded to 48 and 66 bytes, not the real curve sizes. Verify each DER signature with the JDK verifier, and use P-384 and P-521 keys for ES384 and ES512. The 33-byte leading-zero INTEGER case should also be covered deterministically.

integerToBytes silently truncates over-long DER integers instead of rejecting them

When the decoded INTEGER has more bytes than the field length (qLength < bytes.length), the code keeps only the trailing bytes and discards the high-order ones. A malformed or non-canonical DER integer, for example r with an extra leading 0x01 byte, is turned into a different, valid-looking concatenated signature instead of an IOException. Verification then depends on the JDK rejecting the altered value. The conversion should check that the value fits in qLength bytes, allowing only a single leading zero.

Indefinite-length marker reaches new byte[-1] and throws an unchecked exception

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length marker 0x80. readInteger() passes that value straight to read(), where new byte[length] throws NegativeArraySizeException. The decoder's contract reports malformed DER through IOException, which the callers declare, so malformed input to asn1derToConcatenatedRS escapes as a RuntimeException. readNext() has the same problem. readLength should reject negative lengths with an IOException.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing group now yields null count while sibling paths throw IllegalStateException

For a group deleted concurrently, getSubGroupsCount now silently returns null (line 275). In the invalidated path, isUpdated() at lines 73-74 throws IllegalStateException("Not found in database") for the same situation, so the class handles concurrent deletion inconsistently. A null Long is also not a count, so any caller that unboxes the result (for example, comparing it with > 0) will still throw NullPointerException. The change moves the NPE rather than defining the contract for a missing group.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: getSubGroupsCount() returns null, which is not a valid count and can cause NullPointerExceptions when callers unbox it. Although it emphasizes inconsistent missing-group handling rather than explicitly citing the Javadoc contract, it matches the golden concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is not joined before the assertion, and not stopped on failure

The reader thread (lines 139-149) is never joined. The assertion at line 157 runs right after deletedAll.set(true) at line 155, so any exception from a read still in flight when the flag is set is never checked, and the test can pass despite an NPE. Also, the flag is set only on the happy path. If remove() at line 153 throws, deletedAll is never set, the reader loops forever against the server on a non-daemon thread, and the test fails without cleanup. Wrap the deletions in try/finally that sets the flag and joins the thread before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: the reader thread is not joined before asserting, so exceptions from in-flight reads after deletedAll is set can be missed. The additional failure-cleanup concern does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Same concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the paged/searched subgroup methods

The fix only guards getSubGroupsCount(). Three sibling methods still dereference modelSupplier.get() without a null check: getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(firstResult, maxResults) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, firstResult, maxResults) at line 268. If the group was deleted concurrently, isUpdated() is false (the adapter was not invalidated), modelSupplier.get() returns null, and the call throws NullPointerException. This is the same race the PR claims to fix, so the issue is only partially resolved.

Parent lookup can return null and is then dereferenced in the hierarchy builder

At line 47 parentModel comes from session.groups().getGroupById(...) and can be null if the parent was deleted concurrently. It is then used unguarded: at line 51 in canView(parentModel) when admin permissions are disabled; at line 57 in toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full) when the parent is not yet in the map; and at line 60 in populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent), which calls group.getSubGroupsCount() whenever subGroupsCount is true, even when the parent was already in the map. Each of these is an NPE in the same concurrent-access scenario the PR targets. The PR edits this file (only removing an unused helper) but does not add a null check here.

getAttributes and getSubGroups lack the null-supplier guard that getRoleMappings has

getRoleMappings (lines 70-76) returns an empty set when the group supplier is null, with a comment about groups not being loaded. getAttributes (lines 66-68) and getSubGroups (lines 90-92) pass the supplier straight to DefaultLazyLoader. If the group has been deleted and the value is not yet loaded, the loader will call methods such as source.getAttributes() or source.getSubGroupsStream() on null. This reaches GroupAdapter.getAttributes, getFirstAttribute, getAttributeStream and getSubGroupsStream() (line 240) through the same concurrent-deletion race, and the PR does not guard it. This assumes the loader dereferences the supplied source without a null check, which the guard in getRoleMappings suggests.

Test depends on timing and does not deterministically reproduce the NPE

The NPE is a race between a group lookup and a concurrent deletion. The test only has a chance to catch it if the reader thread happens to hit the window while groups are being removed. It can pass on unfixed code, and nothing targets getSubGroupsCount or the subgroup overloads specifically. A deterministic regression test, for example a run-on-server test that obtains a group adapter, deletes the group in another session, and then calls getSubGroupsCount and getSubGroupsStream, would show the fix works and would cover the other unguarded paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets are passed straight to queryset slicing and raise

On the enable_advanced_features branch, `start_offset = cursor.offset` can be negative and is used in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet does not support negative indexing and raises ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any cursor with a negative offset produces a 500. The cursor comes from the client-supplied query string, so an admin can trigger this by crafting a cursor. The comments at lines 876 and 878-879 say Django 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this grants access 'beyond normal pagination bounds'; both claims are false, and the advertised behavior never works.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: negative cursor offsets are used to slice a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative slicing and raises an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError on every non-empty datetime page

get_item_key copies the numeric logic from Paginator: `value = getattr(item, self.key)` followed by `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)`. The endpoint sorts by `-datetime`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime.datetime. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls this key on the first result whenever a page has any rows (via _build_next_values), so with `?optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access user, every non-empty audit log page returns a 500. DateTimePaginator avoids this by converting to a millisecond timestamp. value_from_cursor here also returns the raw cursor integer, which build_queryset would compare against a datetime column even if the key function worked. The optimized path is unusable as written.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime value because the audit logs endpoint orders by -datetime, causing a TypeError. Its additional observations do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared BasePaginator silently clamps negative next-page offsets, leaving cursor arithmetic inconsistent

For next-page cursors, the query now starts at max(0, offset), but build_cursor still receives the raw negative cursor.offset. When the key value is unchanged, _build_next_values computes next_offset = offset + limit from the negative value. The returned page therefore starts at row 0 while the next cursor is computed as if it started at a negative position, so consecutive pages can overlap. Before this change such cursors raised an error; now they return wrong pages silently. BasePaginator is shared by DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other endpoint using them, so this changes behavior well beyond the audit log endpoint. The change is also not a performance optimization, and no tests cover it.

Advanced pagination gated on bare User.is_superuser instead of an active superuser session

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` checks the User model flag directly. Sentry gates superuser behavior on an active superuser session (is_active_superuser(request)), so this bypasses the session-level elevation check. It also introduces a new authorization decision (superuser or global-access member unlocks a different paginator and negative-offset handling) outside the endpoint's permission class, controlled by a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter.

New pagination path and gating logic have no tests and the PR description is empty

The PR adds a new paginator class, a new query-parameter switch, a superuser/global-access gate, and changes to the shared BasePaginator offset handling, but adds no tests. The description is just 'Test 1'. A single test requesting `optimized_pagination=true` with a non-empty audit log would have exposed the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key. Tests should also cover negative cursor offsets, permission gating for non-admin members, and the unchanged default DateTimePaginator behavior.

Performance claims in comments are not backed by any change in query behavior

The comments describe the optimized path as 'high-performance' and 'efficient browsing of large audit datasets'. For non-negative offsets the optimized path issues the same queryset, ordering and slice as DateTimePaginator, and it adds no index, query or caching change. The only behavioral difference is the negative-offset path, which crashes. The comments and the PR title overstate what the change does.

Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but this diff changes no code here

The only change in Cursor.__init__ is a comment saying it 'allows negative offsets' and 'enables efficient reverse pagination'. The code (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged and already accepted negative values before this PR. Rejection of negative offsets happens in the paginators, so the comment describes a behavior that does not come from this line and misleads readers about where the behavior lives.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key with no dedupe

The whole-function lock was the only serialization in BuildIndex. GetIndex returns nil for concurrent first requests, so each one runs a full ListIterator build. For file-backed indexes (size above FileThreshold), two builds now call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time (line 98). Previously the second build ran after the first and failed cleanly on the existing path. Now the two can interleave on-disk creation and fail or leave a bad store. For memory indexes, the second build replaces the first in the cache, orphaning it, and the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double counted. Add a per-key guard (the TODO in search.go mentions this) or re-check the cache under the lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing the BuildIndex lock permits multiple goroutines to build the same expensive index concurrently for the same key. The candidate adds potential consequences without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without the lock, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. This PR adds a new caller of TotalDocs in init (search.go line 216), which runs right after the watch goroutine has started. That goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex, then build, then BuildIndex, and write b.cache concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error that cannot be recovered. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while the newly started watcher goroutine can trigger concurrent BuildIndex writes, potentially causing a fatal concurrent map iteration/write error.

false_positives.candidate:
Build errors in init's errgroup closures are shared-variable races and can be silently dropped

The errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` (declared at line 181) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` from up to `initWorkers` goroutines at once. The closure then does `return err`, which reads that shared variable, so a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build's nil. `init` then reports success while a namespace is missing from the index. `totalBatchesIndexed++` is also an unsynchronized write (lost updates, and the race detector flags it). This now runs inside NewResourceServer, which the code comments say must block startup on failure, so a swallowed error means a silently incomplete index. Use a closure-local error and an atomic counter.

Watch loop dereferences nil event when the events channel is closed, causing a panic

The loop does `v := <-events` and passes `v` to handleEvent without checking whether the channel is open. The SQL poller does `defer close(stream)` when the backend is stopped (b.done). After that, every receive yields nil, and handleEvent immediately reads `evt.Type` (line 226), which panics with a nil pointer dereference. The same pattern in server.go initWatcher (`v.Type` on a possibly nil v) panics too. The watch context is context.Background(), so this loop never exits on its own. Use `v, ok := <-events` and return when ok is false.

Writes made during the initial index build are never indexed

init lists and builds each namespace first, and only afterwards calls WatchWriteEvents. The SQL WatchWriteEvents takes its starting point from the latest resource versions at subscription time (listLatestRVs), so any write committed after a namespace was read but before the subscription is never delivered to the index. The object stays missing from search until it is modified again. This PR makes the build window longer, since the whole build for all namespaces now runs synchronously at construction. The rv returned by build (line 309 onward) is computed for exactly this purpose but discarded here. Subscribe first, build, then replay events with a resource version above each namespace's list version.

Construction now performs DB init, full index build and watcher start synchronously, and can fail

NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle Init (DB open and ping), the full search index build for every namespace above the threshold, and starts the watcher. Any error makes construction fail. Previously this work happened on first RPC, so construction was cheap and a failure only affected calls. The consequences: the caller (module wiring) blocks for the entire build with no timeout (only Stop cancels, and that is not reached during startup); one bad namespace or a transient DB error prevents the whole storage module from starting; and any code that constructs a server before its DB or blob dependencies are ready now fails at construction. The PR asks what this could break, but the diff shows no update to callers and no bounded context for the build. This needs an explicit decision.

Stop no longer gates RPCs, since the Init calls that returned the stop error were removed

Stop stores 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped' in s.initErr. Before this PR every RPC called s.Init, which returned that stored error, so calls after Stop failed fast. This PR removes every s.Init call from the handlers, so nothing reads initErr anymore. After Stop, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List and Search keep reaching the backend. backend.Stop only cancels the poller and does not close the DB. This silently removes the shutdown guard. If it is still needed, check a stopped flag in the handlers or in a shared helper.

Error path after the new Init call leaks started resources

If any step after the new Init call fails, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel. The lifecycle backend may already be initialized, and search init may already have started the event goroutine (search.go line 207), which loops on a context.Background() watch forever. Nothing calls Stop on the discarded server. Call s.cancel() and the lifecycle Stop on the error path.

Span context is still discarded in WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator

The PR is described as fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down, but this file still discards the span context in WriteEvent (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` followed by `b.create(ctx, event)`). ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) do the same. The WriteEvent span is therefore not the parent of the create, update or delete spans, and the DB spans attach to the request instead. Only GetResourceStats was fixed here. Use `ctx, span :=` in these functions.

Postgres skip disables the storage-server startup test without a tracked issue or mention in the description

A postgres branch is added that skips the only test in this file covering the storage-server startup path this PR changes. The skip has a TODO and no tracking issue, and the PR description does not mention disabling it. If construction-time init broke postgres startup, that regression is now hidden rather than fixed. Either fix the test or document the skip with an issue link in the description.

No tests cover the new construction-time failure and concurrency behaviour

The PR changes several behaviours without adding tests: NewResourceServer now returns an error when lifecycle init or the index build fails, RPCs no longer gate on initialization, and the BuildIndex lock was removed. Nothing checks that a failing index build makes NewResourceServer return an error, which would have caught the lost-error race in search.go. Nothing exercises concurrent BuildIndex and TotalDocs under the race detector, which would catch the cache races above.

test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue expects an occurrence whose fingerprint does not match the evaluated group key

Occurrences are produced to Kafka before detector state is committed

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`to_dict()` puts a raw datetime into a dict passed as a Celery task argument
