The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. false_positives.candidate:
Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition

get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing

Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order

The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers

The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s

The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.

The per-segment key type changes from a Redis SET to a sorted set: sadd becomes zadd here, sscan becomes zscan in _load_segment_data, and sunionstore becomes zunionstore in add-buffer.lua. The key names (span-buf:s:{...}) are unchanged and segment keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after, old-version SET keys still exist. New code then hits WRONGTYPE on zadd, on zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin inside the Lua script, and on zscan in the flusher. redis-py pipelines raise on command errors, so process_spans fails for any batch touching a legacy key, and flush_segments can fail for every segment in the same batch. When a member (same payload) already exists in set_key and is also in the source key, for example a redelivered span, its score becomes the sum of two end timestamps (about 3.4e9) instead of end_timestamp_precise. zpopmin uses these scores to choose which spans to evict, so eviction order is corrupted. The same problem applies at line 53 for the parent key. Use AGGREGATE MAX or MIN so scores remain timestamps.

The glossary says span-buf:s:* keys are 'the actual set keys', and the flow above says payloads are added to 'the set'. After this change these keys are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, which is what the eviction and flush logic depends on. The docs should say so.

The PR's purpose is eviction above 1000 spans, but no test inserts more than 1000 spans or checks which spans survive. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, so waiters redo the full load

After Lock() at line 48, the function unconditionally reads and parses assets-manifest.json and then overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. It does this even when a goroutine that held the lock just before has already populated the cache. On a cold start, or after a failed load, N concurrent requests queue on the write lock and each performs the full file read and JSON decode, one after another. The redundant work existed before this change, but the lock now serializes it, so request latency grows with the number of waiters. Re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock in the non-dev case would complete the double-checked pattern that the RLock fast path starts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify incomplete double-checked locking in GetWebAssets: the cache is checked under a read lock but not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing waiting goroutines to redundantly reload assets even if another goroutine has populated the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Dev mode now serializes every request through the exclusive lock

When cfg.Env == setting.Dev, the RLock fast path at lines 45-47 is never taken, so every GetWebAssets call acquires the exclusive write lock at line 48 and holds it across the file open, JSON decode and cache write. Concurrent dev-mode requests that previously ran in parallel are now fully serialized. The impact is limited to local development, but the change in concurrency behaviour is not mentioned and could be avoided by only taking the write lock when a reload is actually needed.

No regression test for the concurrent access fix

The change fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. The race is only detectable by calling GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines under `go test -race`. A test that uses a temporary static root with a valid assets-manifest.json, runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev configurations, and checks the cache behaviour would prevent a regression. Without it, removing the RWMutex would not be caught by CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:

The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of n IDs costs O(n^2) bytes copied and allocated. With the batch size used in the new 40003-annotation test (32767), the final string is roughly 200KB and the loop copies several GB per batch, repeated for every batch and every annotation type. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice.

One bind parameter per ID breaks large batch sizes on MySQL and PostgreSQL

The non-SQLite branch sends one bind parameter per ID. Previously the batch size was a literal in the LIMIT clause and could be any value. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that now makes the DELETE fail on every cycle, and the diff adds no upper bound on the setting. The SQLite workaround only covers SQLite. Either cap the batch size or split the DELETE into statements of bounded parameter count.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

recordStorageDuration is called with name where every other call passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new label value and a new time series that stays in the metrics registry for the life of the process. On a long-running server this grows metric cardinality and memory without bound.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

The legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The request context is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after the unified-storage write completes. The legacy Create therefore almost always sees context.Canceled, the legacy copy is never written, and the only trace is a metric. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The detached goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a background context) before applying the timeout.

Legacy write failures in mode 3 are counted but never logged

In Create the goroutine stores the legacy error in errObjectSt and only records a duration metric; no log line is emitted. Update (line 140), Delete (line 113) and DeleteCollection (line 166) have the same gap. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Since the async legacy write is now the only safety net, failures become invisible except as a counter with no object name or error text, so diverged objects cannot be identified.

Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric

In Create, when the unified-storage write fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage errors are counted against the legacy series and the storage error metric is not updated. Update (line 129) makes the same mistake. Dashboards and alerts comparing the two stores will report wrong numbers.

DeleteCollection records legacy results under the storage metric

The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy results are counted as storage results, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection calls.

Legacy create mutates the same object the storage write used, racing with the response

The goroutine passes obj, the same pointer given to Storage.Create at line 42, to Legacy.Create while the handler continues to serialize the returned object. Legacy create paths typically assign UID, creationTimestamp and other metadata to the object in place. If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

Mode 3 update no longer sends the legacy store the object unified storage persisted

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. Now the raw objInfo is passed to Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated again against the legacy store's own copy. For patch and apply requests the legacy result can differ from what unified stored. Any resourceVersion precondition is checked against the legacy RV, which differs from the unified RV, so legacy updates can fail with a conflict. Both outcomes are silent (see the logging finding), so the two stores can silently diverge.

Dry-run requests are still dispatched to the legacy store

Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection never check options.DryRun before spawning the legacy write. A dry-run request is meant to have no side effects. Unified storage honors it, but the legacy call is dispatched unconditionally with the same options, and this file does not rely on the legacy store honoring DryRun. The legacy goroutine should be skipped when len(options.DryRun) > 0.

One unbounded goroutine per write, not tracked and not drained on shutdown

Each successful write spawns a goroutine that holds the request object and options until the legacy call returns. There is no bound on in-flight legacy writes. Nothing waits for them on shutdown, and Destroy (line 172) calls Legacy.Destroy while those goroutines may still be using Legacy. A slow legacy store causes goroutines and retained objects to grow with the write rate.

Update doc comment describes the old synchronous ordering

The comment says Update writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage, which implies the legacy write is part of the synchronous call. It is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine and its errors are not returned. The Create comment (line 35) also does not say that the legacy write is asynchronous and best-effort, which callers need to know.

Legacy writes in mode 3 are never verified by the tests

Each success case sets up a legacy expectation (for example here), but nothing asserts that it was called: there is no AssertExpectations and no wait for the goroutine. Legacy and storage also share one mock object (lines 53-54 construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock with the same m), so a legacy call would satisfy a storage expectation with the same method name and arguments. A regression that never calls Legacy, or calls it with the wrong object, passes these tests. Since asynchronous legacy behavior is the point of mode 3, tests should wait for the legacy call and check it against a separate legacy mock.

List test is named as 'not implemented' although List is implemented

The case name says listing 'is not implemented', but this PR implements List by calling Storage.List. The case only checks that an error returned by the storage mock is propagated. The name should describe that, for example 'error when listing from the unified store fails'.

New mode 3 subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes

The new mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, which reads the legacy API right after k8s writes (getFromBothAPIs at lines 535 and 547, and later). With legacy writes now fire-and-forget, those reads race the goroutine and nothing waits for convergence. The subtests can be flaky, or fail deterministically if the legacy write fails (see the cancelled-context finding). The legacy-visibility checks should poll (for example with require.Eventually), or the test should document why these reads are unaffected in mode 3.

go.work.sum gets unrelated checksum entries and a duplicated line

The change adds checksums for modules unrelated to mode 3 (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporter and SDK versions, genproto rpc). This suggests a dependency tool was run and its output was committed. The github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery /go.mod line is also added even though an identical line already appears as context just above it, so it is duplicated. The unrelated lines should be reverted and the duplicate removed, or the PR should explain why they are needed.

None of the tests exercise the real decisions, including the skipToken/non-Grafana case where Duplicate is incorrectly allowed, or the federated check that was dropped.

The header comment describes this file as a copy of RuleActionsButtons.tsx with only the View button removed. After this change it takes promRule, uses useGrafanaPromRuleAbility and getEditableIdentifier, and has different identifier and provenance logic, so it has diverged. The stale comment will mislead maintainers about which file to change.

$__range guard now checks the interpolated expression and can be silently bypassed

querySupportsSplitting() is documented (lines 285-286) as refusing to split queries containing `$__range`, because `$__range` must be resolved on the backend against the split time range. This change interpolates templates at the start of runSplitQuery (line 299), so the guard on line 287 now tests the already-interpolated expression. If template replacement resolves `$__range` (it does when request.scopedVars carries `__range`), the token is gone, isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false, and queries like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` get split into chunks. Their results then no longer match what the guard was meant to protect. No test in the diff covers a `$__range` query, so this regression would not be caught. The guard should check the pre-interpolation expression, and the comment at lines 285-286 needs updating since its premise no longer holds.

runShardSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already applies applyTemplateVariables to each target. splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes every shard sub-request to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), and this line interpolates those targets again. The updated shard test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times (1 for the original target plus 4 sub-requests), which confirms the double application, and the assertion makes it look intended. Template replacement is not idempotent: a substituted value containing a `$name` token gets expanded on the second pass. Ad hoc filters are also passed on every pass, and the shard path now forwards request.filters, which it did not do before. The interpolation should happen at one point, or sub-requests should bypass it through an option.

The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs on the raw expression, but the emptiness that matters is the one after interpolation, which this PR now introduces. A query whose expr is a variable resolving to an empty string (e.g. `$query` with an empty value) passes the filter, is classified by isLogsQuery('') as a metric query, and is sent to the backend with an empty expression. The same ordering exists in shardQuerySplitting.ts lines 50-52. Moving the empty-expr filter after the map in both places would make the check match the interpolated value the PR is meant to use.

New test only checks the runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions the change is meant to fix

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only asserts that the expr and step passed to runQuery are interpolated. It does not exercise what interpolating first changes: the isLogsQuery partitioning, querySupportsSplitting (including the $__range guard), and the step/resolution grouping computed by calculateStep. There is no case where a variable expands into a logs query, a step variable drives grouping, or a $__range query stays unsplit. Those are the behaviors the PR is supposed to fix, and they are untested.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, so concurrent new devices can exceed the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices (line 110) and compares with the limit (line 115), then runs the upsert (lines 120-155) with no transaction or lock. Many concurrent logins from new devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of stored devices can exceed deviceLimit by up to the concurrency level. The check-and-insert needs to be atomic, for example in one transaction with a conditional insert, or the overshoot must be documented as acceptable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit without a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device is cached as tagged before the DB write, so a limit-rejected device is admitted on its retry

tagDeviceUI sets the local cache key (line 87) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice returns that error, and Authenticate rejects the login. The cache entry is not removed, so it stays for 29 minutes. The next request from the same device ID hits the cache check at lines 83-85, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and the anonymous login succeeds without the device ever being stored or counted. The same happens after any transient DB error. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or deleted when the write fails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, and an ErrDeviceLimitReached failure leaves the cache entry intact, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Requests without the device ID header are never counted or limited

TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent (lines 120-122). Authenticate only fails on ErrDeviceLimitReached, so an anonymous request that omits the header is neither stored nor rejected, and the limit does not apply to it. The header is client-supplied, so clients can also rotate IDs to get fresh slots. Before this change, tagging was only analytics and this gap did not matter. Now the feature is meant to enforce a limit, so the missing-header case should either be rejected while the limit is active or be documented as outside the limit.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, off the request path. Now Authenticate calls it synchronously with the request context and no timeout. Each first request per device per instance performs a DB write during login, and when a limit is configured each new device also runs a COUNT over the updated_at range (database.go line 110). Slow DB calls now delay or block anonymous page loads, and the panic recovery from the goroutine is gone. The limit-enforcement design needs the synchronous write, but the cost on the hot path, including the uncached COUNT, should be assessed.

No tests cover the Authenticate path, the cache interaction, or updates to existing devices at the limit

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device. Nothing tests that a rejected device retried within the cache window is still rejected, which would have caught the cache bypass in impl.go. Nothing tests that Authenticate returns the error to the caller, or that an existing device still gets its updated_at refreshed (the updateDevice path) once the count has reached the limit. The new enforcement behaviour is therefore only covered at the store level.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented

The device_limit key is read here, but the PR changes no configuration documentation such as conf/defaults.ini or the docs for the [auth.anonymous] section, so operators have no way to learn that the key exists, that 0 means unlimited, or how the 30-day window counts devices. The PR description is also still the unfilled template, including the docs and feature-toggle checklist items.

Dependency injection signature changed; wire files are not part of this diff

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB and builds the store itself, and anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64 that no provider in the graph supplies. If the wire provider set (wire.go or wire_gen.go) still binds anonstore.AnonStore or lists ProvideAnonDBStore, wire generation or compilation will fail. Those files are not in the changed list, so this should be checked.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded by the controller filter, not by I18n.t

The translate override loads only `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)`). The fallback chain's other locales (the site default and :en) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, which is called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation made under `I18n.with_locale` outside a web request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers rendered in jobs, rake tasks) therefore has no guarantee that the fallback yml files are loaded. If the key is missing in the requested locale, the lookup falls back to a locale whose translations were never loaded and returns a 'translation missing' string. The fallback behavior depends on which entry point ran first, which is fragile.

Loading fallback locales does not invalidate the LRU translation cache

The cache at line 71 is keyed only on key, locale, and backend object_id, and is cleared only in `reload!`. Results now depend on which fallback locales are loaded and on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but neither is in the key. If a lookup runs before the fallback locale (e.g. :en) has been loaded, the 'translation missing' result is frozen into `@cache`. When `ensure_loaded!` later loads :en, that stale entry is still served for that locale until the process restarts. The same staleness applies when an admin changes `default_locale`, since cached fallback output for other locales is not recomputed.

Fallback chain is rebuilt and SiteSetting is read on every backend lookup

Fallbacks#translate in the i18n gem calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every backend translate, including the interpolated translations that bypass the LRU cache (`args.length > 0`). Each call reads `SiteSetting.default_locale`, calls `to_sym`, and allocates a new array with `uniq.compact`. This is a small per-translation cost on a hot path. Computing the chain once per locale, or caching it in the hash, would avoid it.

No specs for the new fallback chain, ensure_loaded!, or the set_locale change

This PR changes locale resolution for the whole application: it adds a custom fallback order (user locale, site default, :en), a new `ensure_loaded!` path in the I18n accelerator, a new call in `set_locale`, and it removes `config.i18n.fallbacks` from three environment files. None of this is covered by a spec. Nothing checks that a missing key falls back in the expected order, that fallback locales get loaded, or that the behavior holds in production and profile environments after the config removal. Given the cache and loading issues above, targeted specs are needed before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

They reach the 'grafana-data-egress' event only if (a) ConcreteLogger.FromContext renders contextual attributes from ctx, and (b) ContextualLoggerMiddleware is ordered outside LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. The comment 'returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context' is the New() description. For a nonexistent or already-deleted id, `host.host =` (line 23) or `host.destroy` (line 16) raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a 404. true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
record_for_host does not downcase the input before comparing to lower(host)

The query is `lower(host) = ?` against the URI host, but the input is never downcased. Any mixed-case host fails to match a stored host. Callers include TopicRetriever#invalid_host?, which passes the raw embed_url param (only TopicEmbed normalizes URLs), so an embed_url with an uppercase host is treated as not embeddable and never retrieved. Downcase the host before the lookup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-normalization bug: record_for_host compares lower(host) to an input parameter that is not downcased, causing mixed-case hosts to fail matching.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy host values are copied without normalization or SQL escaping

Values from the old embeddable_hosts setting are inserted verbatim. EmbeddableHost's before_validation strips the scheme and path, and the old allows_embeddable_host? accepted entries like 'https://example.com/1234' (it parsed them with URI). Migrated rows keep those prefixes, so EmbeddableHost.record_for_host, which compares lower(host) to a bare hostname, never matches them. Embeds for those sites silently stop working after upgrade. The value is also interpolated into SQL without escaping, so a host containing an apostrophe aborts the migration. Trailing '\r' from CRLF input is also kept. Normalize each entry (strip scheme, path, whitespace, and '\r') and use bound parameters.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core issue: raw SQL migration bypasses EmbeddableHost normalization, preserving schemes and paths that prevent migrated hosts from matching bare-host lookups. Its additional SQL escaping and whitespace concerns do not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

Fabrication loads every file, so specs still run. true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration aborts when no embed_category row matches, which is the common case

The category lookup `execute(...)[0]['id']` assumes at least one row. The query only matches when site_settings.embed_category holds the name of an existing category. Most installs never set that setting (its default is empty), so the result is empty, `[0]` is nil, and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError. The migration fails on upgrade. The intended fallback to the uncategorized category (`if category_id == 0`, line 14) can never run: it would need a matched row with id 0, and the crash happens first. The uncategorized lookup on line 15 also indexes `[0]['value']` without checking for rows.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unchecked execute(...)[0]['id'] access, which crashes when no embed_category setting matches a row. The candidate adds context about upgrade failure and the unreachable fallback but describes the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
No uniqueness validation or unique index on host

Nothing prevents two rows with the same host, case-insensitively or otherwise. The migration adds no unique index and the model has no validates_uniqueness_of. record_for_host (line 17) calls .first with no ORDER, so if duplicates exist with different categories, the category assigned to imported topics is arbitrary. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness validation and a unique index on lower(host).

category_id is never checked against an existing category

`belongs_to :category` does not verify that category_id points to a real category, and the table has no foreign key. The admin controller passes through any integer (app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb line 24). Deleting a category, or saving a bad id, leaves a host pointing at nothing. TopicEmbed.import then passes that id to PostCreator, so new embed topics get a dangling category. Validate that the category exists.

_ids sideloading yields undefined entries and throws on null

_hydrateEmbedded now maps every *_ids array through _lookupSubType. If the referenced collection is absent from the payload, _lookupSubType returns undefined for each id, and the result is an array of undefined entries. The `hydrated || []` fallback on line 200 never applies because map always returns an array, so the undefined entries survive. The embedding template then renders a row per entry. Separately, `obj[k].map` throws when the _ids value is null. Previously *_ids keys were ignored entirely, so a single null field now breaks hydration of the whole record. Filter out missing entries and guard null before mapping.

Admin CRUD endpoints have no behavioral tests

The only spec asserts that the controller subclasses Admin::AdminController. Nothing covers create, update, or destroy; the category default to uncategorized (controller line 25); the response for an unknown id; validation failures; or the staff-only filter. embedding_controller_spec.rb has the same single inheritance assertion. A regression in the endpoints the admin UI depends on would pass CI. Add request specs for each action, including the failure paths.

PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a silent no-op

`update` renders the current embedding without reading params or saving anything, so the endpoint returns success while changing nothing. The client saveChanges action (admin-embedding controller) calls it with update({}), but the template has no save button, so the action is dead and the endpoint is misleading. Either implement the update or remove the route and the client action.

Hosts saved with a port can never match

The format validator on line 2 explicitly allows an optional :port, and before_validation keeps it. But record_for_host compares against uri.host, which never includes a port. An entry like example.com:8080 is accepted by validation and can never match a referer or embed_url. Either reject ports in validation or compare host and port together.

Host validation rejects TLDs longer than five letters

The regex requires the TLD to be `[a-z]{2,5}`. That rejects valid hosts such as example.technology, example.community, or example.international, and any host without a dotted TLD such as localhost. This is a new validator on a new table, so it blocks legitimate entries that the old free-text setting accepted.

Feed-imported topics lose their category, with no default left to configure

Previously every imported post was placed in SiteSetting.embed_category. That setting is removed here (site_settings.yml, server.en.yml, and the migration's DELETE). TopicEmbed.import now takes the category only from a matching EmbeddableHost. import is also reached from feed polling and import_remote, which do no host check. Feed-imported topics whose URL host is not registered silently land in the uncategorized category, and no admin setting remains to define a default. This is a behavior regression that should be called out or handled.

Failed host deletion gives no feedback

delete() calls destroyRecord().then(...) with no catch. Every other request in this component uses popupAjaxError (see save on line 40). If the delete fails (for example a 403 or 500), the promise rejection is unhandled, the user sees nothing, and the row stays in the list. Add .catch(popupAjaxError).

Test named for embeddable host checks behavior that no longer exists

expandable_first_post? no longer reads embeddable hosts, so the test 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' passes only because the built topic has no TopicEmbed row (has_topic_embed? is false for an unsaved topic). It does not exercise host presence at all, and no test replaces the old 'hosts disabled' coverage. The nested describe on the following lines is also misspelled ('emeddable').

find embedded test changed to id 2, but the fixture always returns fruit 1

The test now calls store.find('fruit', 2), but the /fruits/:id pretender route in create-pretender always returns fruits[0] (apple, id 1), ignoring the id. The assertions therefore check apple's colors. Changing the id suggests coverage of the banana record (color_ids [3]) that does not exist. Either make the fixture honor the id or revert the id to 1.

When cook_method is raw_html, cook returns the raw text unchanged, skipping the markdown pipeline, any sanitizer and the after_post_cook plugin filters. Imported content (RSS items via PollFeed, scraped pages via TopicEmbed.import_remote) is stored this way (topic_embed.rb:22), and PostCreator accepts cook_method from any caller's options with no whitelist (post_creator.rb:216). The cooked value is then emitted unescaped: embed/best.html.erb:19 uses 'raw post.cooked', and normal topic views render cooked as HTML. Any markup that reaches a raw_html post, such as a script tag in a feed item, runs as stored XSS on the forum's own origin for every visitor. Remote HTML needs sanitizing before it is stored as cooked.

RSS and Atom descriptions are almost always entity-escaped (a script tag appears as <script>). After CGI.unescapeHTML those entities become real markup. The result is saved with cook_method raw_html (topic_embed.rb:22) and rendered unescaped (see post.rb:133 and embed/best.html.erb:19), so any feed item can inject script into the forum for all visitors. Escaped content should stay escaped, or be sanitized, never unescaped.

Unauthenticated requests can trigger a full feed download and reimport each time

The throttle is keyed on the full embed_url (lines 26-28). Only the host must match embeddable_host, so a client can vary the path or query string to get a fresh key every time. Each new key then calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute here, which downloads the entire feed and re-imports every item (poll_feed.rb:29, 31-36). The feed fetch and the readability fetch (topic_embed.rb:48) use open() with no timeout. An attacker can therefore keep Sidekiq workers busy with unbounded outbound fetches and DB writes. The feed poll needs its own global throttle or should not run inline per URL.

A retrieve job is enqueued on every request; the throttle only runs inside the job

When no topic exists, every request enqueues a retrieve_topic job, and the 60-second throttle is checked only when the job runs (topic_retriever.rb:27-28). Anonymous requests, and the loading page that reloads every 30 seconds, therefore create unbounded queue entries even when the URL was retrieved moments ago. The throttle check should happen before enqueueing, or duplicate jobs should be deduplicated.

PostCreator.create is called inside the outer Topic.transaction (line 21). PostCreator.create calls enqueue_jobs before returning, which queues process_post and feature_topic_users. Its own comment (post_creator.rb around line 290) says jobs must be enqueued after commit. With Sidekiq, a worker can start before this transaction commits and find no post, so the job silently does nothing. The TopicEmbed row is also created after those jobs are queued.

Shipped migration now uses force: true, which drops an existing table

This changes an existing migration to create_table with force: true. If top_topics already exists with data in any environment where the migration version is not recorded (for example a database built from another branch), this migration drops the table and all its rows without warning. The flag is not needed for a table this migration is supposed to create for the first time and should be removed.

The method_option :category and its only use are deleted. Existing invocations that pass --category or -c now fail with an unknown-option error. The import also changes behaviour: the topic is now built by scraping the article with readability (TopicEmbed.import_remote) instead of a permalink post, and created_at is no longer set on the topic. The PR description is only 'Test 4', so none of this is documented.

feed_polling_enabled defaults to false (site_settings.yml). The 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples never enable feed_polling_enabled, so execute returns early at the first gate and the expectation holds regardless of the gate under test. Only the 'delegates' example enables all three, and it mocks poll_feed. The actual import loop, nil handling and failure behaviour have no coverage.

An href like //cdn.example.com/a.png starts with '/', so the sub(/^\/+/, '') strips both slashes and the result is prefix + '/cdn.example.com/a.png', i.e. http://host/cdn.example.com/a.png. On a large forum this blocks all reads and writes to posts for the duration. The safer pattern is to add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then set the default and NOT NULL constraint.

The key is set with setnx and then given a 60-second expiry in a separate command. If the process dies between the two, the key never expires and that embed URL is throttled permanently for non-staff users. A single atomic SET with NX and EX options would avoid this.

In Ruby, ^ matches at the start of any line. A value such as 'javascript:alert(1)' followed by a newline and 'http://x' passes this check. The later URI() call in absolutize_urls currently rejects it, so no harm follows, but the validation is ineffective and relies on an unrelated exception. The regex should be anchored with \A.

Nothing tests escaping of the article URL in the footer, sanitization of feed or scraped HTML, the unchanged-content update path, or import_remote. true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, the same value as `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` never checks the slot's end. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past the end is accepted. With working hours ending at 17:00 and a 60-minute event, the 16:30 slot passes this check. The fixed host's own end boundary is only enforced here, so a fixed host can be booked beyond their hours in round-robin events, which is the scenario this PR is meant to fix.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the end time is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, causing the working-hours boundary check to validate the slot start rather than its actual end.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length override check compares object references

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares object identity, which is always false for two distinct dayjs instances. The zero-length override early return is therefore dead code. It should use `.isSame(...)` or compare timestamps.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that === compares dayjs object references rather than date values, causing the equality check to fail, and recommend .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check

When a same-day date override exists and the slot lies inside it, execution reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. Existing bookings and calendar busy times are therefore ignored for every slot inside a date override window. Personal events are treated as fixed-host events (isFixed is true when there is no schedulingType), so this affects ordinary personal bookings too: a host with an override 14:00-18:00 who already has a 15:00 booking is still offered 15:00 and can be double-booked. The override should only replace the working-hours check; busy times must still be evaluated.

Split working hours on one weekday reject every slot

`workingHours.find(...)` returns the first entry for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is outside that entry. Working hours come one entry per availability row, so a host with two ranges on the same weekday (for example 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) has every slot outside at least one of those entries. Every slot on that day then hits `return false` at line 150. This check now runs for every fixed host, including personal events, so users with split days get no slots at all. The intended test is 'reject only if no entry contains the slot'. The test suite only uses single-row schedules, so this is not caught.

Override end check ignores slots that start inside the override but run past it

The override boundary test compares `slotStartTime` with the override end instead of `slotEndTime`. A slot that starts inside an override and extends beyond its end (override ends 18:00, 60-minute slot at 17:30) fails all three checks and falls through to `return true` at line 133. The fixed host is then treated as available for time after the override ends. The earlier check at line 119 does use the slot end, so the two checks are inconsistent.

Multiple date overrides on one day make every slot on that day unavailable

`dateOverrides.find` returns the first override whose callback returns truthy, and the callback returns true when the slot lies outside that override. With two overrides on the same date (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the availability UI supports as multiple ranges per date), a slot inside the first range is rejected because the second range reports it as outside, and the converse holds for the second range. Every slot on that day is therefore rejected. The correct semantics is 'available if inside at least one override on that day'. The flag `dateOverrideExist` is also mutated as a side effect inside the predicate, which relies on `find` short-circuiting and is fragile.

Same-day override check depends on the server process timezone

`dayjs(date.start)` is created in local mode, so `.add(...).format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's process timezone. `slotStartTime` is converted with `.utc()` and formats in UTC. On any server whose TZ is not UTC (developer machines, self-hosted deployments), the same-day comparison fails for overrides whose local date differs from the UTC date. The override is then not detected, and the slot falls through to the working-hours/busy logic, so date-override behaviour depends on where the process runs. The shifted value should be put in UTC mode before formatting.

Availability checks use eventType.length instead of the requested duration

`availabilityCheckProps.eventLength` is `eventType.length`, but slot generation at line 451 uses `input.duration || eventType.length`. For events with multiple duration options, the new working-hours and date-override checks compute the slot end from the wrong length, so a 60-minute booking is validated as a 30-minute one. This matters more now that these checks depend on the slot end.

Timezone conversions run inside the per-slot override loop

`dayjs.tz(...)` (which formats through Intl) is evaluated inside the `find` predicate for every override, for every slot, for every fixed host, although the offset depends only on the override. Over a long date range with many overrides this multiplies into a very large number of timezone conversions per getSchedule call. The override windows should be computed once per call.

Timezone-shifted override minutes drop the date and land on the wrong day across midnight

The converted override time is reduced to minute-of-day with `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding the timezone offset, which discards the date. When the shifted time crosses midnight, the slot is attributed to the wrong day. Example: an override 15:00-17:00 on Jan 10 for an organizer in America/New_York (stored as 15:00Z-17:00Z) and an invitee in Asia/Kolkata. The real slots are Jan 11 01:30-03:30 IST. The day filter at line 207 selects the override using the unshifted instant, which falls on Jan 10 IST, and line 219 yields 01:30. The slot is therefore offered (or later dropped by checkIfIsAvailable) on Jan 10, and the override never appears on Jan 11. The full converted timestamp should be computed and bucketed by its own date.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host override fix or for busy times on override days

The PR's headline fix (fixed-host date overrides constraining round-robin slots, and busy times on override days) has no test. The only added assertion is an invitee-timezone variant of an existing single-override scenario. Missing coverage: a round-robin event where a fixed host's override limits availability; an existing booking inside an override still blocking the slot (this would catch the busy-skip bug); split working hours on one weekday; two overrides on one date; and an override that shifts across midnight for an invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic is subtle and currently untested beyond the single happy path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

Only the SMS path increments the column today, so the practical impact is currently small, but the delete condition is broader than the stated intent and will cause data loss once another channel uses the column. The branch should be scoped as `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` plus `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing WorkflowMethods.SMS filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion OR branch, which allows non-SMS reminders to be deleted. The candidate's additional impact qualification does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded DB update inside catch can abort the whole batch

The new `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` in the catch block has no try/catch, and it is not inside any outer try. Before this PR the catch only logged, so it could not throw. Now, if this update fails, the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler rejects. The most plausible trigger is a reminder deleted after `findMany` (for example when its booking is cancelled, which makes Prisma throw P2025), or any transient DB error. The consequence is that every remaining reminder in the batch is skipped for this cron run and the response is an error instead of the normal success response. The increment should be guarded so one bad row does not stop processing of the rest.

The comment says this block deletes 'all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date'. After this PR the same `deleteMany` also deletes reminders whose retryCount is greater than 1, including unscheduled ones that failed twice. The comment is now wrong and does not explain the retry threshold either.

Reminders with no sendTo or empty message never accrue retries

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` (the else branch at line 178 and the catch block). If `sendTo` is null (for example an SMS_ATTENDEE step where `booking.smsReminderNumber` is missing) or the message is empty, nothing is scheduled and retryCount is not incremented. Such a reminder stays unscheduled and is reprocessed on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes, with the template/DB work repeated each time. This is the 'keep retrying until the date is reached' behavior the PR is meant to stop, and the PR leaves this path uncovered. Either count these as failed attempts or delete them explicitly.

The new `OR` in deleteMany combines a predicate that uses the composite index `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` with `retryCount > 1`, which has no index (schema.prisma line 1000 adds the column without one). Postgres can only use a BitmapOr when every arm is indexable, so this cron query now falls back to a sequential scan of WorkflowReminder on every run. That table grows over time, so the cost increases with it. Consider an index on `retryCount` or splitting the delete into two queries.

Retry budget of two attempts is spent within a few cron ticks with no backoff

Each cron tick makes one attempt, and the row is deleted on the first tick after the second failure. Two failures can therefore occur only minutes apart, and a Twilio or network outage longer than that permanently drops the reminder with no log beyond a console line and no alert. The magic `gt: 1` also does not state the 'two failures' rule anywhere in code. The threshold or the lack of backoff should be a deliberate, documented choice.

The PR changes control flow in three places: failed scheduling increments retryCount, errors increment retryCount, and reminders with retryCount > 1 are deleted. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. A test that drives the handler with a mocked twilio.scheduleSMS returning null or throwing, and checks the retryCount updates and the deletion on the next run, would catch regressions such as the catch-block issue above.

In two of the four branches, getBaseConditions returns authConditions or filterConditions as-is, without wrapping them in parentheses. A caller that embeds this result next to other predicates, for example `WHERE ${base} AND status = ...`, gets SQL precedence `A OR (B AND status = ...)`. Rows that the org or team scope should exclude can then be returned. The fix is to wrap the returned fragment in parentheses in every branch so the method always yields one self-contained predicate.

The public `findMany` method was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw SQL fragment. The old method applied the authorization and filter conditions as an AND on every query, so callers could not forget them. Callers now have to write their own `$queryRaw` and interpolate the fragment correctly. Nothing in this diff updates existing callers of `findMany`, so any remaining caller will fail to compile or will silently lose its scope restriction. Either keep a wrapper that always applies the conditions, or update all call sites in this PR.

sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type disableStandardEmails settings

Every other send function in this file takes `eventTypeMetadata` and checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata and always emails the organizer, team members, and attendees. Event types that disable standard emails will still send 'guests added' emails. The handler also does not pass the event type metadata.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor EventType metadata disableStandardEmails flags, causing host and attendee emails to be sent even when standard emails are disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update runs with the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

The EventManager is built from `ctx.user` and that user's credentials. But `booking.references` and the destination calendar belong to the organizer (`booking.userId`). When the caller is a team admin or a matching attendee rather than the organizer, `updateCalendarAttendees` uses the caller's calendars against the organizer's calendar event, so the new guests are not added to the organizer's calendar or the update fails. The handler already loads `booking.user` with `credentials: true` (line 38) and never uses it.

Guests are committed to the DB before the calendar update, with no rollback

The attendees are written at line 92, then `updateCalendarAttendees` runs at line 165 outside any transaction. If the calendar call throws, the new attendee rows stay in the database, the mutation returns an error, and the notification emails at line 168 are never sent. On retry, the same guests now match existing attendees and the request fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid', so the state cannot be repaired from the UI. The calendar update and notifications need to be ordered or wrapped so a failure does not leave partial state.

Email failure is swallowed with a plain console.log and the error object is dropped

The catch block logs a fixed string with `console.log` and ignores `err`. The cause of a failed notification is lost, and the mutation still reports 'Guests added'. The error should be logged with the project logger and the error object included.

No booking status or time check; guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings

After loading the booking, the handler checks only permissions. It does not reject cancelled or rejected bookings, or bookings that have already ended. The UI only offers the action for confirmed upcoming bookings, but the API accepts any booking id. A request for a cancelled booking still writes attendees, updates the calendar event, and sends 'guests added' emails for an event that is no longer happening.

Unbounded guest list enables email spam to all attendees and the organizer

`guests` has no max length, and no rate limit applies. Every successful call sends an email to every existing attendee and the organizer (and team members). Any user who passes the permission check can add an arbitrary number of guests in one call and repeat the call, causing mass invitations sent from the platform. The handler's attendee branch (line 52 of addGuests.handler.ts) also lets any booking attendee, not only the organizer or an admin, trigger this. A maximum array size and a per-booking attendee cap should be enforced.

New guest records are assigned the organizer's timezone and locale

Each new attendee is stored with `timeZone: organizer.timeZone` and `locale: organizer.locale`. The guest's real timezone and locale are unknown, but these values are persisted as if they were the guest's, and later drive how that guest's emails and calendar invites are rendered. Storing a neutral default or leaving the value unset would be more accurate.

Error message is misleading when guests are filtered out as existing or blacklisted

When every submitted guest is already an attendee or is blacklisted, the handler throws 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' ('Emails must be unique and valid'). That text describes a format or duplicate-input error, not 'these addresses are already on the booking' or 'these addresses are blocked'. Blacklisted entries that are mixed with valid ones are dropped silently with no indication to the caller.

No tests for addGuests authorization, filtering, or notification logic

The new handler has a non-trivial permission matrix (organizer, team admin/owner, attendee), a filtering step (existing attendees, blacklist, duplicates), and a calendar and email side effect. None of it is covered by a test in this PR. The inverted admin/owner condition noted above is the kind of bug a basic handler test would catch.

Fallback error message is unreachable and the error text includes the raw error code

`message` is a template string that always contains a non-empty `${err.data?.code}: ...` prefix, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back. The user also sees raw codes such as 'FORBIDDEN: you_do_not_have_permission' or 'BAD_REQUEST: ...'. The fallback should be applied to the translated message, not to the concatenation.

Dialog state persists across open/close, so a stale validation error and old entries reappear

`isInvalidEmail` is set to true on a failed client validation, but `onSuccess` never resets it. Closing the dialog through Escape or the overlay (`onOpenChange={setIsOpenDialog}`) also skips the reset in the Cancel button, so the old emails and the error message remain. When the dialog is reopened, the user sees the stale error and previously entered addresses, which can then trigger the duplicate error on a retry.

Hardcoded English tooltip string bypasses i18n

The remove-email tooltip uses the literal string "Remove email" instead of `t(...)`, so it is not translated, even though this component already uses `t` for its other labels.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use is not enforced atomically

Consumption is a read-decrypt-null-encrypt-write sequence with no transaction or compare-and-set on backupCodes. Two concurrent logins with the same valid code can both read the unconsumed array (line 139), both pass the indexOf check, and both write back, so one backup code yields two sessions. The whole-array write can also resurrect codes that a concurrent disable (which sets backupCodes to null) just cleared. Use a conditional update (for example, compare the old encrypted value in the WHERE clause and check the updated row count) or a transaction with row locking.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: non-atomic backup-code consumption allows concurrent logins using the same code to both succeed, violating one-time-use semantics. The candidate's additional concern and remediation do not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login skips the password check whenever totpCode is non-empty

The password is only verified when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch (line 131) runs whenever `credentials.backupCode` is non-empty, regardless of totpCode. A request that sends email, a valid 10-character backup code, and any non-empty totpCode is authenticated without the password, and the TOTP is never checked either. The login UI clears totpCode in lost-access mode, but the NextAuth credentials endpoint can be called directly. The TOTP branch already has the same password-skip pattern, but this PR adds a second path that needs only the backup code. Password verification should run for CAL users in every branch, so that the backup code or TOTP is an additional factor rather than a replacement for the password.

Backup codes can be dismissed without being saved; 2FA is left enabled with the UI out of sync

The codes are shown only in the DisplayBackupCodes step, which is reached after the enable endpoint has already set twoFactorEnabled=true. The Dialog still receives `onOpenChange`, so Escape, an overlay click, or the X button closes the modal without calling `onEnable` or the 'Close' button. The codes are never rendered again and there is no endpoint to retrieve or regenerate them, so they are lost. The parent is not notified that 2FA is on, so its switch stays unchecked. Toggling it again then fails in setup with TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled. If the authenticator is later lost, the user has no recovery path. The step should ignore dismissal (or require an explicit acknowledgement), and the dismissal path should still notify the parent.

Users who arrive via external-provider TOTP cannot use backup codes

When totpEmail is set (2FA for a Google/SAML sign-in), the footer is only ExternalTotpFooter (Cancel), so there is no 'Lost access' action. The server also blocks backup-only submissions for non-CAL users: in authorize, the ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled check (next-auth-options.ts line 113) fires whenever totpCode is empty. A CAL user who has backup codes and then signs in with Google using the same email goes through loginWithTotp, so they can never use their backup codes and have no recovery path besides their authenticator. Either expose backup codes in this flow and allow a backupCode to satisfy the non-CAL check, or document the limitation.

tabIndex=-1 removes keyboard access to the password visibility toggle in every PasswordField

This change is unrelated to backup codes but applies to the shared PasswordField component used across the app. Setting tabIndex to -1 makes the show/hide button unreachable by Tab, so keyboard-only users cannot reveal a password they are typing. This is an accessibility regression. Drop the change or justify it separately.

No tests exercise backup-code login, backup-code disable, or single-use consumption

The new server logic (backup-code branch in authorize, backup-code branch in disable.ts, code consumption, MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode errors) has no test coverage. The PR checklist says no tests were added, and the only addition is a TODO. The enable/disable e2e flow only checks the download, copy, and close buttons. A regression in backup-code verification or single-use enforcement would go unnoticed, and the password-bypass issue above would not be caught. Add tests for: login with a valid code (consumed afterwards), reuse of a consumed code, wrong code, and disable with a backup code.

Password visibility toggle does nothing because the caller's type="password" overrides PasswordField's type

PasswordField renders `<InputField type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"} ... {...props} />`, so props spread after the computed type. Passing `type="password"` here (replacing the former TextField) forces the input to stay masked. The eye button toggles its icon and label, but the field never shows the password. Remove the explicit type prop.

Assertion is vacuous: expect(promise).toBeTruthy() always passes

`isChecked()` returns a Promise, so `expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` checks that a Promise object is truthy and always succeeds. The FIXME above it acknowledges this. The PR edits this block but keeps the vacuous check, so the enable test does not verify the switch state. Use `await expect(page.locator(...)).toBeChecked()`.

missing_backup_codes text tells locked-out users to generate codes in settings, which is not possible

The message 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' is shown on the login page, where the user is not authenticated. There is no 'generate' action in settings: codes are created only by disabling and re-enabling 2FA, which itself needs a password and TOTP or a backup code. The message points users to a non-existent action.

Copy button reports success without awaiting the clipboard write

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast is shown immediately. If the write is rejected (permissions, insecure context), the user still sees 'Backup codes copied!' and the rejection is an unhandled promise rejection. Await the write inside try/catch and show an error toast on failure.

Submitting an empty backup code in lost-access mode fails silently

With an empty backupCode and empty totpCode, authorize() skips the backup branch and throws SecondFactorRequired. The client handler then calls setTwoFactorRequired(true), which is already true, so nothing changes and no error is shown. The HTML required attribute is disabled by noValidate, and the zod schema does not cover backupCode. Validate that backupCode is non-empty before submitting, or show an error when this case occurs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

Webhook payload destinationCalendar changes shape and empty value is inconsistent

Object-literal import() calls still load every app eagerly, so nothing is lazy

Deferred loading needs thunks (e.g. `googlecalendar: () => import("./googlecalendar")`) with callers invoking them. The PR description gives no goal, so it is unclear whether the intent was laziness. Also, a module whose import rejects produces an unhandled rejection at load time unless that key is awaited, rather than an error at the lookup site.

Previously a synchronous throw from getCalendar inside this forEach propagated and failed the mutation. Now getCalendar is async, so the error is returned from the discarded async callback and becomes an unhandled promise rejection while the mutation reports success. Recurring-cancel calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

Their results and errors are dropped and failures become unhandled rejections. The PR rewrote the sibling non-recurring loop in the else branch to for...of with await but left this one as forEach(async); it should be converted the same way.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the pending deletions

On the paid-cancellation path, `await apiDeletes;` does not wait for the promises inside the array. The handler returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' before calendar and video deletions settle, and their rejections are unhandled. This is pre-existing, but the PR touches these calls and the async change makes the difference observable. Use `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)` if the deletions are meant to complete before responding.

getCalendarCredentials still calls the now-async getCalendar without await

Only getConnectedCalendars currently remembers to await `item.calendar`; any other consumer that uses the field as a Calendar will get undefined methods or a Promise where a value is expected. The PR adds no tests or test updates covering what happens when credential or app lookup or CalendarService construction throws during cancel, reschedule, or video deletion. Those error paths are exactly what changed, so they should have coverage.

CryptoIntegration.init() is global and idempotent: it only runs detection while cryptoProvider is null, and later calls are no-ops. Here it is called with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(), so only providers visible from that loader are considered. If the real provider (Default, Elytron or FIPS) is only visible through another classloader, or is initialized later with a different loader, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider stub becomes the provider for the whole JVM and stays there. Most CryptoProvider methods are placeholder stubs throwing 'Not supported yet.'

getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getOCSPProver, getIdentityExtractorProvider, createECParams, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getSignature, wrapFactoryForTruststore and ECDSACryptoProvider.getPublicFromPrivate all throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."). Any code path that reaches one of these methods then fails with a message that names nothing useful. The class Javadoc ("Simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client") does not mention these gaps. The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. The produced DER is never checked with the JDK's Signature.verify. The key is also always generated as P-256 (KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")), so the ES384 and ES512 cases run with 32-byte R/S values padded to 48 and 66 bytes, not the real curve sizes. true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

The endpoint sorts by `-datetime`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime.datetime. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls this key on the first result whenever a page has any rows (via _build_next_values), so with `?optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access user, every non-empty audit log page returns a 500. DateTimePaginator avoids this by converting to a millisecond timestamp. value_from_cursor here also returns the raw cursor integer, which build_queryset would compare against a datetime column even if the key function worked. The returned page therefore starts at row 0 while the next cursor is computed as if it started at a negative position, so consecutive pages can overlap. Before this change such cursors raised an error; now they return wrong pages silently. BasePaginator is shared by DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other endpoint using them, so this changes behavior well beyond the audit log endpoint.
