true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key with no dedupe

The whole-function lock was the only serialization in BuildIndex. GetIndex returns nil for concurrent first requests, so each one runs a full ListIterator build. For file-backed indexes (size above FileThreshold), two builds now call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time (line 98). Previously the second build ran after the first and failed cleanly on the existing path. Now the two can interleave on-disk creation and fail or leave a bad store. For memory indexes, the second build replaces the first in the cache, orphaning it, and the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double counted. Add a per-key guard (the TODO in search.go mentions this) or re-check the cache under the lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race in BuildIndex caused by narrowing the lock, allowing concurrent goroutines to build the same key without deduplication.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without the lock, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. This PR adds a new caller of TotalDocs in init (search.go line 216), which runs right after the watch goroutine has started. That goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex, then build, then BuildIndex, and write b.cache concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error that cannot be recovered. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu while the newly started watcher can concurrently trigger BuildIndex writes, causing a fatal concurrent map read/write.

false_positives.candidate:
Build errors in init's errgroup closures are shared-variable races and can be silently dropped

The errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` (declared at line 181) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` from up to `initWorkers` goroutines at once. The closure then does `return err`, which reads that shared variable, so a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build's nil. `init` then reports success while a namespace is missing from the index. `totalBatchesIndexed++` is also an unsynchronized write (lost updates, and the race detector flags it). This now runs inside NewResourceServer, which the code comments say must block startup on failure, so a swallowed error means a silently incomplete index. Use a closure-local error and an atomic counter.

Watch loop dereferences nil event when the events channel is closed, causing a panic

The loop does `v := <-events` and passes `v` to handleEvent without checking whether the channel is open. The SQL poller does `defer close(stream)` when the backend is stopped (b.done). After that, every receive yields nil, and handleEvent immediately reads `evt.Type` (line 226), which panics with a nil pointer dereference. The same pattern in server.go initWatcher (`v.Type` on a possibly nil v) panics too. The watch context is context.Background(), so this loop never exits on its own. Use `v, ok := <-events` and return when ok is false.

Writes made during the initial index build are never indexed

init lists and builds each namespace first, and only afterwards calls WatchWriteEvents. The SQL WatchWriteEvents takes its starting point from the latest resource versions at subscription time (listLatestRVs), so any write committed after a namespace was read but before the subscription is never delivered to the index. The object stays missing from search until it is modified again. This PR makes the build window longer, since the whole build for all namespaces now runs synchronously at construction. The rv returned by build (line 309 onward) is computed for exactly this purpose but discarded here. Subscribe first, build, then replay events with a resource version above each namespace's list version.

Construction now performs DB init, full index build and watcher start synchronously, and can fail

NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle Init (DB open and ping), the full search index build for every namespace above the threshold, and starts the watcher. Any error makes construction fail. Previously this work happened on first RPC, so construction was cheap and a failure only affected calls. The consequences: the caller (module wiring) blocks for the entire build with no timeout (only Stop cancels, and that is not reached during startup); one bad namespace or a transient DB error prevents the whole storage module from starting; and any code that constructs a server before its DB or blob dependencies are ready now fails at construction. The PR asks what this could break, but the diff shows no update to callers and no bounded context for the build. This needs an explicit decision.

Stop no longer gates RPCs, since the Init calls that returned the stop error were removed

Stop stores 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped' in s.initErr. Before this PR every RPC called s.Init, which returned that stored error, so calls after Stop failed fast. This PR removes every s.Init call from the handlers, so nothing reads initErr anymore. After Stop, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List and Search keep reaching the backend. backend.Stop only cancels the poller and does not close the DB. This silently removes the shutdown guard. If it is still needed, check a stopped flag in the handlers or in a shared helper.

Error path after the new Init call leaks started resources

If any step after the new Init call fails, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel. The lifecycle backend may already be initialized, and search init may already have started the event goroutine (search.go line 207), which loops on a context.Background() watch forever. Nothing calls Stop on the discarded server. Call s.cancel() and the lifecycle Stop on the error path.

Span context is still discarded in WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator

The PR is described as fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down, but this file still discards the span context in WriteEvent (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` followed by `b.create(ctx, event)`). ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) do the same. The WriteEvent span is therefore not the parent of the create, update or delete spans, and the DB spans attach to the request instead. Only GetResourceStats was fixed here. Use `ctx, span :=` in these functions.

Postgres skip disables the storage-server startup test without a tracked issue or mention in the description

A postgres branch is added that skips the only test in this file covering the storage-server startup path this PR changes. The skip has a TODO and no tracking issue, and the PR description does not mention disabling it. If construction-time init broke postgres startup, that regression is now hidden rather than fixed. Either fix the test or document the skip with an issue link in the description.

The PR changes several behaviours without adding tests: NewResourceServer now returns an error when lifecycle init or the index build fails, RPCs no longer gate on initialization, and the BuildIndex lock was removed. Nothing checks that a failing index build makes NewResourceServer return an error, which would have caught the lost-error race in search.go. Nothing exercises concurrent BuildIndex and TotalDocs under the race detector, which would catch the cache races above.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition

get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

Error-handling test asserts the failing batch is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring

The docstring says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages'. Offsets 100 and 101 both complete: the first raises, the worker logs it and completes the offset in its finally, and the second succeeds. The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. It passes only because the commit thread's first cycle fires about one second after creation while the test checks after roughly 0.2 seconds. On a slower run the commit happens and the test fails. The test should wait for the commit and assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102.

Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing

Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order

The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers

The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s

The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.

The key names (span-buf:s:{...}) are unchanged and segment keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after, old-version SET keys still exist. New code then hits WRONGTYPE on zadd, on zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin inside the Lua script, and on zscan in the flusher. redis-py pipelines raise on command errors, so process_spans fails for any batch touching a legacy key, and flush_segments can fail for every segment in the same batch. When a member (same payload) already exists in set_key and is also in the source key, for example a redelivered span, its score becomes the sum of two end timestamps (about 3.4e9) instead of end_timestamp_precise. zpopmin uses these scores to choose which spans to evict, so eviction order is corrupted. The same problem applies at line 53 for the parent key. Use AGGREGATE MAX or MIN so scores remain timestamps.

Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no metric or log, and it replaces an observable limit

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin silently deletes the lowest-scored (earliest-ending) entries. The buffer.py change also removes the old flush-time guard, which logged an error and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded. Segments that used to be dropped and logged are now silently truncated, and operators have no signal that spans are being discarded. Add a counter or log for the number of evicted spans.

Redirect chains deeper than 1000 now stop early, leaving set_span_id at an intermediate span, so later spans are attached to the wrong segment with no error or metric. Re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock in the non-dev case would complete the double-checked pattern that the RLock fast path starts.

If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. None of this is covered by a spec. This template has no next/previous controls, so for any group with more than 50 members the members beyond the first 50 cannot be seen. Before this change, non-automatic groups returned all members and automatic groups returned up to 200. This is a functional regression for larger groups. Either add pagination to this page or request the full list here.

members endpoint response changed from an array to an object, breaking existing clients

GET /groups/:name/members.json previously returned a bare JSON array. It now returns {members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}. This is a public endpoint, so any existing API client or script that iterates the top-level array will break. The default page size of 50 also silently truncates results for clients that previously received every member of a non-automatic group. Nothing in this PR versions the endpoint or documents the change.

The rewritten create action sets name and visible but never reads params[:alias_level]. The admin group form shows the alias_level combo-box for new groups too (it is not inside {{#if id}}), and asJSON sends alias_level. An admin who picks a value for a new group has it silently discarded and the group is saved with the default. The update action handles this with 'group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?', and create should do the same. No spec covers it.

Changed members endpoint contract has no test coverage in this PR

The members action's response shape, default limit, limit/offset handling and total count were all changed, and automatic groups now paginate like others. No spec change in this PR covers any of this (the groups controller spec is not touched). Tests should assert the {members, meta} shape, that total reflects the full membership, and that limit/offset select the right page for both automatic and non-automatic groups.

Offset clamp uses the stale user_count, leaving an empty page after removing the last member

findMembers clamps offset to the user_count from before the request. Take a group with 51 members on page 2 (offset 50) and remove the one member on that page. removeMember then calls findMembers, which clamps to the old user_count of 51 and keeps offset 50. The server returns an empty page with total 50, so the admin sees an empty page and a page counter past the last page. record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save reads the current value and writes back the incremented one. Two concurrent signups for the same blocked address can both read N and both write N+1, losing an increment. Use an atomic update (for example BlockedEmail.update_counters(record.id, match_count: 1) or a SQL increment) together with the last_match_at update.

The candidate narrows this to the non-atomic match_count increment, which is a concrete manifestation of the golden comment's concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored, so it matches addresses where the domain is only a substring

Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) matches the domain anywhere after an '@'. With a whitelist containing gmail.com, an address like x@gmail.com.attacker.net satisfies the check and passes, which defeats the whitelist. With a blacklist containing spamclub.com, a@spamclub.com.example.org is also rejected. This logic was moved here verbatim from User, but this PR rewrites it into a new validator and it is a security control, so the pattern should be anchored to the end of the address (for example matching '@domain' followed by end of string, case-insensitively).

The candidate gives the same root cause and fix direction as the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so changing the case of an address bypasses it

A blocked entry 'bad@spamclub.com' does not match 'Bad@spamclub.com', and the unique index on blocked_emails.email is also case-sensitive, so rows differing only by case can coexist and .first picks one arbitrarily. Anyone blocked can register again by changing the case of any letter. The codebase already has Email.downcase (used in users_controller#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), so both the stored value and the lookup should be normalized the same way.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? lets a blocked address bypass the blocklist by changing letter case. The extra details about normalization and the unique index do not change the core issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed the .title float rule from the header without replacement

The diff deletes the `.title { float: left; }` rule inside `.d-header`. Nothing in the PR restores positioning for the title element, and the PR does not mention the removal. float: right on the small-action button is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container

`.small-action` now gets `@include flexbox()` (added in this PR), and the `button` inside it still relies on `float: right`. Beyond adding flexbox, the PR changes `.small-action-desc` padding from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` to `0 1.5%`, drops `margin-top: 5px`, changes the `.custom-message p` margin from `5px 0` to `0`, and removes `padding-top: 4px` from `> p`. None of these follow from switching to flexbox, and the PR gives no reason for them. They change the visible spacing of every small-action notice and should be split out or justified.

`order` only affects flex or grid items. Nothing in this change makes the parent of `.extra-info-wrapper` a flex container, so `@include order(2)` on line 30 may have no effect. PR description is a placeholder and the performance claim is unsupported

The description reads only 'Test 5', and the title says the change optimizes header layout performance. The PR contains no measurement, benchmark, or before/after evidence. The diff also changes header, topic title, small-action notices, and badges, and gives no visual verification. website_name leaks the website domain and path for TL0 users that anonymous viewers should not see

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), so for a TL0 user seen by an anonymous viewer the raw website URL is omitted on purpose. The new `website_name` attribute is added to the public attribute list (line 43) but not to that untrusted list. `include_website_name` (lines 153-155) only checks `website.present?`, so for the same user the serializer now emits `website_name`, which contains the host and, with this PR, the full URL path (e.g. `example.com/user`). The untrusted-attributes spec (spec line 11) also omits `website_name`, and the TL0 fixture sets no website, so the existing test cannot catch this. Result: the anti-spam hiding of new users' websites for anonymous visitors is bypassed, and the domain and path are exposed in public user JSON and the profile header.

Same-parent-domain check matches unrelated sites that share a multi-label public suffix

The branch at lines 144-146 treats two hosts as the same site when they have the same label count and everything after the first label matches. Take an instance at `mysite.github.io` and a profile website `other.github.io/about`. Both hosts have 3 labels and `github.io == github.io`, so the full path is shown for an unrelated site (`other.github.io/about` instead of `other.github.io`). The same happens for `mysite.co.uk` vs `other.co.uk`. The intent was www./forum. siblings under one registrable domain, but the check does not account for public suffixes, so it shows paths for other sites on shared hosting domains.

Hostname comparison is case-sensitive, so the same-domain path rule can miss

`URI#host` returns the host as written and does not lowercase it. A website such as `http://Example.com/user` on an instance whose hostname is `example.com` fails `website_host == discourse_host` at line 141. It then falls through to the else branch, which returns plain `Example.com` with no path, even though the domain matches. Both sides should be normalized (e.g. with `downcase`) before comparing.

website_name is not refreshed after the user saves a new website, so the header can show the old domain

The template now renders `model.website_name` (user.hbs line 66), which is computed only on the server. Previously the controller derived the name from `model.website`, which updated reactively. `save()` only copies `bio_excerpt` from the response (line 210), so after a user changes their website in preferences, `website_name` on the shared model stays stale. The profile header keeps showing the old domain until the user record is refetched, which a sibling-route transition may not do.

Branches and edge cases of website_name are untested

The new specs only cover one website (`example.com/user`) against three hostnames. Not covered: the equal-label-count branch for `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` (serializer lines 144-146), a blank website where `website_name` should be nil, an unparseable website, and mixed-case hosts. The untrusted-attribute spec (line 11) also does not include `website_name`, so the TL0 anonymous visibility problem is not checked. Regressions in the branch logic or visibility rules would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring match, so look-alike origins are accepted

discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1 checks whether the sender origin is a substring of discourseUrl, not whether it equals it. If discourseUrl is 'https://forum.example.com/', a page at 'https://forum.example.co' passes the check and can send 'discourse-resize' messages. The impact is limited to setting the iframe height, but this is the only origin validation in the embed script and it is wrong. The comparison should parse discourseUrl and compare origins for equality.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same origin-validation bug: indexOf/substring matching can be bypassed by look-alike origins instead of requiring exact origin equality. The examples differ, but the underlying issue and fix are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ALLOWALL is not a valid X-Frame-Options value

The only valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM. Browsers ignore unrecognized values, so this line only appears to allow framing by accident, and it overwrites any app-wide frame policy with a meaningless string. To allow framing, the header should be removed (for example response.headers.delete('X-Frame-Options')), not set to an invalid value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments target the same code issue: setting X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL. The golden comment frames it as disabling clickjacking protection, while the candidate explains ALLOWALL is an invalid value that browsers ignore, undermining frame protection. Same underlying bug despite different emphasis.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Article URL interpolated unescaped into stored HTML footer

The URL is placed unescaped into an href attribute and a text node of the footer, which is then stored as raw HTML. The only check is that the URL starts with http(s):// (line 11). Characters such as single quote, equals and parentheses are legal in URL paths and can pass URI parsing, so a feed link like http://example.com/'onmouseover='alert(1) produces an anchor with an injected event handler. The URL should be HTML-escaped before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS issue: an unescaped URL is interpolated into stored HTML (href and text), allowing event-handler injection. It omits the separate nil-contents NoMethodError, but the core vulnerability matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
'<%- end if %>' is a syntax error; the best view cannot render

The block opened on line 2 is closed with 'end if', which is not valid ERB/Ruby for closing a conditional. It compiles to 'end if ;', where the modifier 'if' has no condition, so the template raises SyntaxError whenever it is rendered. Every request for an existing embedded topic (the @topic_view branch) fails. It should be '<%- end %>'.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the invalid `end if` ERB/Ruby closer and state it should be `end` to close the conditional.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One bad feed item aborts the whole poll; nil content is not guarded

The loop has no per-item rescue. If any item raises (for example i.content is nil, which is possible for entries with only a summary, so nil.scrub raises; or TopicEmbed.import raises on a PostCreator or permission error), the remaining items are never imported. The job is also scheduled with retry: false, so the failure is dropped until the next hourly run hits the same item again.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same core bug: i.content can be nil (e.g., summary-only entries), so calling scrub raises a nil error. The extra discussion about loop failure and retries is additional context, not a different issue.

false_positives.candidate:
CGI.unescapeHTML turns escaped feed markup into live HTML

RSS and Atom descriptions are almost always entity-escaped (a script tag appears as <script>). After CGI.unescapeHTML those entities become real markup. The result is saved with cook_method raw_html (topic_embed.rb:22) and rendered unescaped (see post.rb:133 and embed/best.html.erb:19), so any feed item can inject script into the forum for all visitors. Escaped content should stay escaped, or be sanitized, never unescaped.

Unauthenticated requests can trigger a full feed download and reimport each time

The throttle is keyed on the full embed_url (lines 26-28). Only the host must match embeddable_host, so a client can vary the path or query string to get a fresh key every time. Each new key then calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute here, which downloads the entire feed and re-imports every item (poll_feed.rb:29, 31-36). The feed fetch and the readability fetch (topic_embed.rb:48) use open() with no timeout. An attacker can therefore keep Sidekiq workers busy with unbounded outbound fetches and DB writes. The feed poll needs its own global throttle or should not run inline per URL.

A retrieve job is enqueued on every request; the throttle only runs inside the job

When no topic exists, every request enqueues a retrieve_topic job, and the 60-second throttle is checked only when the job runs (topic_retriever.rb:27-28). Anonymous requests, and the loading page that reloads every 30 seconds, therefore create unbounded queue entries even when the URL was retrieved moments ago. The throttle check should happen before enqueueing, or duplicate jobs should be deduplicated.

PostCreator enqueues jobs inside an open transaction

PostCreator.create is called inside the outer Topic.transaction (line 21). PostCreator.create calls enqueue_jobs before returning, which queues process_post and feature_topic_users. Its own comment (post_creator.rb around line 290) says jobs must be enqueued after commit. With Sidekiq, a worker can start before this transaction commits and find no post, so the job silently does nothing. The TopicEmbed row is also created after those jobs are queued.

Shipped migration now uses force: true, which drops an existing table

This changes an existing migration to create_table with force: true. If top_topics already exists with data in any environment where the migration version is not recorded (for example a database built from another branch), this migration drops the table and all its rows without warning. The flag is not needed for a table this migration is supposed to create for the first time and should be removed.

--category option removed with no replacement and no documentation

The method_option :category and its only use are deleted. Existing invocations that pass --category or -c now fail with an unknown-option error. The import also changes behaviour: the topic is now built by scraping the article with readability (TopicEmbed.import_remote) instead of a permalink post, and created_at is no longer set on the topic. The PR description is only 'Test 4', so none of this is documented.

Gate tests pass for the wrong reason; poll_feed itself is untested

feed_polling_enabled defaults to false (site_settings.yml). The 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples never enable feed_polling_enabled, so execute returns early at the first gate and the expectation holds regardless of the gate under test. Only the 'delegates' example enables all three, and it mocks poll_feed. The actual import loop, nil handling and failure behaviour have no coverage.

Protocol-relative URLs are rewritten to a wrong absolute URL

An href like //cdn.example.com/a.png starts with '/', so the sub(/^\/+/, '') strips both slashes and the result is prefix + '/cdn.example.com/a.png', i.e. http://host/cdn.example.com/a.png. The same problem exists for img src (line 71). Protocol-relative links should keep their host, or be resolved with URI.join against the article URL.

Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the posts table under lock

On PostgreSQL releases before 11, add_column with default: 1 and null: false rewrites the entire posts table while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a large forum this blocks all reads and writes to posts for the duration. The safer pattern is to add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then set the default and NOT NULL constraint.

setnx and expire are not atomic; a crash leaves the throttle key without a TTL

The key is set with setnx and then given a 60-second expiry in a separate command. If the process dies between the two, the key never expires and that embed URL is throttled permanently for non-staff users. A single atomic SET with NX and EX options would avoid this.

URL validation uses ^ instead of \A, so it matches any line

In Ruby, ^ matches at the start of any line. A value such as 'javascript:alert(1)' followed by a newline and 'http://x' passes this check. The later URI() call in absolutize_urls currently rejects it, so no harm follows, but the validation is ineffective and relies on an unrelated exception. The regex should be anchored with \A.

Test name says 404 but asserts only non-success; referer mismatch is untested

The example 'is 404 without an embed_url' does not set a host, so it fails on the host check and never exercises the missing-parameter path. It only asserts not-success, so it does not verify a 404. There is also no example for a referer whose host differs from embeddable_host, which is the main access check in ensure_embeddable.

Spec asserts raw HTML is stored and rendered verbatim

The assertion post.cooked.should == post.raw locks in the behaviour that imported content is stored as-is with no sanitization. Nothing tests escaping of the article URL in the footer, sanitization of feed or scraped HTML, the unchanged-content update path, or import_remote. The security-relevant paths of this feature are not covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

It now uses a constant 10 MB for every upload type, so admin-configured limits for attachments and images are ignored in the browser. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same problem: it replaced the max_image_size_kb setting with the constant. The 'type' argument is no longer used for the size check at all.

false_positives.candidate:
Request-controlled 'type' ends up unquoted in a shell command via the tempfile name

For API URL uploads, the tempfile is created at line 55 with the name prefix 'discourse-upload-#{type}', where 'type' is the unvalidated params.require(:type) value. The new code passes tempfile.path to OptimizedImage.downsize, and convert_with (optimized_image.rb, around line 161) joins the instructions and runs them through backticks with the path unquoted. A 'type' containing shell metacharacters such as $(...), backticks, or ';' therefore becomes executed shell code. This is reached when an API caller uploads an image by URL that is larger than max_image_size_kb. It needs an API key, but it is still command execution that did not exist before this PR. Validate 'type', and pass arguments to the external process as an argv array (system, Open3) instead of a shell string.

Oversized images are uploaded anyway when downsizing fails or stalls

The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times and ignores its return value. convert_with returns false (and swallows exceptions) on any failure, such as a missing binary, an unsupported format, or a corrupt file. After the loop there is no re-check of the size, so an image that is still above max_image_size_kb is passed to Upload.create_for as-is. The site's hard limit is therefore no longer enforced on the server. The input and output are also the same path, so a failed or partially written conversion overwrites the user's file with truncated data, and the next pass works on that damaged file. Check the result of each pass, stop on failure, and reject the upload if it is still over the limit.

URL download cap is now a fixed 10 MB, decoupled from max_image_size_kb

The download limit for API URL uploads changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to 10.megabytes. Two consequences. First, non-image files fetched by URL can now be up to 10 MB regardless of the admin's limit. Second, if an admin raises max_image_size_kb above 10 MB, images between 10 MB and the new limit are rejected at download time (the rescue nil turns the failure into a nil tempfile), which is the opposite of what the feature is meant to allow. Derive the download cap from the setting, or justify the constant.

Animated-GIF detection depends on the tempfile path, so animated GIFs get flattened

The animated branch in optimize is chosen by matching the GIF extension against 'from', which is the request tempfile path. Rack multipart tempfiles are typically created without the original extension, so the check fails for uploaded GIFs even when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. downsize_instructions then uses '#{from}[0]', which keeps only the first frame. The result is that an oversized animated GIF is silently reduced to a still image on upload. Determine animation from the original filename or from the file contents, and pass that decision explicitly.

New downsizing behavior and changed limits have no tests, and the PR description is a placeholder

The PR adds a server-side loop that rewrites uploaded files, changes the public OptimizedImage downsize/optimize API, and replaces the download and client size limits with constants. No specs were added or updated. The description is just 'Test 1'. Nothing covers an image above the limit being reduced below it, the loop giving up after five attempts, a failed convert, the GIF branch, or the duplicate downsize signature (which a spec calling the width/height form would have caught).

Synchronous API uploads run up to five full convert and optimize passes in the request

For synchronous API uploads, the request thread now performs up to five ImageMagick conversions, each followed by ImageOptim.optimize_image! (which runs several external optimizers), on an image up to the 10 MB download cap, before responding. Each pass rewrites the whole file. A single pass with a scale factor computed from the size ratio, or moving the reduction into the deferred job, would avoid this cost.

Unsubscribe writes notification_level directly, so auto-tracking can silently undo it

`tu.save!` changes notification_level without going through `TopicUser.change`. `TopicUser.change` also sets `notifications_reason_id` (user_changed) and `notifications_changed_at`, and publishes the change on MessageBus. Here the reason stays NULL for any topic whose level the user never explicitly set. `TopicUser.update_last_read` (the CASE expression in topic_user.rb) and `TopicUser.auto_track` both switch a topic to tracking when `notifications_reason_id IS NULL` and the user's viewing time passes the auto-track threshold. So after a user clicks the unsubscribe link and the topic is muted, the next read can flip it back to tracking, and the promise in the email to stop notifications is silently broken. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic.id, notification_level: ...)` instead.

The action mutates notification_level, but it is reachable via GET (config/routes.rb: `get 't/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe'` and `get 't/:topic_id/unsubscribe'`). Rails' forgery protection does not cover GET, so any page that embeds the URL (for example an img tag on another site) will mute a logged-in user's topic. Mail link scanners and prefetchers will also trigger the mutation without the user clicking. A state change like this should be a POST (with a GET confirmation page), or should use a signed token like the existing email/unsubscribe/:key flow.

`TopicUser.find_by` can return nil (for example if the row was never created or was removed), and `tu.notification_level` is then called without a guard, which raises NoMethodError and returns a 500. Using `TopicUser.change`, which creates the row when it is missing, would avoid this and also fix the persistence problem noted for the save! call.

The email copy says 'You will stop receiving notifications for <title>', but for users at tracking or watching the action sets notification_level to regular. Regular still sends notifications for replies and mentions, so those users keep getting notified. Only users already at regular are muted. Either mute for every level or change the wording.

`user_id = user.is_a?(User) ? user.id : topic` falls back to `topic`, which is the topic id, instead of `user`. TopicsController calls `TopicUser.track_visit! topic_id, user_id` with integer ids, so `user_id` becomes the topic id. The update then hits (or creates) the topic_users row for whichever user has the same id as the topic, and the real user's last_visited_at is never recorded. This predates the PR, but the PR edits this same method (line 125), so the fix belongs in this change.

The unsubscribe_link string now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}. html_part (line 67) and body (line 90) call I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args), and template_args only contains unsubscribe_url if the caller passed it. Any caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link: true without unsubscribe_url, including plugins that use this public builder, will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument while building the email. Either default the URL in the builder or render the topic line only when the URL is present.

The diff rewrites the summary routes and drops `post_number: /<digits>/` from their constraints (both `t/:slug/:topic_id/summary` and `t/:topic_id/summary`). The unsubscribe feature has nothing to do with summary URLs, and the change is not mentioned. Either revert it or explain why it is safe, since the constraint's effect on a route with no post_number segment is not obvious.

The route is declared as a top-level `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', ...)`. Ember derives the default template name from the route name (topicUnsubscribe, or topic-unsubscribe), not from the path topic/unsubscribe, so the new templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs is likely not the template used for this route. The page could render blank or fall back to the application template. Either rename the template to match the route or nest the route under the topic resource as this.route('unsubscribe'). I have not verified the resolver behavior in the running app.

Nothing covers the new action: the logged-out redirect, the 301 slug redirect that must happen before any state change, the notification_level transitions (tracking or watching to regular, regular to muted), or a missing TopicUser row. The message_builder_spec change only passes an extra argument and does not assert that the link appears in the body or HTML. A spec that re-reads the topic_user row after unsubscribe would have caught the auto-track persistence bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check

When a same-day date override exists and the slot lies inside it, execution reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function. Existing bookings and calendar busy times are therefore ignored for every slot inside a date override window. Personal events are treated as fixed-host events (isFixed is true when there is no schedulingType), so this affects ordinary personal bookings too: a host with an override 14:00-18:00 who already has a 15:00 booking is still offered 15:00 and can be double-booked. The override should only replace the working-hours check; busy times must still be evaluated.

Split working hours on one weekday reject every slot

`workingHours.find(...)` returns the first entry for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is outside that entry. Working hours come one entry per availability row, so a host with two ranges on the same weekday (for example 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) has every slot outside at least one of those entries. Every slot on that day then hits `return false` at line 150. This check now runs for every fixed host, including personal events, so users with split days get no slots at all. The intended test is 'reject only if no entry contains the slot'. The test suite only uses single-row schedules, so this is not caught.

Override end check ignores slots that start inside the override but run past it

The override boundary test compares `slotStartTime` with the override end instead of `slotEndTime`. A slot that starts inside an override and extends beyond its end (override ends 18:00, 60-minute slot at 17:30) fails all three checks and falls through to `return true` at line 133. The fixed host is then treated as available for time after the override ends. The earlier check at line 119 does use the slot end, so the two checks are inconsistent.

Multiple date overrides on one day make every slot on that day unavailable

`dateOverrides.find` returns the first override whose callback returns truthy, and the callback returns true when the slot lies outside that override. With two overrides on the same date (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00, which the availability UI supports as multiple ranges per date), a slot inside the first range is rejected because the second range reports it as outside, and the converse holds for the second range. Every slot on that day is therefore rejected. The correct semantics is 'available if inside at least one override on that day'. The flag `dateOverrideExist` is also mutated as a side effect inside the predicate, which relies on `find` short-circuiting and is fragile.

Same-day override check depends on the server process timezone

`dayjs(date.start)` is created in local mode, so `.add(...).format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's process timezone. `slotStartTime` is converted with `.utc()` and formats in UTC. On any server whose TZ is not UTC (developer machines, self-hosted deployments), the same-day comparison fails for overrides whose local date differs from the UTC date. The override is then not detected, and the slot falls through to the working-hours/busy logic, so date-override behaviour depends on where the process runs. The shifted value should be put in UTC mode before formatting.

Availability checks use eventType.length instead of the requested duration

`availabilityCheckProps.eventLength` is `eventType.length`, but slot generation at line 451 uses `input.duration || eventType.length`. For events with multiple duration options, the new working-hours and date-override checks compute the slot end from the wrong length, so a 60-minute booking is validated as a 30-minute one. This matters more now that these checks depend on the slot end.

Timezone conversions run inside the per-slot override loop

`dayjs.tz(...)` (which formats through Intl) is evaluated inside the `find` predicate for every override, for every slot, for every fixed host, although the offset depends only on the override. Over a long date range with many overrides this multiplies into a very large number of timezone conversions per getSchedule call. The override windows should be computed once per call.

Timezone-shifted override minutes drop the date and land on the wrong day across midnight

The converted override time is reduced to minute-of-day with `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding the timezone offset, which discards the date. When the shifted time crosses midnight, the slot is attributed to the wrong day. Example: an override 15:00-17:00 on Jan 10 for an organizer in America/New_York (stored as 15:00Z-17:00Z) and an invitee in Asia/Kolkata. The real slots are Jan 11 01:30-03:30 IST. The day filter at line 207 selects the override using the unshifted instant, which falls on Jan 10 IST, and line 219 yields 01:30. The slot is therefore offered (or later dropped by checkIfIsAvailable) on Jan 10, and the override never appears on Jan 11. The full converted timestamp should be computed and bucketed by its own date.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host override fix or for busy times on override days

The PR's headline fix (fixed-host date overrides constraining round-robin slots, and busy times on override days) has no test. The only added assertion is an invitee-timezone variant of an existing single-override scenario. Missing coverage: a round-robin event where a fixed host's override limits availability; an existing booking inside an override still blocking the slot (this would catch the busy-skip bug); split working hours on one weekday; two overrides on one date; and an override that shifts across midnight for an invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic is subtle and currently untested beyond the single happy path.

The server also blocks backup-only submissions for non-CAL users: in authorize, the ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled check (next-auth-options.ts line 113) fires whenever totpCode is empty. A CAL user who has backup codes and then signs in with Google using the same email goes through loginWithTotp, so they can never use their backup codes and have no recovery path besides their authenticator. Either expose backup codes in this flow and allow a backupCode to satisfy the non-CAL check, or document the limitation.

tabIndex=-1 removes keyboard access to the password visibility toggle in every PasswordField

This change is unrelated to backup codes but applies to the shared PasswordField component used across the app. Setting tabIndex to -1 makes the show/hide button unreachable by Tab, so keyboard-only users cannot reveal a password they are typing. This is an accessibility regression. Drop the change or justify it separately.

No tests exercise backup-code login, backup-code disable, or single-use consumption

The new server logic (backup-code branch in authorize, backup-code branch in disable.ts, code consumption, MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode errors) has no test coverage. The PR checklist says no tests were added, and the only addition is a TODO. The enable/disable e2e flow only checks the download, copy, and close buttons. A regression in backup-code verification or single-use enforcement would go unnoticed, and the password-bypass issue above would not be caught. Add tests for: login with a valid code (consumed afterwards), reuse of a consumed code, wrong code, and disable with a backup code.

Password visibility toggle does nothing because the caller's type="password" overrides PasswordField's type

PasswordField renders `<InputField type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"} ... {...props} />`, so props spread after the computed type. Passing `type="password"` here (replacing the former TextField) forces the input to stay masked. The eye button toggles its icon and label, but the field never shows the password. Remove the explicit type prop.

Assertion is vacuous: expect(promise).toBeTruthy() always passes

`isChecked()` returns a Promise, so `expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` checks that a Promise object is truthy and always succeeds. The FIXME above it acknowledges this. The PR edits this block but keeps the vacuous check, so the enable test does not verify the switch state. Use `await expect(page.locator(...)).toBeChecked()`.

missing_backup_codes text tells locked-out users to generate codes in settings, which is not possible

The message 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' is shown on the login page, where the user is not authenticated. There is no 'generate' action in settings: codes are created only by disabling and re-enabling 2FA, which itself needs a password and TOTP or a backup code. The message points users to a non-existent action.

Copy button reports success without awaiting the clipboard write

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast is shown immediately. If the write is rejected (permissions, insecure context), the user still sees 'Backup codes copied!' and the rejection is an unhandled promise rejection. Await the write inside try/catch and show an error toast on failure.

Submitting an empty backup code in lost-access mode fails silently

With an empty backupCode and empty totpCode, authorize() skips the backup branch and throws SecondFactorRequired. The client handler then calls setTwoFactorRequired(true), which is already true, so nothing changes and no error is shown. The HTML required attribute is disabled by noValidate, and the zod schema does not cover backupCode. Validate that backupCode is non-empty before submitting, or show an error when this case occurs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Office365 createEvent always uses the first destination calendar, so other hosts' invites fail

For COLLECTIVE events event.destinationCalendar now holds one calendar per host, but this code always takes the first entry (line 73) and never checks which credential is running. CalendarManager.createEvent forwards credential.id, and EventManager passes destination.externalId, but that externalId is only echoed back in the result and never reaches the service. For a team member's Office365 account the URL becomes /me/calendars/<organizer's calendar id>/events, which does not exist in that account, so the member never gets the event. The same pattern exists in Lark createEvent (calendarId taken from destinationCalendar[0], around lines 128-129 of the Lark service) and in CalDAV createEvent (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts filters calendars by the first destination's externalId; for a member's account nothing matches, no object is created, and the call still returns success). Only the Google service selects by credentialId, so the collective fix works for Google only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same defect: credentialId is not actually plumbed into non-Google createEvent implementations (Office365/Lark/CalDAV), so they ignore the per-host credential and use the first destination calendar, breaking collective events. The candidate describes the runtime consequence of the signature/contract mismatch the golden flags.

false_positives.candidate:
Google deleteEvent falls back to 'primary' instead of the event's calendar

When externalCalendarId is falsy, the expression searches destinationCalendar for an entry whose externalId equals that falsy value. It never matches, so calendarId becomes undefined and the code falls back to 'primary'. The previous code used event.destinationCalendar?.externalId here. On cancel, the delete goes to the user's primary calendar instead of the calendar holding the event. Google returns 404 and deleteEvent resolves silently, so the event stays on the real calendar with no error. This is reachable for references without externalCalendarId, including those the new EventManager code creates without it.

Google Meet description patch uses selectedCalendar, which can now be undefined

The insert uses 'selectedCalendar || "primary"', but the patch call below uses the raw selectedCalendar. When no destination matches the credential, the patch gets calendarId undefined. The patch is not awaited and has no error handling, so the hangout link description update silently fails for events inserted into primary. The same resolved calendarId should be used in both calls.

Google createEvent ignores destinations stored without a credentialId

The lookup matches destinations only by cal.credentialId === credentialId. Legacy DestinationCalendar rows with credentialId null never match, so the event goes to 'primary' instead of the configured externalId. The previous code used calEventRaw.destinationCalendar.externalId directly. EventManager's no-credentialId branch (createEvent(c, event) with no destination) makes this path reachable, so users with legacy destination rows get their bookings created in the wrong calendar.

Unguarded destructured element can throw when no destination calendar exists

mainHostDestinationCalendar comes from array destructuring, so its static type is DestinationCalendar, not DestinationCalendar | undefined. When evt.destinationCalendar is null or empty and the location is Google Meet, this line dereferences undefined and throws a TypeError inside create(). The previous code used evt.destinationCalendar?.integration, which was safe. Booking creation fails for these events. Use mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration.

externalCalendarId is dropped for destinations created without a destination id

createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent(c, event) without destination.externalId in the no-credentialId branch, the fallback branch, and for other_calendar integrations. CalendarManager.createEvent then returns externalId undefined, so result.externalId is undefined and the booking reference is saved without externalCalendarId. The previous code persisted evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId. Later update and delete calls then have no calendar id to work with (see the Google updateEvent and deleteEvent findings).

updateLocation writes calendar references with no credentialId or externalCalendarId

CalendarManager.updateEvent returns only appName, type, success, uid, updatedEvent, originalEvent, calError and calWarnings. It never returns externalId or credentialId, so result.externalId and result.credentialId are always undefined here. editLocation.handler persists these via references.create, so the new calendar reference rows lack credentialId and externalCalendarId. The previous code fell back to evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId and externalId. A later cancel then takes the legacy no-credentialId path in handleCancelBooking, which deletes using all calendar credentials of that type and no calendar id.

Webhook payload destinationCalendar changes shape and empty value is inconsistent

evt is spread into webhook payloads (sendPayload with ...evt), so destinationCalendar in BOOKING_CANCELLED and other webhooks changes from a DestinationCalendar object or null to an array. This is an undocumented breaking change for webhook consumers. Empty is now [] here but null in handleNewBooking (BOOKING_CREATED/REQUESTED), so consumers checking for null get different values per event type. The e2e expectation change from null to [] in webhook.e2e.ts (line 249) confirms the public payload changed.

Cancel loop repeats recurring and legacy deletions once per calendar reference

The former single if was turned into a loop over all calendar references, but the recurring branch does not depend on the reference. For a recurring series cancelled with allRemainingBookings, it deletes every updated booking's events across all user calendar credentials once per reference, so a collective series with N references issues N times the deletes and pushes duplicate entries into apiDeletes. The legacy no-credentialId branch likewise re-runs for each reference lacking credentialId. The loop should be restructured so the recurring deletion runs once.

Team members' calendars are silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null

evt.destinationCalendar is null when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar. Then evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...) is a no-op, so for a COLLECTIVE event the team members' destination calendars are never added. EventManager sees no destinations and falls back to a single calendar for the organizer, so the other hosts never get the event. Initialise the array before pushing, or build the combined list in one place.

Calendar update failures are no longer logged

The console.error(message) in the catch block was removed, but the message is still built with the error details. Failures in updateAllCalendarEvents now return error result objects without any log entry, so the cause of a failed calendar update is lost.

organization.slug removed from dynamic-group user select without explanation

The findMany for dynamic group users dropped 'organization: { select: { slug: true } }'. The PR description does not mention it. If any code later in handleNewBooking reads organization.slug for dynamic-group bookings, it now gets undefined. Confirm there are no remaining readers or restore the select.

loadUsers catch-all turns client errors into a generic 500

Any error that is not an HttpError or PrismaClientKnownRequestError, including the new plain Error for an empty dynamicUserList (which is a client input problem), is rethrown as HttpError 500 'Unable to load users'. The original message is discarded, and a request validation problem looks like a server fault. Prisma known errors are mapped to 400, which is also a questionable classification for database failures.

Multi-destination calendar creation has no tests

createAllCalendarEvents now loops over several destinations, fetches credentials from the DB for other hosts, and handles the no-credentialId path differently. updateAllCalendarEvents also loops over multiple references. The only test-file change is one e2e expectation. Several regressions listed above (missing externalCalendarId, dropped credentialId, wrong calendar selection) would be caught by unit tests that run EventManager with a two-destination collective event against mocked calendar services.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach in requestReschedule turns calendar failures into unhandled rejections

Previously a synchronous throw from getCalendar inside this forEach propagated and failed the mutation. Now getCalendar is async, so the error is returned from the discarded async callback and becomes an unhandled promise rejection while the mutation reports success. The calendar deleteEvent calls are also not awaited before sendRequestRescheduleEmail runs. Use for...of with await so errors are handled and deletions finish before the email is sent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core bug: an async operation inside forEach is not awaited, so failures become unhandled promise rejections instead of being caught. The candidate prompt explicitly flags the need to await and handle errors, matching the golden concern about wrapping the await in try-catch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective for calendar errors

Before this PR getCalendar was synchronous, so a throw from the CalendarService constructor inside this sync forEach callback reached the try/catch and was logged. Now getCalendar is async: the throw becomes a rejected promise returned by the async callback, which forEach discards. The catch never sees it and it surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection. The deletions are also not awaited, so the function returns true and sends the reschedule email while the old calendar event/meeting is still being deleted. Use for...of with await inside the try.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that async callbacks inside forEach are not awaited, so rejections bypass try/catch and cleanup/deletions race with subsequent logic. The candidate's calendar-specific example is the same underlying issue and recommends the same fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Object-literal import() calls still load every app eagerly, so nothing is lazy

Each `import("./...")` is a property initializer in the object literal, so every app module is requested as soon as this file is evaluated. Awaiting at the call sites only defers the wait; it does not avoid loading the apps. Deferred loading needs thunks (e.g. `googlecalendar: () => import("./googlecalendar")`) with callers invoking them. The PR description gives no goal, so it is unclear whether the intent was laziness. Also, a module whose import rejects produces an unhandled rejection at load time unless that key is awaited, rather than an error at the lookup site.

forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective for calendar errors

Same change as in the vital reschedule: getCalendar is now async, so errors thrown while creating the calendar service escape the try/catch on line 124-139 and become unhandled rejections. The deleteEvent/deleteMeeting calls are not awaited before the function returns true and sends the reschedule email. Use for...of with await inside the try so failures are logged and ordering is preserved.

Recurring-cancel calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

The outer `.forEach(async (credential) => ...)` does not return its promise, so the handler continues without waiting for it. The final `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` copies apiDeletes before these callbacks reach their `apiDeletes.push(...)` calls, so these per-occurrence calendar deletions are never awaited. Their results and errors are dropped and failures become unhandled rejections. The PR rewrote the sibling non-recurring loop in the else branch to for...of with await but left this one as forEach(async); it should be converted the same way.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the pending deletions

On the paid-cancellation path, `await apiDeletes;` does not wait for the promises inside the array. The handler returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' before calendar and video deletions settle, and their rejections are unhandled. This is pre-existing, but the PR touches these calls and the async change makes the difference observable. Use `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)` if the deletions are meant to complete before responding.

getCalendarCredentials still calls the now-async getCalendar without await

getCalendarCredentials stays synchronous and stores `getCalendar(credential)` directly, so each returned `calendar` field is a Promise<Calendar | null>, not a Calendar. Only getConnectedCalendars currently remembers to await `item.calendar`; any other consumer that uses the field as a Calendar will get undefined methods or a Promise where a value is expected. Make this function async and await the calendar, or document that the field is a Promise.

Async conversion changes error propagation in cancel and reschedule paths with no test updates

getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, deleteMeeting, deleteEvent and payment app lookup all changed from synchronous to async, and several callers moved from sync forEach to async callbacks. The PR adds no tests or test updates covering what happens when credential or app lookup or CalendarService construction throws during cancel, reschedule, or video deletion. Those error paths are exactly what changed, so they should have coverage.
